title: Robust and Scalable UAV-UGV Planning for Aerial Monitoring under Energy and Precedence Constraints
summary: We consider planning for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) teams in aerial monitoring missions with ordering requirements on the monitoring points to be visited by the UAV. The system consists of multiple UAV-UGV teams, each comprising one UAV and one UGV. UAV energy limitations are modeled through endurance, defined as the maximum flight time on a full battery. The UGVs serve as mobile charging stations and transport the UAVs between consecutive aerial tours. Given a set of monitoring points subject to ordering constraints and the teams' initial and terminal positions, the objective is to minimize mission completion time while satisfying UAV energy limits and the required visit order under bounded travel-time disturbances that may arise during execution. Unlike prior work, the plan jointly determines vehicle routes and their timing, allowing teams to slow down as needed to satisfy the ordering constraints. We develop a polynomial-time algorithm that generates efficient solutions to the underlying NP-hard planning problem. We establish feasibility guarantees, characterize the algorithm's computational complexity, and evaluate its performance via numerical comparisons.

Introduction Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are used in various domains such as agriculture and environmental monitoring (e.g., tokekar2016sensor, ren2019uavmonitoring ). However, their limited energy restricts missions defined over large areas or long time-horizons. Using unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) as mobile charging stations addresses this limitation by providing a flexible alternative to fixed recharging infrastructure. Recently, energy-constrained planning of UAV-UGV teams has gained significant attention (e.g., yu2018algorithms,ropero2019terra,ramasamy2021cooperative,chen2021delivery, er2026energy, er2026rspect, fowler2026prospect ). However, these methods generally assume that points of interest may be visited in any order. In practice, aerial monitoring missions may require some locations to be visited before others. In multi-robot task allocation, such ordering requirements are formalized as cross-schedule dependencies korsah2013comprehensive . Exact methods have addressed vehicle-routing problems with temporal synchronization bredstrom2007branch , while polynomial-time sequencers handle task allocation under temporal and spatial constraints gombolay2018fast ; however, these approaches generally do not model vehicle energy. Similarly, bischoff2020multi schedules cooperative tasks using greedy construction and local search, but focuses on task scheduling rather than energy-constrained spatial planning. More recently, sojo2024optimal computes optimal precedence-constrained plans for heterogeneous UAV teams under energy limits, though its computational complexity grows significantly with team size and recharging relies on static infrastructure. In this paper, we propose a heuristic algorithm for robust UAV-UGV planning in aerial monitoring missions with precedence constraints. The goal is to minimize the overall mission completion time while respecting the energy constraints and the required visit order under bounded travel-time disturbances. We formulate this planning problem as a mixed-integer program, which is NP-hard. Our main contribution is an efficient heuristic (Alg. alg:precept ) that jointly determines vehicle routes and their timing, with formal guarantees on feasibility and worst-case time complexity (Theorem thm:main ). We validate our approach via numerical comparisons against branch-and-cut, simulated annealing, and a heuristic baseline that assigns all locations that are weakly connected by precedence constraints to the same team. Problem Formulation sec:problem_formulation We consider an aerial monitoring mission executed by multiple UAV-UGV teams. The energy-constrained UAVs must visit a set of monitoring points, supported by the UGVs which serve as mobile charging stations and transport the UAVs between take-off and landing locations. Two features distinguish this formulation from prior work (e.g., er2026rspect, fowler2026prospect ). First, precedence requirements constrain the order in which the monitoring points may be visited. Second, the plan selects not only where the vehicles go but how long each leg takes, allowing a team to slow down if needed rather than reroute to satisfy these ordering constraints. title: Spa-Bench: A Real-Robot Benchmark for Spatial Grounding in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising route toward general-purpose robotics by transferring semantic knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into language-conditioned control. However, most VLA evaluations emphasize aggregate manipulation success under changes in objects, instructions, or environments, leaving unclear how reliably these policies ground spatial descriptions in the physical scenes where they act. We therefore ask a sharper question: how reliably can current VLAs translate spatial descriptions into appropriate real-robot behavior? To investigate this, we introduce Spa-Bench, a real-robot benchmark that evaluates spatial grounding across six tabletop tasks covering Object State, Relative Size, Referential Description, Relational Placement, Ordinal Position, and Counting. Our primary evaluation compares in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) spatial configurations while retaining training support for the relevant objects, concepts, and actions, reducing object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure. Four diagnostic conditions further probe physical execution, sensitivity to wording, object-task associations, and recognition that no action is required. We release 4,092 episodes collected on the SO-101 robot arm: 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 real-robot evaluation rollouts from five state-of-the-art VLA policies. Across the three fully evaluated policies, success falls from 67.5-73.3% on ID spatial configurations to 40.7-52.0% on OOD spatial configurations, while matched direct instructions improve success by 28.3-40.0 percentage points. These results show that the evaluated VLAs can often execute the required manipulations but lack robust spatial grounding. Project materials, including videos, code, and benchmark data, are available at https://justintiensmith.github.io/Spa-Bench/.

Project materials, including videos, code, and benchmark data, are available at . vision-language-action models, robot learning, spatial grounding, robot evaluation, VLA benchmarking Introduction Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot learning. By connecting pretrained vision-language representations to robot actions, these models can transfer semantic knowledge acquired from internet-scale data into language-conditioned control brohan2023rt2,black2025pi05,nvidia2025gr00t,fang2026molmoact2 . This transfer promises robots that can respond to new objects, instructions, and environments without requiring a separately trained policy for every behavior. Policies evaluated on existing benchmarks have demonstrated increasingly broad manipulation capabilities, including generalization across objects, instructions, visual conditions, and task sequences zhang2024vlabench,zhou2025liberopro,gao2026stargen . Nevertheless, completing a manipulation task does not by itself establish that a policy has correctly interpreted the spatial structure of its environment. Spatial understanding in existing benchmarks is typically embedded within an overall task-success metric and is consequently entangled with object recognition, language interpretation, and motor execution. If a policy fails to place a green pen to the left of a red block, for example, the failure could arise from incorrect spatial grounding, failure to identify the objects, an unsuccessful grasp, or an inability to execute the required placement due to an inadequate number of demonstrations spanning the full workspace. Furthermore, benchmarks that introduce a fixed scene to mitigate some of these issues introduce a different problem: Success may result from memorizing recurring object locations or action patterns rather than from grounding the instructed spatial relation. In this work, we use spatial grounding to describe the ability to map language about properties, positions, quantities, and relations in the current physical scene to an appropriate target, goal configuration, or decision not to act. We study this capability through the following question: How reliably can current VLAs ground spatial descriptions into appropriate actions in the real world? Answering this question requires more than measuring success on an ordinary held-out task. A test task that simultaneously introduces an unfamiliar object, instruction, spatial concept, or physical behavior cannot reveal which of these changes caused a failure. A diagnostic spatial benchmark should instead establish familiarity with the constituent objects, concepts, and manipulation behaviors before evaluating whether the policy can use the relevant spatial information in a different physical configuration. We introduce the Spatial Grounding Benchmark (Spa-Bench), a controlled real-robot benchmark designed around this principle. Spa-Bench comprises six tabletop tasks evaluating the grounding of Object State, Relative Size, Relational Placement, Referential Description, Ordinal Position, and Counting. All tasks use the same robot embodiment, workspace, receptacle, and broad pick-and-place action family. The principal source of variation is therefore the scene-grounded rule that determines which object should be manipulated, where it should be placed, or whether movement is even required. Spa-Bench evaluates policies in ID and OOD spatial configurations. ID configurations measure whether a policy has acquired the spatially grounded behaviors represented in its demonstrations. OOD configurations change the association between a spatial concept and its task argument while preserving training support for the relevant objects, physical actions, and spatial concepts. We implement this controlled split through a withheld-cell design: each component of an OOD evaluation configuration appears elsewhere in training, but their particular combination is reserved for evaluation (see Fig.~ fig:withheld_cell_construction ). The purpose of this construction is to reduce object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure. To characterize spatially grounded performance beyond the primary ID--OOD comparison, Spa-Bench includes four additional diagnostic conditions that probe complementary aspects of policy behavior. Direct-manipulation controls remove the need for spatial inference while preserving the requested robot motion. Prompt-paraphrase trials restate both OOD spatial and direct-manipulation instructions on the same scenes, testing whether their performance gap depends on exact wording. Cross-task-object rollouts vary the usual association between an object and task. Finally, no-intervention scenes test whether a policy can recognize when no action is required. Spa-Bench contains 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations, with 200 demonstrations for each task. We evaluate five fine-tuned state-of-the-art policies that are drawn from four different VLA architectures: VLA-0, MolmoAct2, , GR00T-N1.7 Frozen LLM (GR00T-N1.7 F-LLM), and GR00T-N1.7 Full Fine-Tune (GR00T-N1.7 F-FT). Three policies complete the full 900-rollout evaluation protocol, producing 2,700 evaluation episodes, while two partial baselines contribute 192 episodes. In total, we release 4,092 SO-101 episodes, including the demonstrations, rollout videos, task specifications, and documented scene layouts. Across the three fully evaluated policies, ID spatial-configuration success ranges from 67.5 to 73.3 , but success decreases to 40.7 --52.0 in OOD spatial configurations. On the OOD spatial configuration matched scene subset, direct-manipulation instructions achieve 81.7 --89.2 success, showing that many of the physical behaviors are executable even when the policy fails under a spatially grounded instruction. Performance is strongly task dependent: all three policies fail every OOD Counting trial, almost always without acting; other tasks are dominated by target-selection or spatial-outcome errors. The direct manipulation advantage also persists when both instruction types are paraphrased, revealing that the state-of-the-art VLAs we evaluate do not exhibit robust spatial grounding. In summary, our core contributions are: We introduce Spa-Bench, a six-task real-robot benchmark for evaluating spatial grounding across ID and OOD physical configurations. We develop a controlled evaluation protocol that combines a withheld-cell split with four diagnostics that probe physical execution, wording sensitivity, object context, and action gating. We evaluate five fine-tuned VLA policies and release 4,092 SO-101 episodes, including 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 evaluation rollouts, together with task specifications and scene layouts. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-language-action models (VLAs) connect pretrained multimodal representations to robot actions with the goal of transferring semantic and visual knowledge into closed-loop control. RT-2 helped establish this formulation by representing actions as tokens and co-fine-tuning a vision-language model on web and robot data, demonstrating transfer to novel objects, instructions, and semantically specified behaviors brohan2023rt2 . OpenVLA subsequently introduced an open-source 7-billion-parameter VLA trained on large-scale robot data and designed for adaptation to downstream embodiments kim2024openvla . In parallel, coupled a pretrained vision-language backbone to a flow-matching action expert for generating continuous action chunks across multiple embodiments black2025pi0 . More recent VLAs have targeted open-world generalization, heterogeneous robot data, embodied reasoning, and practical deployment. extends through heterogeneous co-training on robot trajectories, verbal instructions, semantic predictions, and web data black2025pi05 . The GR00T-N1.7 family uses a dual-system architecture in which a vision-language module interprets the scene and instruction while a diffusion transformer produces continuous actions nvidia2025gr00t . VLA-0 investigates whether continuous actions can instead be generated directly as numerical text without introducing a specialized action vocabulary or action head goyal2025vla0 . MolmoAct2 connects an embodied-reasoning vision-language model to a flow-matching continuous-action expert fang2026molmoact2 . Because these models differ in pretraining data, training objectives, action representations, and fine-tuning procedures, Spa-Bench compares complete policy systems rather than isolating individual architectural choices. Each fine-tuned policy is evaluated under the same controlled spatial configurations and diagnostic conditions to characterize its spatial generalization. Simulation and Reasoning Benchmarks Simulation benchmarks have enabled scalable evaluation of language-conditioned robot behavior. RLBench provides a broad collection of vision-guided manipulation tasks and automatically generated demonstrations james2019rlbench , while ALFRED evaluates grounded instruction following over compositional household activities shridhar2019alfred . LIBERO studies declarative and procedural knowledge transfer across lifelong-learning task suites liu2023libero . RoboCasa expands language-conditioned manipulation to diverse household activities in simulated kitchens nasiriany2024robocasa , and BEHAVIOR-1K targets long-horizon everyday activities involving physical and semantic state changes li2024behavior1k . VLABench further evaluates semantic knowledge, spatial relationships, physical understanding, and long-horizon reasoning across numerous tasks and objects zhang2024vlabench . VIMA-Bench more explicitly separates forms of generalization, including a combinatorial split that evaluates unseen object--texture pairings whose individual components appear during training jiang2023vima . These benchmarks establish task breadth and scalable evaluation, but spatial grounding is generally one component of overall task success and therefore remains entangled with perception, planning, and execution. title: REMM: Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation
summary: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to retain task-relevant history while revising conclusions no longer supported by physical evidence. Retaining observations alone does not specify which completed conditions should be withdrawn after a disturbance or which obligations require repair. We introduce REMM, Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor. REMM separates an append-only evidence history from revisable task state and explicitly links derived relations and completed conditions to their supporting facts. When accepted evidence changes a supporting fact, it withdraws dependent conclusions and schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries without updating the executor. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall. Complementary video diagnostics show improved grounding of retained history into the next instruction, including comparisons with $π_{0.5}$-compatible high-level planner adaptations. These results support revisable memory as a practical interface for continued manipulation without policy retraining. Project: https://revanthsenthil.github.io/remm/.

Introduction sec:intro Long-horizon manipulation requires more than executing a sequence of independent skills. Each action changes the world in which subsequent decisions are made, and information needed later may no longer be directly observable: which object was handled first, what remains inside a container, or where an object was placed before becoming occluded. Such tasks therefore require decisions that depend on interaction history under partial observability~ robomme,memoryvla . Yet retaining history alone is insufficient. A previously valid relation may cease to hold after a slip, human intervention, or environmental rearrangement. A robot must therefore preserve what happened while revising what is currently supported by the available evidence. Generalist robot policies have substantially improved the execution of individual manipulation skills~ rt2,octo,openvla,pi05,g05 . Recent models further extend language-conditioned control to long-horizon settings; in particular, G0.5 provides an autoregressive interface that interleaves reasoning and action generation within a single policy~ g05 . However, a capable executor does not by itself determine what should happen next when the relevant evidence is old, hidden, or contradicted by a subsequent physical intervention. Recent work equips manipulation systems with temporal context through learned memory banks, sparse visual events, or retrieved keyframes ~ memoryvla,eventvla,memer . Hierarchical systems instead place memory and reasoning above the motor policy: HiMe ~ hime maintains editable multimodal memory, while HyMeS ~ hymes and BATON baton steer reusable or frozen skills using external verification and transition-aware memory. These methods establish that memory can extend a policy beyond its immediate observation. They also sharpen a different question: after evidence changes, which earlier conclusions should change with it? Closed-loop planners can incorporate success, scene, or human feedback into subsequent decisions~ innermonologue ; structured world representations encode relational scene state~ conceptgraphs ; and dynamic memories can add, delete, or modify stored relations as new evidence arrives~ robomemory . Yet these capabilities do not explicitly track which physical relations support previously completed task conditions. If such a relation changes without revising its downstream consequences, the controller can retain an internally coherent but physically stale task state. We therefore consider an intervention-grounded process memory in which physical relations, derived scene state, and completed task conditions are connected through explicit support dependencies. When verified evidence changes an upstream relation, its affected consequences can be selectively withdrawn. These dependencies are supplied by task and physical semantics rather than learned through causal discovery; their use as recorded justifications is related to truth maintenance~ doyle1979 , while remaining distinct from causal world models that learn or probabilistically infer manipulation outcomes~ causalworld,cobrapmm . We introduce , Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory layer around a frozen G0.5 executor. preserves an append-only evidence history while maintaining a separate projection of currently supported state. It records causal dependency links from physical relations to derived and completed task conditions; when verified evidence supersedes a parent relation, invalidates affected descendants, identifies the broken task obligation, and schedules a bounded recovery instruction at the next verified stationary skill boundary. This produces an inspectable path from physical intervention to memory revision and changed control without -specific parameter training. We evaluate on real-robot tasks involving transport disruptions, delayed sequence recall, and hidden-object rearrangement. The evaluation separates retention from revision: sequence and hidden-object tasks test whether decision-relevant history persists through delay and occlusion, while transport interventions test whether previously valid task state is correctly withdrawn and repaired after the world changes. Beyond end-to-end task success, we measure change acceptance, dependency revision, recovery timing and destination, physical repair, and the observed memory-to-control trace. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57 to 91 in intervention recovery and from 43 to 70 in sequence recall, while completing all four of its hidden-object trials.\\ Our contributions are threefold: a formulation of revisable embodied memory that separates recorded execution history from currently supported task state and represents intervention-sensitive dependencies from physical relations to derived and completed task conditions; , a supervisory system that propagates dependency invalidation and dispatches nominal or recovery instructions to a frozen G0.5 policy without -specific parameter training; and a controlled real-robot evaluation that traces observed changes through memory revision to subsequent control decisions across transport, sequence-recall, and hidden-object manipulation tasks. Related Work sec:related Memory for Vision--Language--Action Control Policy-integrated approaches make history part of action generation. MemoryVLA retrieves perceptual and cognitive tokens from a learned memory bank~ memoryvla ; EventVLA learns when to preserve sparse visual evidence~ eventvla ; and Chameleon and ChainVLA propagate compact event or execution state across action queries~ chameleon,chainvla . These methods learn representations for retention and retrieval inside the policy. RoboMME shows that their benefit depends strongly on whether a task requires temporal, spatial, object, or procedural memory~ robomme . uses a different boundary: it leaves G0.5 frozen, does not learn a memory-conditioned action model, and studies explicit revision of task state between bounded skills. Hierarchical approaches place memory above the executor. MemER trains a high-level visual policy to select keyframes and predict subtasks for a separately trained ~ memer . HiMe divides control among an Executor, a working-memory Sentry, and a Planner that retrieves and edits multimodal memory~ hime . HyMeS uses executable memory-management heuristics and multimodal completion checks to steer a Markovian VLA~ hymes , while BATON uses a frozen VLA with subtask exploration and transition-aware memory~ baton . These systems are the closest architectural context for . Our question is narrower than general memory management: whether storing explicit parents for derived and completed task conditions allows a verified intervention to revise exactly the downstream obligations that no longer hold. Closed-Loop State Revision and Recovery Robotic planners have long used feedback to reconsider high-level action. Inner Monologue conditions an LLM planner on success detection, scene description, and human feedback~ innermonologue ; schedules emerging tasks using priorities, dependencies, interruption, and resumption~ zhou2026mathcalp3versatileembodiedagents ; and PhyAgentOS couples persistent session state with verification and replanning~ phyagentos . These works establish closed-loop supervisory control, but their task scheduling or model-mediated replanning does not by itself expose which physical fact sustained a completed condition. connects these levels explicitly and preserves the active atomic skill while inserting, deferring, or retargeting a recovery at a skill boundary. Structured memories provide the complementary world-state representation. ReMEmbR indexes spatially and temporally grounded experience for navigation~ remembr ; ConceptGraphs builds open-vocabulary object--relation graphs for planning~ conceptgraphs ; and RoboMemory revises relevant neighborhoods of temporal, spatial, semantic, and episodic memory~ robomemory . does not claim the first relational memory or editable knowledge graph. It adds an append-only evidence ledger, an active projection, and typed links from physical relations to derived scene and task conditions. Those links draw on two related traditions. Truth-maintenance systems retain justifications and withdraw conclusions when their support becomes inactive~ doyle1979 . title: Visual-Wi-Fi Navigation to Signal-Emitting Devices
summary: Indoor navigation to task-relevant targets remains difficult when the target is small, occluded, or visually indistinct. Meanwhile, smart appliances, mobile devices, and IoT tags emit Wi-Fi signals during everyday communication, providing a pervasive but underused spatial cue. We study visual-Wi-Fi navigation, where a robot reaches a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment using onboard visual observations and Wi-Fi packets overheard from the device, without connecting to the device or modifying infrastructure. Realizing this requires pose-dependent Wi-Fi observations during closed-loop policy learning and reliable spatial cues from bearing measurements corrupted by indoor multipath propagation on a moving robot. We present WiFiSpaces, which extends the Habitat embodied simulator with online ray-traced Wi-Fi sensing, rendering Wi-Fi observations for a robot-mounted antenna array at continuous poses during policy rollouts. On top of it, we build ViFiNav, a localization-aware navigation framework: an online source-localization algorithm exploits robot motion to disambiguate and robustly aggregate bearings from multiple viewpoints into a confidence-aware source estimate, and a learned policy fuses this evolving estimate with depth observations and learns to act on it as it is refined. Experiments show that exploiting robot motion is key to accurate source estimates, and that fine-tuning on ray-traced Wi-Fi observations in WiFiSpaces improves the success rate of ViFiNav. The policy transfers zero-shot to unseen scene datasets, and we deploy it on a real robot with a Wi-Fi sensor built from a commodity router, without any real-world training.

Introduction sec:intro Navigation in unmapped environments often involves locating and reaching task-relevant targets, including everyday connected devices such as smart appliances and mobile devices. While visual navigation has made substantial progress~ wijmans2022ver,kim2023topological,khanna2024habitat , it remains difficult when the target is small, occluded, visually indistinct, or has no direct visual manifestation~ young2025enhancing . A vision-only agent then lacks an explicit spatial cue and must rely on weak semantic priors or broad exploration, producing inefficient trajectories. Meanwhile, the growing prevalence of connected devices creates a new sensing opportunity: many indoor targets already emit wireless signals as part of their normal communication, which can be overheard by a robot-mounted receiver to provide complementary spatial cues. As shown in Fig.~ fig:task , we study visual--Wi-Fi navigation: in an unmapped environment, an embodied agent uses onboard visual observations and Wi-Fi packets overheard from the target's existing traffic to navigate to the physical location of a signal-emitting target device. The target is defined by the Wi-Fi source location and need not be visible. Unlike audio cues, which require the target to actively and continuously emit informative sound and are susceptible to environmental noise~ chen2020soundspaces,chen2022soundspaces,shi2025towards , wireless signals are emitted by ordinary devices as a by-product of communication and propagate through and around obstacles~ hunter2023wiros,mundra2024wisensehub , providing spatial cues beyond visual line of sight. Among wireless technologies, we focus on Wi-Fi because it is the most pervasive: ultra-wideband (UWB) and Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) localization typically require dedicated anchors or tags to be deployed and calibrated~ grosswindhager2017uwb,zhao2021uloc,zhang2025bridge , whereas most household and personal devices, including IoT tags, already communicate over Wi-Fi (Fig.~ fig:task ), and their packets can be overheard by a commodity Wi-Fi router without connecting to the device or its network~ gringoli2019free,hunter2023wiros . Wi-Fi is a deployment choice, not a requirement: the same setting arises for any wireless modality that carries spatial cues beyond line of sight. However, autonomous navigation with Wi-Fi signals raises two key challenges. The first challenge is to obtain pose-dependent Wi-Fi observations at scale for learning-based embodied navigation: during rollouts they must track the agent's continuous pose, including heading, while reflecting the source location and the 3D geometry that shapes propagation, reflection, and blockage. Precomputed radio maps do not fit: they tabulate the signal on a discrete grid and would have to be rebuilt every episode as the source moves, over poses that are policy-dependent and unknown in advance. To address this, we propose , to our knowledge the first embodied navigation simulator to provide online Wi-Fi observations at the agent's current pose, by extending Habitat with a Wi-Fi sensor built on physics-based ray tracing~ sionna ; synchronizing agent state with the wireless scene at every step and reusing scene geometry across episodes makes online ray tracing practical for closed-loop policy learning. The second challenge is to turn noisy Wi-Fi measurements into reliable spatial cues on a moving robot. Each overheard packet yields channel state information (CSI) at the router, from which a bearing to the source can be estimated~ kotaru2015spotfi,hunter2023wiros , but indoor multipath makes single-vantage bearings heavy-tailed: in , about of raw bearings are off by more than (Fig.~ fig:loc_analysis_a ), consistent with real deployments~ kotaru2015spotfi,xie2019md,eleftherakis2024spring+ , and acting on such an estimate commits the robot to the wrong part of the scene. To address this, we present , a localization-aware visual--Wi-Fi navigation framework: an online Wi-Fi source localization algorithm resolves the directional ambiguity of the small antenna array using the robot's natural motion and robustly aggregates multi-view bearings into a confidence-aware source estimate, and, rather than heuristically following each intermediate estimate, a learned multimodal policy fuses this evolving cue with visual observations and learns to act on it in closed loop. In summary, our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt,topsep=1pt,parsep=0pt] A complete system for visual--Wi-Fi navigation, which we formulate as reaching a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment from visual observations, odometry, and Wi-Fi packets overheard from its existing traffic, without modifying the target device or infrastructure. , an embodied navigation simulator that provides online ray-traced Wi-Fi observations synchronized with continuous agent poses during policy rollouts. An online Wi-Fi source localization algorithm coupled with a reinforcement-learned policy that learns to act on its evolving estimates. Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment: fine-tuning in improves the success rate of over the same policy without Wi-Fi fine-tuning, and the policy generalizes zero-shot across indoor scene datasets; the same policy is further deployed on a real robot with a commodity-router Wi-Fi sensor~ gringoli2019free,hunter2023wiros , without any real-world training. Related Work Embodied navigation with vision and sound. Visual navigation has been widely studied, including PointGoal savva2019habitat,wijmansdd,ye2021auxiliary,wijmans2022ver , ObjectGoal chaplot2020object,khanna2024habitat,ko2025context , ImageGoal kim2023topological , and vision-language navigation long2025instructnav , but relies on target visibility or learned semantic priors and degrades to weakly guided exploration when the target is small, occluded, or has no visual manifestation. Audio-visual navigation~ chen2020soundspaces,chen2022soundspaces,shi2025towards adds sound cues, but requires the target to actively and continuously emit informative sound. Wi-Fi signals, in contrast, are emitted by ordinary devices as a by-product of their normal traffic and provide spatial cues beyond visibility. Wireless localization and navigation. Indoor localization with Wi-Fi biswas2010wifi,xiong2013arraytrack,kotaru2015spotfi,xie2019md,ayyalasomayajula2020deep,jiokeng2020ftm,eleftherakis2024spring+ , UWB grosswindhager2017uwb,zhao2021uloc , and BLE zhang2025bridge is well studied; Wi-Fi is attractive for its commodity availability, but existing systems rely on site-specific data biswas2010wifi,ayyalasomayajula2020deep or calibrated anchors xiong2013arraytrack,kotaru2015spotfi,xie2019md,jiokeng2020ftm,eleftherakis2024spring+ , limiting map-free use. Robot motion has been exploited to synthesize larger apertures for angle-of-arrival (AoA) estimation jadhav2022wireless , but with active coordination with the Wi-Fi infrastructure hunter2023wiros,mundra2024wisensehub and for localization or tracking rather than closed-loop navigation. Classical radio source seeking~ twigg2012rss,charrow2014cooperative couples an RF estimate with a model-based controller, but does not fuse it with visual observations in a learned policy or formulate the problem as an embodied navigation task with standardized episodes and metrics. Prior navigation works using indoor mmWave cellular links~ yin2022millimeter,yin2024zero,li2025digital need dedicated base stations and suffer severe wall attenuation, require hard-to-obtain link-state labels, and train on precomputed radio maps rather than pose-dependent observations during closed-loop execution. Wireless-aware simulation platforms. As summarized in Table~ tab:simulator_comparison , embodied simulators~ savva2019habitat,shen2021igibson,kolve2017ai2,IsaacSim provide navigation tasks, visual observations, and policy-learning interfaces but do not model radio propagation, whereas wireless simulators~ sionna,WirelessInSite,chen2026rfdt model propagation with high fidelity but are not embodied environments. Recently, SimART~ yan2026simart couples a robotics simulator with Sionna ray tracing for outdoor 6G sensing but does not target indoor navigation, and concurrent work~ lu2026rfcues trains an RF-guided navigation policy with Habitat and Sionna but evaluates it only in simulation. instead embeds Wi-Fi sensing in the step loop of an embodied simulator: CSI for a robot-mounted antenna array is rendered at every agent pose in indoor scenes and exposed as an observation synchronized with visual observations and actions, so policies can be trained and evaluated closed-loop. Task Definition sec:task We consider visual--Wi-Fi navigation: an agent must reach a stationary Wi-Fi-emitting device at an unknown location in an unmapped indoor scene, using only onboard observations. Unlike PointGoal and ObjectGoal navigation, neither a goal vector nor a visual description of the target is available: the target is identified only by its MAC address, and its location must be inferred from Wi-Fi measurements overheard from it, while visual observations provide the scene context needed to reach it. At each step , the agent receives , where is an egocentric visual observation (RGB-D) and is Wi-Fi CSI, a complex-valued channel response across antennas and orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) subcarriers (Sec.~ sec:sim ), and its onboard odometry pose in an episode-local frame, and acts with the standard Habitat action space (move forward, turn left, turn right, stop). An episode is specified by a scene, an initial agent pose, and a target location; the target location is used by the simulator to generate Wi-Fi observations and by the evaluator to measure success, but is never exposed to the agent. An episode succeeds if the agent executes stop within a success distance of the source within the maximum episode length of 500 steps. title: StereoEngine: Scaling Stereo Bimanual Robot Data without Stereo Cameras
summary: Stereo vision is increasingly used for robotic manipulation, with a growing body of work incorporating it into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, the scarcity of large-scale, real-world stereo datasets remains a fundamental bottleneck for scaling such policies. Recent generative monocular-to-stereo methods target settings such as VR content and autonomous driving. No prior work produces realistic synthetic stereo data for robotic manipulation, where stereo supervision has come predominantly from simulation. We propose StereoEngine, which introduces two complementary methods to synthesize stereo data for robotic manipulation. In the first, we warp a monocular (left) video into the right view using estimated depth and inpaint the disoccluded regions with a video diffusion model, lifting monocular demonstrations into stereo pairs without training on real stereo. In the second, we render a stereo pair in simulation and jointly generate both photorealistic views, producing consistent left-right data without any real video as input. StereoEngine outperforms existing baselines in generated stereo quality, and using its synthetic data for policy mid-training or task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves downstream bimanual manipulation. Project website: https://stereoengine.github.io

Introduction 1pt 2pt Imitation learning from teleoperated demonstrations has enabled increasingly capable bimanual manipulation systems~ aloha2_2024,intelligence2025pi05,intelligence2026pi07steerablegeneralistrobotic . Recent stereo-conditioned policies extend this by taking stereo observations as input and exploiting binocular views to improve spatial reasoning, including challenging cases such as transparent objects~ han2026stereopolicyimprovingroboticmanipulation,deng2026stereovlaenhancingvisionlanguageactionmodels . However, scaling these stereo-conditioned policies to the point where they can be used for large-scale general imitation learning remains difficult, as large-scale robot datasets are overwhelmingly monocular and single-arm~ open_x_embodiment_rt_x_2023,fang2026molmoact2actionreasoningmodels,wu2026robocoinopensourcedbimanualrobotic . The few datasets captured with stereo cameras, such as DROID~ khazatsky2024droid , are single-arm which means no large-scale bimanual stereo dataset exists. Collecting stereo demonstrations at comparable scale would require expensive stereo rigs and costly re-teleoperation. This motivates scalable methods to synthesize stereo data without additional real-world collection~ mandlekar2023mimicgen,xue2025demogen,yu2025real2render2realscalingrobotdata,chen2026craft . While monocular-to-stereo synthesis has emerged as a promising direction~ zhao2024stereocrafter,dai2025svg,lu2026grt , existing works target domains outside of robotic manipulation, such as VR/AR content~ 2024spatialdreamer,yu2025mono2stereobenchmarkempiricalstudy,qiao2025genstereo,xing2025stereoworldgeometryawaremonoculartostereovideo . Reconstruction-based novel-view synthesis (e.g., NeRF~ mildenhall2020nerf , 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl3Dgaussians ) requires multi-view datasets and per-scene optimization on static scenes, unlike our dynamic single-view setting. Methods that train on stereo pairs draw on simulation data that suffers from domain gaps or on only a small number of real pairs~ huang2025restereodiffusionstereovideo . To our knowledge, no prior work synthesizes realistic stereo data directly from real robot video data. To address the data bottleneck, we present , a scalable framework for synthesizing photorealistic stereo data for bimanual manipulation using video diffusion. provides two independent methods. When a real monocular demonstration exists, we convert it into a stereo pair by warping the left view and inpaint the disoccluded regions which are the surfaces that become visible in the right view but were never observed in the left. This preserves the appearance of the real data, though every generated pair remains tied to an existing demonstration. When no real video exists, we instead generate both views from a simulated trajectory, which allows data generation for entirely new tasks and configurations. Together, the two methods lift the abundant monocular data that already exists and generate new data where none exists, without ever training on real stereo correspondences. We evaluate across 480 real-world rollouts spanning five bimanual manipulation tasks. See Figure~ fig:teaser for a visualization of the diverse synthetic stereo pairs produced by . Using ExStereo~ liu2027exstereo and StereoVLA~ deng2026stereovlaenhancingvisionlanguageactionmodels as our downstream policies, mid-training~ liu2027exstereo them on data---an intermediate stage between a policy's large-scale pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning---or fine-tuning them on it directly, consistently improves manipulation performance and generalization over baselines. The contributions of are: -L, a monocular-to-stereo pipeline whose inpainter is trained without any real stereo pairs, using warp-derived masks, partial arm masks, and disparity dropout. -S, which jointly generates both left and right views from simulation, needing no real video. A large-scale bimanual robot stereo dataset released from both methods. Real-world experiments showing that data improve stereo-conditioned policies through both large-scale mid-training ( -L) and task-specific fine-tuning ( -S). Related Work Stereo Vision in Computer Vision sec:related_stereo Stereo vision offers an efficient way of recovering 3D structure from image pairs where depth is obtained by estimating the disparity between a rectified left--right pair. This means obtaining 3D information from ordinary RGB cameras without active depth sensors. Recent stereo matching has shifted toward general-purpose foundation models with strong zero-shot generalization, largely by leveraging priors from monocular depth foundation models to generalize across unseen domains and remain reliable on transparent, reflective, and textureless surfaces~ wen2025stereo,Bartolomei_2025_CVPR,guo2024stereo . These advances make stereo an accurate and deployable source of 3D geometry well suited to robotics. In this work, we leverage these benefits for robot manipulation by generating large-scale stereo data so that stereo-conditioned policies can scale for training. Monocular-to-Stereo Generation Monocular-to-stereo generation synthesizes a right-eye view from a monocular left video, originally for immersive 3D content~ xie2016deep3dfullyautomatic2dto3d . Most methods require stereo pairs for training, either from large-scale stereo datasets that are expensive to obtain or from synthetic renders with a large domain gap from real video~ zhao2024stereocrafter,yu2025mono2stereobenchmarkempiricalstudy,qiao2025genstereo,xing2025stereoworldgeometryawaremonoculartostereovideo ; training-free~ wang2024stereodiffusion,dai2025svg,shi2026dissolvestereocoarsedepthinjection and recent self-supervised~ lu2026grt variants relax this requirement. However, all of these only convert an existing left video and cannot produce stereo pairs where none exists. As summarized in Table~ tab:comparison , addresses both limitations: it needs no stereo pairs, operates on real robot data, and jointly generates both photorealistic views without any real footage. Stereo Vision in Robotics Stereo perception offers a practical route to 3D geometry in manipulation, recovering structure on materials where active depth sensors fail, such as transparent, specular, and textureless surfaces. Stereo can also yield cleaner geometry than active depth sensors, as we show later in Section~ ssec:warping . Prior work adapts stereo depth estimation to these challenging conditions~ wei2024droma,bai2024cleardepth and uses stereo depth for downstream grasping and tracking~ yu2025pogs . More recently, stereo has been integrated into imitation and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies. ActiveGlasses~ zou2026activeglasseslearningmanipulationactive reconstructs a point cloud from the stereo pair through a stereo matcher and feeds that to the policy, while StereoPolicy~ han2026stereopolicyimprovingroboticmanipulation and StereoVLA~ deng2026stereovlaenhancingvisionlanguageactionmodels consume the stereo images directly. All of these methods can benefit from large-scale stereo demonstrations, yet none address how such data can be obtained at scale. Stereo demonstrations can be teleoperated on a stereo rig, but this requires stereo hardware on every platform and teleoperation for every new task. instead generates the stereo data needed to train these policies without additional real-world collection. Video Generation in Robotics Video generation models have recently been used to scale robot data, either as world models that generate demonstrations for policy learning~ jang2025dreamgen,gao2026dreamdojo,ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot,nvidia2025cosmosworldfoundationmodel,ye2026robodream or as data engines that augment existing demonstrations while keeping the robot trajectory fixed~ yu2023scaling,robosplat,liu2025DCODA,chen2026ropa . A related group of methods conditions video diffusion on simulation to synthesize new configurations or diverse demonstrations~ mandlekar2023mimicgen,yu2025real2render2realscalingrobotdata . Closest to our setting is CRAFT~ chen2026craft , which generates a video from Canny edges~ canny1986edge of a simulated bimanual episode together with a real reference image. However, all of these generate only monocular video, and is the first to extend video generation for robot data to stereo pair synthesis. title: Verifier-Mediated Multi-LLM Coordination for Multi-Robot Path Planning
summary: Foundation models are increasingly used for high-level multi-robot task planning, yet independently generated symbolic plans can become jointly infeasible after geometric grounding because of shared spatial and temporal constraints. We study execution-aware coordination of large-language-model (LLM) planners for multi-robot navigation. We compare a centralized architecture, in which one LLM jointly reasons over the robot team, with a decentralized multi-LLM architecture in which each robot independently proposes a task plan. A geometric verifier grounds the candidate plans into robot trajectories, detects predicted inter-robot conflicts, and converts conflict information into structured feedback for targeted replanning. This verifier-mediated architecture separates semantic task reasoning from execution-level feasibility while enabling iterative coordination among LLM planners. Experiments in CARLA and on Crazyflie aerial robots evaluate coordination performance as task complexity increases and characterize the trade-offs between centralized reasoning, decentralized verifier-mediated coordination, and physical executability.
full_text: Verifier-Mediated Multi-LLM Coordination for Multi-Robot Path Planning Vivek Khatana , Zijian Song , Naira Hovakimyan , Petros Voulgaris \\ \ vkhatana, zijians4, nhovakim\ @illinois.edu \\ \ vkhatana, pvoulgaris\ @unr.edu \\ Department of Mechanical Science and Engineering, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA \\ Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Nevada, Reno, NV, USA Foundation models are increasingly used for high-level multi-robot task planning, yet independently generated symbolic plans can become jointly infeasible after geometric grounding because of shared spatial and temporal constraints. We study execution-aware coordination of large-language-model (LLM) planners for multi-robot navigation. We compare a centralized architecture, in which one LLM jointly reasons over the robot team, with a decentralized multi-LLM architecture in which each robot independently proposes a task plan. A geometric verifier grounds the candidate plans into robot trajectories, detects predicted inter-robot conflicts, and converts conflict information into structured feedback for targeted replanning. This verifier-mediated architecture separates semantic task reasoning from execution-level feasibility while enabling iterative coordination among LLM planners. Experiments in CARLA and on Crazyflie aerial robots evaluate coordination performance as task complexity increases and characterize the trade-offs between centralized reasoning, decentralized verifier-mediated coordination, and physical executability. Introduction Foundation models provide a flexible interface for semantic reasoning, task decomposition, and high-level planning in robotic systems. In multi-robot settings, however, a plan that is individually meaningful for each robot may still be jointly infeasible after geometric grounding. Independently generated routes can intersect in space and time, violate shared workspace constraints, or create execution conflicts that are not apparent at the symbolic planning level. These failures motivate an execution-aware coordination mechanism between foundation-model reasoning and physical robot motion. A key architectural question is whether multi-robot foundation-model planning should be centralized or decentralized. A centralized planner can reason over the complete team state and generate coordinated plans jointly, but its context and decision space grow with team and task complexity. In contrast, decentralized planners provide modularity and local reasoning, but they require an explicit coordination mechanism to resolve conflicts between independently generated plans. Recent multi-robot LLM frameworks coordinate robot teams through centralized or decentralized symbolic reasoning and inter-agent communication~ chen2024centralized,huang2025compositional . However, such symbolic coordination does not by itself ensure that the resulting plans remain physically feasible after geometric grounding. This work studies verifier-mediated multi-LLM coordination. Each robot-level LLM proposes a symbolic task plan, which is grounded into an executable trajectory by a geometric planning layer. A shared execution-level verifier evaluates the grounded trajectories for obstacle and inter-robot conflicts. When a conflict is predicted, the verifier converts the failure into structured feedback---including the affected agents, conflict location, and conflict time---and returns this information to the appropriate LLM planner for targeted replanning. This creates a closed coordination loop between foundation-model reasoning and robot execution without requiring unrestricted natural-language negotiation. The framework is illustrated in Fig.~ fig:architecture . The main contributions of this work are: We formulate centralized and decentralized LLM-based architectures for multi-robot task planning under shared execution constraints. We introduce a verifier-mediated coordination mechanism that converts predicted geometric conflicts into structured feedback for targeted multi-LLM replanning. We empirically study coordination and task completion performance across increasingly complex multi-robot tasks in CARLA~ Dosovitskiy17 and demonstrate transfer of the planning--verification--execution framework to Crazyflie~ bitcraze_crazyflie20 aerial robots. Relation to prior work. Recent work has explored centralized and decentralized LLM-based multi-robot symbolic reasoning and coordination~ chen2024centralized,huang2025compositional,li2026survey , as well as feedback and constraint-guided refinement of LLM-enabled robotic behavior~ madaan2023selfrefine,huang2022innermonologue,ravichandran2026safety . Our focus is different: we use an external execution-level verifier to evaluate grounded multi-robot trajectories, detect physical conflicts, and return structured agent-specific geometric feedback for targeted multi-LLM replanning. Verifier-Mediated Multi-Robot Planning sec:LLM_mediation Multi-Robot Task and Path Representation We represent the robot environment by a graph , where nodes denote admissible symbolic states and edges denote valid transitions. Robot is assigned a task containing its start , goal , required targets , and task-specific constraints . The LLM generates a symbolic plan where denotes the planner context, including prior execution-level feedback when available. Each symbolic plan is grounded and passed to a local geometric planner, where maps symbolic states to geometric anchors in the robot's state space and is a local geometric planner used to connect grounded waypoints, such as an A -based planner~ carlagrp . The resulting route is subsequently associated with the robot execution trajectory . Centralized and Decentralized LLM Architectures In the centralized architecture, a single LLM receives the joint team task and generates all robot plans simultaneously, This exposes the planner to the global coordination problem but increases the size of the joint planning context. In the decentralized architecture, robot has its own LLM planner as in . The planners need not directly negotiate in unrestricted natural language. Instead, their candidate trajectories are coupled through a shared execution-level verifier. Execution-Level Conflict Verification and Feedback For every robot pair , the verifier evaluates the trajectories and requires where is a prescribed separation threshold. The verifier can additionally check robot-obstacle constraints using the same grounded trajectories. If condition~ is violated, the verifier identifies a predicted and constructs a structured feedback object where and denote the predicted conflict time and location, is the minimum predicted separation between robots and , and the superscript denotes the planning iteration . Replanning is targeted to the affected agent while feasible plans from other agents may be retained. The process terminates when all candidate trajectories satisfy the execution-level constraints. Multi-Robot Evaluation CARLA Experiments We first evaluate the proposed centralized and decentralized multi-LLM planning architectures in CARLA~ Dosovitskiy17 using a structured road-network graph (shown in Fig.~ fig:multi_target_complexity ). We evaluate two environment representations: raw coordinate descriptions and a neighbor-list representation. In the raw-coordinate representation, the environment is provided to the LLM through the serialized geometric positions of the graph nodes. In the neighbor-list representation, each node is instead described by its adjacent nodes, , thereby explicitly encoding the admissible graph connectivity. We consider a two-agent multi-target navigation problem. Each agent begins at an assigned start node, visits all designated target points in any order, and returns to its start node. The agents share the road network and must avoid inter-agent conflicts during execution. To evaluate increasing task complexity, we consider target sets of size nodes. A trial is declared successful only if both agents visit all assigned target points and remain collision-free. Our experiments use an inter-agent separation threshold of m; a trial is declared unsuccessful if the distance between the agents falls below this threshold at any time. We compare centralized and decentralized planning under the same task conditions. In the centralized architecture, a single LLM jointly generates plans for both agents. In the decentralized architecture, each robot is assigned an independent LLM planner that reasons over its own task and tentative trajectory. Coordination is achieved through iterative verifier-mediated replanning as described in Section~ sec:LLM_mediation . At the end of each planning iteration, the agents exchange their tentative paths, which are evaluated by a prediction-based collision checker using a time-indexed distance criterion (cf.~ ). If an inter-agent conflict is detected, the predicted conflict location and time index are communicated to the corresponding LLM, which replans its trajectory while the other agent retains its current plan (cf.~ ). This process is repeated until no predicted inter-agent conflict is detected. Performance is evaluated using three primary metrics: (i) expected success time, defined as the average planning time over successful trials; (ii) expected successful path length, defined as the average path length over successful trials; and (iii) expected planning time, defined as the average planning time over all trials. For decentralized planning, the reported planning time is averaged across the two LLM planners. Fig.~ fig:comparison highlights the trade-off between centralized and decentralized LLM coordination as task complexity increases. For smaller target sets, centralized planning incurs lower planning overhead, whereas the performance gap narrows for larger target sets as decentralized planning benefits from its modular structure. The results also show that the environment representation matters: neighbor-list inputs consistently produce graph-valid routes with path lengths comparable to centralized planning, while raw-coordinate inputs provide greater geometric flexibility but are more susceptible to invalid waypoint generation. Insights from CARLA Experiments The CARLA experiments reveal several system-level trade-offs in foundation-model-based multi-robot planning. First, centralized planning is computationally efficient for the two-agent tasks considered here because a single LLM reasons jointly over the complete multi-agent state and can account for inter-agent interactions during plan generation. In contrast, decentralized planning introduces additional communication and replanning overhead through verifier-mediated coordination. As task complexity increases, however, the performance gap between the two architectures becomes smaller, suggesting that the additional coordination overhead of decentralized planning is partially offset by its modular planning structure. Second, the environment representation provided to the LLM has a significant effect on planning reliability. The neighbor-list representation consistently produces graph-valid feasible routes with similar path lengths across the two planning architectures, whereas coordinate-based descriptions occasionally produce shorter trajectories but are more susceptible to invalid or out-of-map waypoints. This illustrates a trade-off between geometric flexibility and symbolic validity. Finally, collision-free task completion became more difficult as the number of target points increased, consistent with longer trajectories, larger waypoint-ordering spaces, and more frequent inter-agent conflicts. These factors also increase the difficulty of resolving conflicts through iterative replanning, highlighting the importance of explicit execution-level feasibility checking. title: Structure-Aware Matching for Robust UAV Thermal-to-Satellite Geo-Localization
summary: UAV thermal-to-satellite geo-localization localizes UAVs by matching real-time thermal images against georeferenced satellite images, enabling autonomous navigation in GNSS-denied and low-visibility conditions. However, substantial cross-modal disparities in color, brightness and viewpoint hinder conventional appearance-based methods from establishing reliable correspondences. While existing approaches predominantly address global modality shifts, they overlook the invariant scene structures inherently shared between thermal and satellite views. To bridge this gap, we propose SAMF, a Structure-Aware Matching Framework that explicitly exploits stable cross-modal structural cues to improve UAV thermal geolocalization. Specifically, the Directional Structure Enhancement Module (DSEM) strengthens robust structural representations by capturing directional and low-frequency spatial patterns, and the Modality-Aware Affine Remapping Module (MARM) subsequently applies affine correction to these enhanced features, further promoting cross-modal alignment. Additionally, we introduce the Thermal-UAV-Paired benchmark derived from the Thermal-UAV dataset. Extensive experiments on both the Boson-nighttime and Thermal-UAV-Paired datasets show that SAMF achieves state-of-the-art performance. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness and synergistic complementarity of DSEM and MARM. The code and dataset are released at: https://github.com/YuxinWang879/SAMF.git.

Specifically, the Directional Structure Enhancement Module (DSEM) strengthens robust structural representations by capturing directional and low-frequency spatial patterns, and the Modality-Aware Affine Remapping Module (MARM) subsequently applies affine correction to these enhanced features, further promoting cross-modal alignment. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness and synergistic complementarity of DSEM and MARM. The code and dataset are released at: . UAV geo-localization, thermal imagery, cross-modal image matching, structure-aware matching. Introduction eliable geo-localization is essential for autonomous UAV flight and mission execution. However, in extreme environments involving complex electromagnetic confrontation or geographic occlusion, Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals may be blocked, interfered with or spoofed, making it difficult for UAVs to continuously obtain reliable position information ref1,ref2 . To reduce dependence on GNSS, cross-view geo-localization determines the UAV’s location by matching images captured in real time by the UAV with geo-tagged satellite images ref3 . In recent years, UAV-to-satellite cross-view geo-localization has received increasing attention. Existing studies mainly focus on daytime visible-light scenarios and improve the matching capability between UAV images and satellite images through feature representation, local information modeling or cross-view alignment ref6,ref7,ref8,ref9 . However, when UAVs operate at night or under low-light conditions, visible-light images often fail to preserve sufficient scene details. In contrast, thermal images are less affected by illumination variations and can continuously capture ground scenes. Therefore, cross-view matching between UAV thermal images and satellite images has emerged as a pivotal problem for UAV autonomous localization in low-visibility conditions ref4 . Due to significant differences in color, brightness, and texture between thermal and satellite images ref4 , even if they correspond to the same geographic location, their appearance may differ greatly. The above differences, combined with variations in viewpoint, scale, and direction, make it highly challenging to establish reliable matching relationships between two types of images. Current methods for UAV thermal-to-satellite geo-localization can be broadly categorized into two groups according to how they address the modality discrepancy between thermal and satellite images. The first category focuses on reducing the modality distribution gap between thermal and satellite images, mainly through domain-adversarial training ref10 , conditional-GAN-based image synthesis ref11 , and sparse generative models ref12 . For example, Xiao et al. ref4 integrated these techniques into a thermal geo-localization framework and achieved competitive geo-localization performance on the Boson-nighttime dataset. The second category bypasses feature distribution alignment and instead directly models the geometric transformation between thermal images and satellite images through deep homography estimation. STHN ref13 estimates a fine-grained homography matrix based on coarse retrieval results to achieve pixel-level geometric alignment, while UASTHN ref14 further introduces an uncertainty-aware mechanism to automatically identify and discard unreliable matches in geometric estimation. While existing approaches have advanced the task through distribution alignment and geometric estimation, the intrinsic structural cues shared between satellite and thermal imagery have not been fully exploited. In reality, these cues are pivotal for robust cross-modal matching. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:boson_examples , despite significant discrepancies in radiometry, local texture, and brightness, thermal and satellite images preserve consistent large-scale scene structures. Specifically, attributes such as surface orientation, region boundaries, terrain trends, and global spatial layouts exhibit strong structural coherence across modalities. Unlike appearance features that are highly sensitive to sensor characteristics, these structural cues reflect the spatial organization of ground scenes and thus demonstrate superior cross-modal stability ref15,ref16 . Therefore, rather than attempting to directly bridge the global modality gap, leveraging these stable structural cues provides a more effective mechanism to mitigate appearance inconsistencies. To this end, we propose a Structure-Aware Matching Framework (SAMF) that explicitly models and leverages these stable structural cues to enhance the accuracy and reliability of UAV thermal geo-localization. Specifically, SAMF incorporates a Directional Structure Enhancement Module (DSEM) to reinforce robust structural representations by exploiting directional and low-frequency spatial information. Complementing this, a Modality-Aware Affine Remapping Module (MARM) is introduced to perform modality-specific affine corrections on the structure-enhanced features, further mitigating residual cross-modal discrepancies. We validate SAMF on the Boson-nighttime dataset and the newly constructed Thermal-UAV-Paired dataset. The Boson-nighttime dataset was originally established by Xiao et al. ref4 . To rigorously evaluate our proposed method, we introduce the Thermal-UAV-Paired dataset, which is derived from the Thermal-UAV dataset ref17 by establishing precise one-to-one correspondences between thermal UAV images and satellite imagery. Experimental results demonstrate that SAMF achieves state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks. Furthermore, ablation studies verify the effectiveness and complementarity of the DSEM and MARM modules, confirming that exploiting stable cross-modal structures significantly bolsters geo-localization performance. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We propose a Structure-Aware Matching Framework tailored for UAV thermal-to-satellite geo-localization. SAMF explicitly leverages stable cross-modal structural cues to substantially improve localization accuracy and reliability under low-visibility conditions. We introduce a Directional Structure Enhancement Module to extract and reinforce invariant spatial structures across modalities. By capturing surface texture orientations, weak boundary trends, and coarse-grained layouts, DSEM ensures robust performance even in weak-texture and low-semantic environments. We design a Modality-Aware Affine Remapping Module to perform lightweight modality alignment on the structure-enhanced features. MARM effectively mitigates cross-modal feature discrepancies while preserving spatial structures, forming a complementary processing pipeline with DSEM. We construct and release the Thermal-UAV-Paired benchmark based on the Thermal-UAV dataset. Comprehensive evaluations on both the Boson-nighttime and Thermal-UAV-Paired datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our proposed framework. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:related work reviews related studies on cross-view UAV geo-localization, cross-modal feature alignment, and spatial structural feature learning. Section~ sec:methodology introduces the overall framework of SAMF and its main modules. Section~ sec:experiments presents the experimental settings, comparison results, and ablation analysis. Finally, Section~ sec:conclusions concludes this paper. RELATED WORK sec:related work This section provides an overview of related works covering cross-view UAV geo-localization, cross-modal feature alignment, and spatial structure feature learning. Cross-View UAV Geo-Localization Cross-view geo-localization usually estimates the location of a query image by matching it against a large-scale geo-tagged reference database. Early studies established the task framework for ground-to-satellite and UAV-to-satellite matching, and improved the correspondence between different views through feature representation, feature aggregation, and metric learning ref3,ref5,ref6,ref7 . Subsequent studies have improved UAV--satellite matching through different mechanisms, including pose estimation with satellite imagery ref18 , UAV--satellite view synthesis ref19 , local-pattern modeling ref20 , feature segmentation and regional alignment ref21 , and cross-view consistent attention ref22 . Research on reference-image representation, geography-aware sampling, and benchmark construction has also improved the robustness of localization systems to viewpoint and scene variations ref23,ref24,ref25 . These methods have advanced UAV--satellite cross-view geo-localization, but most of them are developed for daytime visible-light images. Their matching processes still rely substantially on color, texture, and local appearance cues, whose stability decreases under insufficient illumination and nighttime imaging conditions. Thermal infrared sensing can capture ground scenes with limited dependence on ambient illumination and therefore provides an alternative observation modality for UAV geo-localization in low-visibility conditions ref4 . Existing thermal-to-satellite geo-localization studies mainly reduce the difficulty of cross-modal matching from two perspectives. The first line, represented by Xiao et al. ref4 , reduces the overall distribution discrepancy between thermal and satellite images by combining domain-adversarial training ref10 , conditional GAN-based image-to-image translation ref11 , and sparse GAN-based thermal image generation ref12 , together with data augmentation. The other group estimates the geometric transformation between the two views after coarse retrieval and performs fine-grained localization through homography modeling and local matching ref13,ref14 . Other studies have used multimodal data augmentation to improve robustness to complex imaging conditions, or combined zero-shot retrieval with local feature matching to extend the applicability of thermal geo-localization ref15,ref26 . These studies have advanced the task from the perspectives of distribution alignment, geometric estimation, and generalization capability. However, they generally treat cross-modal differences as an overall distribution shift or a geometric transformation, failing to exploit the invariant structural cues shared across thermal and satellite modalities. This limitation restricts model performance in weak-texture and low-semantic scenes, where appearance information is scarce and stable structural cues are indispensable. Cross-Modal Feature Alignment Reducing feature distribution discrepancies between heterogeneous modalities is a common strategy in cross-modal matching. title: Gamma: Grounded Multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit for Memory-Intensive Manipulation
summary: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies fail on memory tasks, behaviour that depends on events observed long before the current frame, because their training data is overwhelmingly Markov and mapping episodic memory directly to action chunks is hard. Yet the same policy, finetuned once to follow a privileged oracle's grounded-subgoal text, nearly solves these tasks: the difficulty lies entirely in mapping memory to a grounded symbolic subgoal. Existing work entrusts this stage to a single VLM that selects keyframes and reasons over raw frames, and falls far short of the oracle: key identities and dynamics are buried in noisy pixels, the reasoning spans hundreds of frames in an unbounded context, and hallucination corrupts the memory itself. We instead present GAMMA (Grounded multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit), which builds the stage as a collaborating two-agent memory system: a detector tool (SAM-3) for spatial grounding, a VLM writer that distils each replan window into one grounded text line, an append-only text memory bank, and a VLM reasoner that reads the bank and emits the next grounded subgoal at the oracle's cadence, wrapped in a propose-verify harness that admits, defers, corrects, or rejects every agent claim against mechanical visual evidence, at training-corpus construction and at deployment alike. On a sixteen-task memory-manipulation suite GAMMA recovers a large fraction of the oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed, reaching the ceiling on several tasks, and transfers with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark.
