On a sixteen-task memory-manipulation suite recovers a large fraction of the oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed, reaching the ceiling on several tasks, and transfers with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark. Introduction sec:intro Vision--language--action (VLA) policies pretrained on large manipulation corpora~ pi05,openvla,rt2 now solve a wide range of tabletop tasks from a single language instruction. Their training data, however, is overwhelmingly Markov: the correct action chunk is a function of the current observation and the instruction. Robot tasks in homes and factories are frequently not of this kind. An agent that watched a demonstration must reproduce it after the visual evidence is gone; an agent that saw a container shuffle must remember which container now hides which object; an agent asked to press a button after the fourth pass of a moving object must count. On a recent memory-manipulation benchmark~ robomme instantiating sixteen such tasks, the policy~ pi05 , finetuned end-to-end, succeeds on only a small fraction of episodes (Table~ tab:motivation ). Two observations make this failure a well-posed problem. First, finetuning the policy on the benchmark under the standard instruction leaves success low even when a memory module injects past frames into it ( end-to-end, for the best memory-VLA architecture; Table~ tab:motivation ): the mapping from a long episodic history to an action chunk lies far from the distribution the policy was pretrained on. Second, the benchmark~ robomme ships the same policy finetuned once to condition on a privileged oracle's grounded-subgoal text, one grounded sentence per action chunk such as ``pick up the container at that hides the green cube'', and it nearly solves the suite ( ): a grounded subgoal returns the data to the pretraining distribution, Markov, simple and direct, since the behaviour is again a function of the current observation and one instruction-like sentence. Subgoal-to-action is thus solved by the pretrained VLA's own low-level control; learning memory-to-action directly would couple that control with high-level memory reasoning, the hard part, whereas decomposing the problem as \[ \; \; \; \; \] isolates the genuinely unsolved stage and inherits the policy's motor competence without further training. The problem is therefore to produce the oracle's subgoal stream (content, coordinates, and timing) from raw episodic observation. The natural candidate for this first stage is a single VLM over the episode's frames, as in keyframe-memory pipelines such as MemER~ memer : select a small set of informative frames, then reason over them to produce the next subgoal. Benchmark results show that this family falls well short of the oracle (Figure~ fig:teaser ), and our tick-level analysis (Section~ sec:diagnosis ) explains why. (i)~Keyframe selection loses information: nothing guarantees the decisive frame survives selection, the selector's policy is opaque, and a dropped frame is unrecoverable. (ii)~VLMs are weak at precise spatial grounding: grounded subgoals carry exact coordinates, and a off by a few pixels sends the policy to the wrong one of identical objects. (iii)~Reasoning over raw frames is hard: the key object's identity and motion are buried in redundant background, and the frame-token context grows without bound. (iv)~VLMs hallucinate: a VLM asserts what is plausible rather than what is observed, uniquely damaging in a memory system, where one false fact enters the record and poisons every decision downstream. The first three failures share a root---pixels are the wrong medium for episodic memory---and the fourth demands that whatever medium replaces them be verifiable. We therefore build the memory stage as , a grounded multi-agent system rather than a single model (Figure~ fig:system ). A segmentation-based detector (SAM-3~ sam3 ), called as a tool on every frame, supplies the precise coordinates a VLM produces unreliably. A VLM writer (agent-1) runs once per replan tick and distils its window of sampled frames, their detections, the memory so far and the planner's expected next subgoal into at most one grounded text line, or none when the window shows no task-relevant change. The append-only text memory bank is the only history carrier: faithful (every line is evidence-gated against its own frames), compact (hundreds of steps become a handful of lines) and transparent (every coordinate in it came from the detector). A VLM reasoner (agent-2) reads the bank alone, without pixels, and emits the next grounded subgoal, trained to match the oracle stream verbatim at its cadence. Grounded text alone does not remove failure (iv): in closed loop the finetuned writer completed actions on a learned schedule rather than on evidence, and both agents cited coordinates they could not know (Section~ sec:diagnosis ). Because the bank is symbolic and grounded, every such claim is checkable, and we therefore wrap both agents in a propose--verify harness (Section~ sec:harness , Algorithm~ alg:harness ): every claim the agents make (an event line proposed for memory, a completion that would advance the plan, a cited coordinate) is checked against mechanical visual evidence and admitted, deferred until its evidence appears, corrected to the evidence-consistent value, or rejected. The same contract generates the supervision (Section~ sec:targets ): a target line exists only at the window that shows its evidence and cites only coordinates visible in the writer's inputs, so the agents are trained on the verified distribution the harness enforces at deployment; the reasoner is further trained on banks written by the trained writer rather than on ground-truth banks, so its training distribution matches deployment. Across the full suite, recovers a large fraction of the oracle ceiling with the policy fixed ( average success against the oracle's , of the privileged ceiling, Table~ tab:main ), reaching it on several tasks. Because the memory is readable text, every failure can be attributed to a bank line or its absence, yielding design principles validated in closed loop (Section~ sec:diagnosis , Appendix~ app:rounds ). Contributions. (1)~A decomposition argument, backed by a controlled end-to-end-versus- oracle gap under one fixed policy, locating the difficulty of VLA memory tasks in the memory-to-grounded-subgoal stage. (2)~ , a grounded multi-agent memory system (detector tool, VLM writer, append-only text bank, VLM reasoner) that replaces opaque keyframe selection with verified symbolic memory, and whose propose--verify harness is a general contract under which every agent claim (event, progress or grounding) takes effect only after a mechanical evidence check that admits, defers, corrects or rejects it, applied identically at corpus construction and at deployment. (3)~State-of-the-art memory-task performance with a fixed policy on RoboMME, transfer with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark, and a tick-level diagnostic protocol that turns closed-loop failures into attributable, fixable memory defects. Related Work sec:related Vision--language--action policies. Imitation policies for manipulation~ act,diffusionpolicy and their scaled, language-conditioned successors~ rt1,rt2,palme,octo,openvla, openvlaoft,robomamba,pi0,pi05 map the current observation and an instruction to short action chunks, from training data dominated by tasks fully observable in the current frame~ robomimic,contextvla . We treat the fixed subgoal-conditioned policy (Section~ sec:problem ) as a competent executor and study the memory stage above it. Memory for embodied agents. Partial observability in control has classically been met with architectural memory~ drqn,merlin,gtrxl,amago,rmt,ttt,elmur : representations that are latent, and so cannot be inspected, audited, or corrected at deployment. In VLAs, recent work compresses past frames into the policy's context~ contextvla or attaches a memory module to the backbone or recurrent queries~ memoryvla,rememvla ; a growing 2026 line gives VLAs explicit memory~ unimemvla,eventvla,weavela,aura,agm,hime , audits show frozen VLAs barely deploy the history they encode~ pbnr , and a contrasting line argues for continuous latent reasoning~ crvla . Closest to us, MemER~ memer keeps an episodic memory of VLM-selected keyframes and reasons over the selection with a second VLM pass. We share the decompose-to-subgoal philosophy but replace pixel memory with verified grounded text and selection with per-tick writing: nothing is discarded, and every remembered fact is a checkable sentence. Benchmarks. Standard manipulation suites~ metaworld,rlbench,calvin,libero,robocasa evaluate long-horizon chains whose sub-tasks are individually Markov, so strong policies need no episodic store. Recent benchmarks target the missing dimension~ mikasarobo,robocerebra,rmbench ; RoboMME~ robomme isolates episodic memory itself: sixteen tasks built around counts, orders, swaps, and demonstrated routes, with a privileged grounded-subgoal oracle that upper-bounds subgoal-conditioned execution. RoboMemArena~ rma adds 26 long-horizon kitchen tasks in four memory families. We adopt RoboMME's tasks, success predicates, and oracle cadence of one subgoal per action chunk, and evaluate on both. VLM agents with tools and verification. LLM planners over robot skills~ saycan,codeaspolicies choose the next step from language; Inner Monologue~ innermonologue showed that textual observations fed back into the loop make it robust, a precursor of our text bank, and append-only natural-language memories underpin open-ended agents~ generativeagents,voyager . Like tool-using agents~ toolformer,react and visual programs~ visprog,vipergpt , our system delegates what the model does poorly: SAM-3~ sam3 supplies pixel-exact grounding, and evidence extractors the percepts sparse-frame VLM inference reads at chance. Verification of model output ranges from self-critique~ reflexion,selfrefine to trained process verifiers~ verifystep , model judgments of model text; the harness instead admits a claim by a mechanical check against perception. An episode is scored by the environment's success predicate. title: LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs
summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn compact latent world models without pixel reconstruction. Existing JEPA pipelines typically train visual representations and action-conditioned dynamics before adding a control policy or solver. We introduce LeWAM, an end-to-end JEPA for control with: (1) a joint training objective over next latent state prediction and action flow matching, and (2) an isotropic Gaussian constraint on the latent state, enabling a single model to support direct policy execution and efficient planning by evaluating sampled actions with its learned latent dynamics. Compared with prior JEPAs in visual planning, LeWAM improves success rate from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks, and plans 32.3 times faster. On behavior cloning tasks in simulation and physical robots, LeWAM is also competitive with established methods. Interpretability analyses show that LeWAM learns control-relevant representations and action distributions effectively guiding test-time planning and control.

Introduction sec:introduction Visual control requires autonomous agents to complete tasks by selecting actions based on visual observations of the world. World models address this challenge by predicting the consequences of candidate actions, allowing agents to anticipate how the world will evolve before executing them. Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs)~ lecun2022apath offer a compact world modeling paradigm where future world states are predicted in latent space rather than by reconstructing pixels. Recent works such as ~ zhou2024dinowm and ~ maes2026lewm demonstrate the promise of applying action-conditioned latent world models to downstream control. These pipelines obtain visual features from pretrained encoders~ zhou2024dinowm,assran2025vjepa2 , or train representations from scratch with distributional regularizers such as ~ balestriero2025lejepa,maes2026lewm to prevent collapse. However, these methods alone do not reliably retain control-relevant information; JEPAs can favor temporally persistent distractors~ sobal2022slowfeatures , while action-conditioned dynamics may retain extraneous observation information~ brandfonbrener2023inverse . Control with these models typically requires an online solver such as the cross-entropy method (CEM)~ rubinstein1999cem or a separately trained action predictor. When initialized with a broad Gaussian prior over action sequences, CEM demands extensive rollouts to identify viable candidates, particularly as action dimensionality or planning horizon grows~ huang2021cemgd . Contact transitions also complicate local action optimization because the dynamics can switch between modes~ pang2023contactplanning . A post-trained action predictor can provide direct control, as in ~ nguyen2026gcidm , or guide action search, as in ~ wang2026prism . Training these predictors on frozen JEPA embeddings leaves action supervision disconnected from visual representation learning. We introduce , an end-to-end JEPA that jointly learns representation, action-conditioned dynamics, and a stochastic policy in a single training stage (Figure~ fig:intro ). Training combines two ingredients: a joint training objective over next-latent-state prediction and action flow matching, and ~ balestriero2025lejepa to regularize the latent states. A Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT)~ liang2025MoT predictor uses clean actions for latent dynamics prediction and noisy actions for policy learning through flow matching, so both objectives train the shared visual representation. Consequently, LeWAM supports both direct policy execution and visual planning by refining action sequences sampled from its learned policy. Our contributions are threefold: To our knowledge, the first JEPA that jointly learns representation, action-conditioned latent dynamics, and stochastic policy, using a joint prediction objective, one weight for latent-space regularization, and approximately 17M parameters. A planning procedure that jointly imagines the consequences of actions and how to act in the resulting states, which samples candidate action sequences from the learned action distribution and refines them with gradient descent through learned dynamics. Across ten heterogeneous simulated environments, improves goal-reaching success over ~ maes2026lewm , particularly on contact-rich tasks. Four-task comparisons extend these gains to longer goal horizons and show faster planning. On goal-agnostic task completion in simulation and physical robot execution, performs competitively with established baselines. Linear probes reveal decodable physical-state and action information, recorded-action rollouts visualize its learned dynamics, and planner ablations measure the gains from its stochastic action proposals. title: OGPO: Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization for Recoverable Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose OGPO, an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose , an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have shown strong potential for language-conditioned robotic manipulation by scaling supervised action prediction on large-scale robot datasets~ rt1,rt2,openvla . Most existing VLA policies are adapted to downstream tasks through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), where the model is optimized to predict expert actions from visual observations and language instructions on demonstration trajectories~ openvlaoft,octo,pi0,pi05 . Although this paradigm is simple and stable, it treats demonstrations primarily as step-wise action labels for trajectory-level imitation. As a result, policies trained purely with SFT tend to reproduce demonstration-specific action paths and remain inherently bounded by the coverage and quality of demonstration data. As shown in Figure~ fig:case-pertuation , when execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories, such policies may suffer from compounding errors in long-horizon tasks and lack explicit guidance for recovering toward task-progress states~ dagger . Recent studies have explored reinforcement learning (RL) to further improve pretrained VLA policies beyond supervised imitation, including iterative online RL fine-tuning~ ire-vla , PPO/GRPO-style policy-gradient optimization~ vla-rl,simplevlarl,pirl , residual policy learning~ selfimproving , and RL-based policy distillation~ rpd . By optimizing task-level rewards, RL can in principle encourage goal-directed behaviors that are not directly captured by step-wise action imitation. However, existing RL-based VLA post-training methods typically require costly environment rollouts and suffer from limited sample efficiency, making them difficult to scale for real-world robotic post-training. In this work, we study whether VLA policies can acquire goal-directed recoverability purely from offline robot data, without requiring additional online interaction. We define this ability as recovering toward task-progress key states when execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. Our key insight is that offline demonstrations should not be used merely as action sequences to imitate; they also contain implicit evidence about which task-progress states are reachable and which behaviors move the policy toward them. Based on this insight, we propose , an offline goal-conditioned policy optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Specifically, we retain SFT as a lightweight action prior to preserve low-level action feasibility and language-action alignment, while introducing an offline goal-conditioned RL objective to learn key-state reachability from existing trajectories. To turn offline data into goal-reaching supervision, adaptively relabels trajectories with task-progress key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to guide both policy optimization and value estimation. Instead of supervising the policy to imitate every action along the demonstration path, this objective trains the policy to reach task-progress states under goal-conditioned rewards. In this way, shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to improve goal-directed recoverability under feasible off-demonstration deviations while avoiding the high interaction cost of online RL. We evaluate OGPO on LIBERO~ libero and MetaWorld~ metaworld , and further test robustness and recoverability on LIBERO-Plus~ liberoplus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct benchmark with mid-execution perturbations. The results show that OGPO consistently improves over SFT baselines, especially on long-horizon and difficult tasks, while achieving stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and execution-time deviations. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate VLA post-training from the perspective of goal-directed recoverability and identify the limitation of trajectory-level SFT in recovering toward task-progress states under execution deviations. Second, we propose OGPO, an offline goal-conditioned policy optimization framework that adaptively relabels fixed robot trajectories with task-progress key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards, allowing the policy to learn and optimize goal-directed behaviors beyond step-wise action imitation. Third, we conduct extensive experiments on standard manipulation, distribution-shift, and mid-execution perturbation benchmarks, demonstrating that OGPO consistently improves task performance, robustness, and goal-directed recoverability without requiring additional online interaction. Related Works VLA post-training aims to adapt pretrained vision-language-action policies to downstream robotic manipulation tasks while preserving their general action priors and improving task-specific performance. Existing approaches mainly follow two directions: SFT and RL. Supervised Fine-tuning for VLA Policies SFT has become a dominant post-training strategy for adapting pretrained VLA policies to downstream robotic tasks. In this paradigm, the model is fine-tuned on expert demonstration trajectories by minimizing a supervised action prediction loss conditioned on visual observations and language instructions. Existing VLA models instantiate this paradigm with different action representations and prediction objectives. OpenVLA~ openvla discretizes continuous robot actions into action tokens and optimizes the policy with a next-token prediction objective using cross-entropy loss. Octo~ octo predicts continuous action chunks through a diffusion-based action head trained with a diffusion loss. ~ pi0 and ~ pi05 further adopt flow-matching objectives for continuous action-chunk prediction. Recent studies such as OpenVLA-OFT~ openvlaoft improve SFT-based adaptation by introducing continuous action representations, action chunking, parallel decoding, and regression-based imitation objectives. Despite these advances, SFT remains inherently constrained by the coverage and quality of demonstration data: it primarily learns to reproduce expert actions along demonstrated trajectories, and thus provides limited support for generalizing to unseen states, handling execution perturbations, and mitigating long-horizon compounding errors~ dagger . Reinforcement Learning for VLA Post-training Recent works have explored RL as an additional post-training stage after SFT. By optimizing task-level rewards through online rollouts, RL allows VLA policies to move beyond the behavior distribution of expert demonstrations and potentially acquire more robust behaviors under distribution shift~ rlwhat . For example, iRe-VLA~ ire-vla alternates between online RL and supervised learning to improve policy performance while maintaining training stability. Other methods apply PPO- or GRPO-style policy-gradient optimization to VLA models~ vla-rl,simplevlarl,pirl , aiming to enhance long-horizon decision-making and task success through outcome-driven rewards. In addition, residual RL methods improve pretrained VLA policies by learning lightweight corrective policies around frozen generalist models~ selfimproving , while RL-based policy distillation methods leverage VLA teachers or RL experts to obtain more specialized policies~ rpd . More recent studies further explore simulator- or world-model-based reinforcement fine-tuning to reduce the cost of direct real-world interaction~ worldenv,vlarft,wmpo,wovr . Although these methods demonstrate the promise of RL for improving VLA policies beyond SFT, they typically rely on online rollouts, real-world interaction, or simulator-based policy evaluation, making them costly and sample-inefficient for long-horizon robotic tasks. Our distinction. In this work, we combine the benefits of SFT and RL in a fully offline VLA post-training framework. Different from prior methods that rely mainly on action imitation, online rollouts, or simulator-based policy evaluation, OGPO extracts goal-reaching and failure-aware supervision directly from offline robot data. This enables VLA policies to improve goal-directed recoverability without additional environment interaction. To the best of our knowledge, OGPO is the first framework that integrates SFT regularization with offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning for recoverable VLA post-training. Method In this section, we present OGPO, an offline goal-conditioned policy optimization framework for recoverable VLA models. OGPO operates in three stages. First, it relabels offline trajectories into key-state-centered goal-reaching segments, thereby exposing the task-progress structure hidden in demonstrations. Second, it converts segment-level completion labels into goal-conditioned process rewards, which provide dense learning signals for value estimation. Third, it performs offline advantage-weighted policy optimization with SFT regularization, enabling the policy to improve toward goal-reaching behaviors while preserving feasible action priors. title: Cubic Spline Interpolation for Smooth Trajectory Generation in Autonomous Motion Systems
summary: We presented a program that automates the construction and solution of the cubic spline interpolation problem for a sequence of position-time waypoints, producing trajectories that are continuous in position, velocity, and acceleration and therefore avoid the infinite-acceleration problem inherent to piecewise-linear waypoint following. By assembling the interpolation and continuity conditions into a single linear system and solving directly for the spline coefficients, the program removes the need to manually derive per-segment equations for each new waypoint set. We illustrated the approach on free-form curve drawing and signature digitization, two tasks that use the same underlying machinery required for smooth robot and drone trajectory generation. Future work includes extending the implementation to multi-axis trajectories with explicit velocity and acceleration bounds, adopting the more computationally efficient tridiagonal solution method for larger waypoint sets, and evaluating the approach quantitatively against alternative trajectory generation methods.
full_text: Trajectories for robots, drones, and other autonomous vehicles must pass through a sequence of prescribed waypoints while remaining physically realizable, meaning the underlying position signal should have continuous velocity and acceleration. Piecewise-linear interpolation between waypoints violates this requirement: velocity changes discontinuously at each waypoint, implying infinite acceleration. We describe a program that fits piecewise cubic splines to a set of waypoints specified as position-time pairs , enforcing continuity of the function value, first derivative, and second derivative across segment boundaries. The spline coefficients are obtained by assembling the interpolation and continuity conditions into a single linear system and solving for the unknown coefficients directly, removing the need to derive the per-segment equations by hand. We demonstrate the approach on two illustrative tasks: generating smooth free-form paths from a sparse set of user-specified points, and reconstructing continuous digital traces of handwritten signatures from sampled pen positions. We discuss the computational cost of the direct linear-system approach relative to the classical tridiagonal (moment-based) formulation, and outline the extensions needed to apply this method to multi-axis robot and drone trajectories subject to velocity and acceleration limits. : cubic splines, trajectory generation, motion planning, smooth interpolation, autonomous vehicles Introduction A recurring problem in robotics, computer animation, and autonomous vehicle control is generating a trajectory that passes through a specified sequence of waypoints while producing motion that is physically executable. A naive solution connects consecutive waypoints with straight line segments (piecewise linear interpolation). This is simple to compute, but it is unsuitable for actuated physical systems: at each interior waypoint, the direction and often the magnitude of the velocity vector changes instantaneously. Since acceleration is the time derivative of velocity, a discontinuous velocity implies an infinite acceleration at that instant, which no real actuator, motor, or propulsion system can produce. This limitation motivates the use of smoother interpolants. A trajectory that is continuous (continuous position and velocity) removes the infinite-acceleration problem at the position level, but a trajectory that is continuous (continuous position, velocity, and acceleration) is preferable for most physical systems, since acceleration commands are what feedback controllers on robots and drones ultimately track. Piecewise cubic polynomials are the lowest-degree polynomials that can be joined together to form a globally curve while still leaving enough free parameters to interpolate an arbitrary sequence of waypoints; this is the classical cubic spline deboor2001 . In more demanding aerial robotics applications, still higher continuity (up to the fourth derivative, or ``snap'') is used so that the commanded thrust and body rates vary smoothly, as in minimum-snap trajectory generation for quadrotors mellinger2011 . Cubic splines represent the simplest member of this family: they guarantee only continuity, but they are correspondingly cheaper to compute and are sufficient for many ground robot, camera path, and animation applications where jerk and higher derivatives are not explicitly constrained. In this work we describe a program that automates the construction and solution of the cubic spline interpolation problem for a set of waypoints given as pairs. Rather than deriving the spline coefficients for each new set of waypoints by hand, the program assembles the full linear system of interpolation and continuity constraints, and solves for the coefficient vector directly. We apply the resulting tool to two tasks that are not typically framed as robotics problems, but which exercise exactly the same underlying interpolation machinery: (1) generating smooth free-form curves (``abstract drawings'') from a small set of user-supplied points, and (2) reconstructing a smooth digital trace of a handwritten signature from a sparse set of sampled points lying on the signature. Both tasks illustrate that once a program can turn an arbitrary list of waypoints into a curve, the same machinery is directly reusable for generating feasible motion commands for physical autonomous systems. Related Work Cubic spline interpolation is a classical topic in numerical analysis; de Boor's text deboor2001 remains the standard reference for both the theory (existence, uniqueness, and optimality properties of the interpolating spline) and the numerical construction of splines via divided differences and B-spline recursions. The formulation used in this paper follows the direct polynomial-coefficient construction described there, rather than the B-spline basis. In robotics and aerial vehicle control, piecewise polynomial trajectories are widely used to convert a sequence of waypoints into a reference signal that a lower-level controller can track. Mellinger and Kumar mellinger2011 generate trajectories for quadrotors by minimizing the integral of the square of the fourth derivative (snap) of position, subject to waypoint and boundary constraints, using piecewise polynomials of higher degree than cubic. Their formulation illustrates the general pattern followed here: waypoint interpolation constraints plus derivative-continuity constraints at segment boundaries, assembled into a linear system whose solution gives the polynomial coefficients. Cubic splines correspond to the special case where only continuity up to the second derivative is required, which reduces the polynomial degree needed per segment from the degree required for minimum-snap trajectories, at the cost of not directly controlling jerk or snap. Cubic splines and related low-order piecewise-polynomial curves have also been used outside of vehicle motion planning for exactly the same reason they are useful here: they turn a sparse set of sample points into a smooth, evaluable curve. In signature processing, cubic splines have been used to smooth the raw, jagged pen-position sequences captured by a digitizing tablet before further feature extraction saffar2018 , and Bézier variants of piecewise cubics have been used to vectorize and reconstruct handwritten signature contours. This is directly analogous to the signature-digitization application described in Section~ sec:applications of this paper, where a small number of sampled points on a signature are used to reconstruct a continuous curve. Problem Formulation We are given a set of waypoints , with , where plays the role of the interpolation parameter (typically time, but the same formulation applies to any monotonically increasing parameterization such as arc length). The goal is to construct a function that: passes through every waypoint, i.e., for all ; is twice continuously differentiable on , i.e., . The cubic spline construction represents as piecewise cubic polynomials, one per interval : This introduces unknown coefficients . These are determined by the following conditions: Interpolation conditions ( equations). Each segment must match the waypoint values at both of its endpoints: First-derivative continuity ( equations). At each interior waypoint, the velocity computed from the segment on the left must match the velocity computed from the segment on the right: Second-derivative continuity ( equations). Similarly, acceleration must match across each interior waypoint: These conditions total equations, two short of the unknowns. The remaining two degrees of freedom are fixed by a choice of boundary condition at the two ends of the trajectory. Common choices include: Natural boundary conditions: and , which impose zero curvature (and, in a trajectory-tracking context, zero commanded acceleration) at the start and end of motion. Clamped boundary conditions: and are set to specified values, useful when a known initial or final velocity is required (e.g., a robot starting or ending at rest, or matching the velocity of an adjoining trajectory segment). Matrix Formulation All continuity and interpolation equations, together with the two boundary equations, are linear in the unknown coefficients. They can therefore be written as a single matrix equation where stacks the unknowns , is a sparse matrix built entirely from the waypoint times (evaluating the appropriate powers of at each row), and collects the waypoint values and the boundary-condition constants, with zeros elsewhere. Once and are assembled, the coefficient vector is recovered as This is the approach implemented in our program: rather than deriving the entries of and by hand for each new set of waypoints, the program constructs and programmatically from the input list of pairs and computes the matrix inverse (or, equivalently, solves the linear system) to obtain all spline coefficients in one step. Implementation The program accepts a list of waypoints as pairs. For waypoints, it constructs the matrix and right-hand-side vector described in Section~3.1 by iterating over each segment and each continuity condition, then solves Equation~ eq:linear-system for the coefficient vector . The resulting per-segment cubic coefficients are stored and can be evaluated at any query time by locating the containing segment and evaluating Equation~ eq:segment . Algorithm~ alg:spline summarizes the procedure. Computational note. Solving the full system by direct matrix inversion costs arithmetic operations in general. The classical alternative formulation of the cubic spline problem reduces the unknowns to the second derivatives (moments) at the waypoints, which produces a tridiagonal system solvable in time via the Thomas algorithm deboor2001 . For the waypoint counts used in this work the cost of direct inversion is not a practical bottleneck, but the tridiagonal formulation would be preferable for applications with large numbers of waypoints or real-time replanning requirements, such as online trajectory replanning for a drone reacting to a dynamic environment. Applications sec:applications We demonstrate the spline-fitting program on two tasks that require converting a sparse set of sample points into a smooth, continuous curve. Free-form path synthesis Given a small number of waypoints placed by hand, the program produces a smooth curve passing through all of them. Signature digitization A handwritten signature can be represented as a sequence of pen positions sampled over time as the signature is written. Treating these samples as waypoints, the program fits a cubic spline to reconstruct a continuous digital trace of the signature from a reduced set of points. Cubic splines have previously been used in the signature-processing literature specifically to smooth raw, noisy pen-position sequences prior to further analysis saffar2018 ; the present application uses the same underlying interpolation for a related purpose, converting a sparse point set into a continuous curve suitable for digital storage or display. Discussion and Limitations The formulation presented here treats each spatial axis independently: a waypoint sequence produces a scalar function . Extending this to multi-dimensional trajectories, as required for planar or 3D robot and drone motion, is done by fitting an independent cubic spline to each coordinate axis ( , , and, for aerial vehicles, ) using the same set of waypoint times . Because all axes share the same knot sequence, the resulting vector-valued trajectory is in each component and therefore has well-defined, continuous velocity and acceleration vectors. Two limitations are worth noting. First, the cubic spline construction used here enforces only continuity and does not explicitly bound the magnitude of velocity or acceleration, nor does it constrain jerk; a trajectory that is technically feasible in the continuity sense may still command acceleration

title: VLMs are Native Action Models: Unleashing the Manipulation Capabilities of VLMs with Explicit Action-Space Grounding
summary: Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already exhibit strong visual, spatial and reasoning capabilities relevant to robotic manipulation. The key challenge in turning pretrained VLMs into generalist manipulation policies is to expose these capabilities through an appropriate action interface. Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified trainable policy, but typically introduce learned action tokens, action heads, or action experts whose semantics must be learned from robot data pretraining. In contrast, modular foundation-model-based manipulation methods can exploit pretrained VLM capabilities for zero-shot manipulation, but rely on external planning and control scaffolds that are not end-to-end trainable as a unified continuous-action policy. In this work, we introduce EASG, an Explicit Action-Space Grounding framework that bridges these two paradigms. By projecting a tool center point (TCP)-centered action frame into the wrist camera observation and expressing actions in the form of VLM's native textual generation interface, EASG makes the semantics of a continuous robot action space directly observable in the VLM's perceptual context. This allows pretrained VLMs to directly generate executable robot actions using their existing visual-spatial reasoning capabilities, without robot-action pretraining or additional action modules. Besides, the same action interface supports direct fine-tuning with robot trajectories, allowing the models to continuously improve beyond their manipulation capabilities unleashed by EASG. Overall, EASG enables zero-shot manipulation and generalization across object positions, categories, and robot embodiments, while supporting effective fine-tuning in the same continuous action space. These results demonstrate that, given an appropriate action interface, pretrained VLMs can themselves serve as native action models for robotic manipulation.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments l 0.36 fig:real-setup Experimental Setup. To study both the native zero-shot capability and the extensibility of VLM-based manipulation, we conduct real-world experiments on a 6-DoF UR3 robot with a wrist-mounted RGB-D camera and an external camera. We construct a task suite spanning rigid, articulated, deformable, precise, and long-horizon manipulation, and organize it into two groups of different difficulty. Task Group 1 contains relatively simple tasks, whereas Task Group 2 includes more challenging tasks requiring greater precision, more complex interactions, or longer-horizon execution. We find that pretrained VLMs with EASG exhibit non-trivial zero-shot capability on Task Group 1 but generally fail on Task Group 2. Accordingly, we use Task Group 1 to characterize native VLM manipulation and Task Group 2 to evaluate capability extension through robot-data fine-tuning. title: Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning for Long-Tailed Robotic Policies
summary: In the practical deployment of vision--language--action policies, handling long-tailed task distributions is a common challenge due to the highly imbalanced composition of robot demonstration datasets. To investigate this issue, we study the head-task action bias in shared robot policies, particularly focusing on its relationship with task-specific visual evidence. Our experimental analysis shows that, when the visual evidence required by a tail task is insufficient, the policy increasingly falls back on action patterns reinforced by data-rich head tasks, resulting in degraded performance on under-represented tasks. Motivated by this observation, we propose Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning, a training framework for long-tailed robot policies. Our method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence using instruction-related and action-related signals, and constructs counterfactual observations by removing the selected evidence. The resulting counterfactual predictions are used to strengthen the association among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with the supervision adaptively adjusted according to the number of demonstrations available for each task. The proposed framework requires neither additional training data nor region-level annotations and incurs no additional computation during deployment. Extensive experiments across simulated benchmarks, different VLA architectures, and real-world robot platforms demonstrate that our method robustly and consistently improves long-tailed robot policy learning, particularly for tail tasks, while maintaining reliable performance on head tasks.

The resulting counterfactual predictions are used to strengthen the association among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with the supervision adaptively adjusted according to the number of demonstrations available for each task. The proposed framework requires neither additional training data nor region-level annotations and incurs no additional computation during deployment. Introduction Vision--language--action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising foundation for generalist robot policies, integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation within a unified framework brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0,MaSZHK26 . Robot demonstration datasets, however, can be highly imbalanced across manipulation skills openx2024 . Similar to the long-tailed category distributions observed in datasets such as iNaturalist vanhorn2018inaturalist , robot task distributions can be skewed toward a few data-rich head tasks, leaving many tail tasks with limited demonstrations zhu2026beyond . Long-tailed learning addresses unequal supervision through approaches such as resampling, loss reweighting, and decoupled representation and classifier learning cui2019classbalanced,kang2020decoupling,ma2022delving . However, most of these methods are developed for classification and are difficult to apply directly to VLAs due to differences in task formulation and model architecture. zhu2026beyond propose Approaching-Phase Augmentation (APA) for long-tailed VLA learning, but it relies on additional tools, such as object detection and image inpainting, increasing the complexity of the approach.Moreover, APA primarily mitigates the problem through data augmentation, without directly constraining VLAs' reliance on head-task action bias. However, comparing the results of policies trained on the balanced FULL dataset and the long-tailed LT dataset (see Appendix~ app:dataset_distribution ), we find that tail-task performance drops substantially under LT, as shown in Fig.~ fig1 (a). Interestingly, some head tasks perform worse under FULL than under LT: more complete and diverse training data do not yield uniform improvements across all tasks. This leads us to consider whether the long-tailed multi-task learning problem is related to how different tasks jointly influence a shared policy. We further visualize the model's attention during inference. Figures~ fig1 (b) and (c) show that head tasks attend reasonably well to visual evidence associated with the target object, but may exhibit more dispersed visual attention due to cross-task interference. Tail tasks face a more severe problem: they struggle to establish reliable task-specific visual grounding. Through the toy experiment in Section~ sec:toy_experiment , we find that when such evidence is insufficient, the model must still produce an action, and the shared policy tends to fall back on frequent action patterns in the training data, giving rise to a head-task action bias. Thus, tail tasks do not merely suffer from insufficient data exposure; during decision-making, shared action priors associated with head tasks are more likely affect the visual evidence needed for the current task. This finding raises a new question: [t] 0.39 0pt [t] 0.57 Thus, we introduce Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning ( ) , Without requiring additional annotations or training data, directly uses the original data and a relation-aware counterfactual branch to identify visual evidence relevant to decisions during rollouts. It constructs counterfactual samples by removing key relational tokens and strengthens the associations among task instructions, visual relations, and actions through counterfactual training. Crucially, evidence guides both counterfactual construction and supervision in , which adaptively assigns weaker regularization to head tasks and stronger supervision to tail tasks according to the number of demonstrations. Our contributions: 1)We reassess the conventional view that tail-task failures arise from data scarcity and show through a toy experiment that, when task-specific visual grounding is insufficient, tail-task predictions fall back on action bias shaped by head tasks. 2) We propose , which suppresses tail tasks’ reliance on action priors via counterfactual supervised training to build their task-specific evidence, without requiring extra annotations or additional training data. 3) We evaluate on two VLA policies in LIBERO-Core-LT and on two real-world robot platforms, Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, with macro-averaged gains and task-specific outcomes reported. Related Work Long-Tailed Learning. Long-tailed recognition studies class imbalance that biases models toward head classes zhang2023survey . Representative approaches include class-balanced re-weighting cui2019classbalanced , decoupled representation and classifier learning kang2020decoupling , and prior-based logit adjustment menon2021logitadjustment . LDAM adjusts classification margins according to class frequencies cao2019ldam , Balanced Softmax addresses label distribution shift ren2020balanced , and DisAlign combines adaptive score calibration with prior-based re-weighting zhang2021disalign . Feature augmentation methods enrich tail classes through transferable class-generic variations chu2020feature , learned semantic augmentation directions li2021metasaug , or head-class feature displacements wang2021rsg . Contrastive methods improve representation geometry: PaCo introduces learnable class-wise centers cui2021paco , while BCL balances inter-class contributions zhu2022balanced . These methods primarily address discrete class imbalance rather than long-tailed state and behavior distributions in sequential robotic manipulation. Robotic Foundation Models. Robotic foundation models build on large vision and language models touvron2023llama2,zhai2023sigmoid,oquab2024dinov2 . PaLM-E integrates visual, state, and textual inputs for embodied reasoning and planning driess2023palme . Robot policies span autoregressive, diffusion-based, and continuous generative approaches. RT-1 brohan2023rt1 scales Transformer-based behavior cloning through action tokenization, while RT-2 brohan2023rt transfers Internet-scale vision-language knowledge to robotic control. OpenVLA kim2024openvla combines a pretrained language model with SigLIP and DINOv2 features and trains on Open X-Embodiment demonstrations openx2024 . MiniVLA belkhale2024minivla adopts a lightweight Qwen2.5-0.5B backbone, while OpenVLA-OFT improves adaptation and inference through parallel decoding, action chunking, and continuous regression kim2025oft . Diffusion policies generate continuous actions through iterative denoising chi2023diffusion . Octo ghosh2024octo trains a Transformer-based diffusion policy on diverse robot trajectories for adaptation to new observation and action spaces. black2025pi0 combines flow matching with a pretrained vision-language model for cross-embodiment control, while black2025pi05 broadens task and environment coverage. SmolVLA uses a compact architecture and asynchronous inference for efficient training and deployment shukor2025smolvla . Despite these advances, training data can remain imbalanced across tasks, states, and behaviors, motivating further investigation into how long-tailed distributions affect visuomotor representations and action prediction. title: LeapBot-JAC: Joint Action Chains for World Action Models
summary: Action-chunking policies predict future controls but execute only a prefix before replanning. How should a fixed action-token budget be organized to support execution? We propose LeapBot-JAC, which allocates sparse future-control references and dense execution targets within one shared action expert. Both chains are supervised by demonstrated controls and jointly denoised at aligned physical-time positions. Directed attention allows execution tokens to read reference tokens subject to the host's visibility constraints. JAC adds neither action tokens nor parameters and retains the host's world-modeling process; both chains participate in inference, while only the execution chain drives the robot. On LIBERO, JAC reaches 98.3% success with FastWAM and LeapBot-WA, up from 97.0% and 97.3%. On zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, their success rates improve from 53.5% to 70.4% and from 73.1% to 77.3%, respectively. RoboTwin and two real-world tasks provide additional deployment evaluations. Single-training-seed comparisons and FastWAM ablations support action-role organization as a practical design choice under a fixed action-token budget.
full_text: Action-chunking policies predict future controls but execute only a prefix before replanning. How should a fixed action-token budget be organized to support execution? We propose LeapBot-JAC, which allocates sparse future-control references and dense execution targets within one shared action expert. Both chains are supervised by demonstrated controls and jointly denoised at aligned physical-time positions. Directed attention allows execution tokens to read reference tokens subject to the host's visibility constraints. JAC adds neither action tokens nor parameters and retains the host's world-modeling process; both chains participate in inference, while only the execution chain drives the robot. On LIBERO, JAC reaches 98.3 success with FastWAM and LeapBot-WA, up from 97.0 and 97.3 . On zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, their success rates improve from 53.5 to 70.4 and from 73.1 to 77.3 , respectively. RoboTwin and two real-world tasks provide additional deployment evaluations. Single-training-seed comparisons and FastWAM ablations support action-role organization as a practical design choice under a fixed action-token budget. Introduction Action-chunking policies predict a sequence of future robot controls, but closed-loop deployment often executes only a short prefix before querying the policy again. ACT and Diffusion Policy exploit sequence generation for temporally coherent behavior while using temporal ensembling or receding-horizon execution to incorporate new observations~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion . Predictions beyond the executed prefix can still influence the current output through the model's internal dependencies. The resulting design question is how to organize those predictions: should every token have the same temporal density and deployment role? World action models (WAMs) couple robot control with learning environment dynamics. Motus supports multiple video--action modeling modes~ bi2025motus ; LingBot-VA uses causal video--action generation~ li2026lingbotva ; Fast-WAM retains video co-training while omitting future-video generation at inference~ yuan2026fastwam . These approaches primarily organize world representations and their interaction with control. Within an existing action expert, the organization of a fixed number of control predictions remains a separate design choice. We study action-role organization under a fixed action-token budget. Dense predictions preserve near-term control resolution, whereas sparsely sampled control targets span a longer interval using fewer tokens. Combining these roles provides a way to expose execution to a temporally extended reference without adding an action expert or expanding its token sequence. The reference consists of robot controls, not semantic subgoals or executable waypoints; its role is to condition the jointly generated execution chain. We propose (Joint Action Chains, JAC). A sparse reference chain and a dense execution chain share input projections, Transformer layers, an output head, and every action forward pass. Both chains are supervised by demonstrated controls and evolve together during denoising, with independent noise samples at a common noise level. Physical-time positions align the two target sequences. A directed role mask permits to read while blocking direct access in the reverse direction, subject to the host's legal attention edges. Only the execution prefix is sent to the robot. This construction reorganizes action prediction while preserving the host's world-modeling process. Prior work already explores joint generation of high-level intent and executable actions~ li2026lawa,hao2025chd . JAC's focus is more specific: directly supervised control references and dense execution coexist within one existing action expert at a fixed token budget. We assess task success across two hosts and examine how information-flow direction, reference weight, and reference stride affect performance. Our contributions are threefold. (1) Action-role allocation: we formulate sparse reference and dense execution prediction within a fixed action-token budget, separating the supervision span from the executed prefix. (2) Shared-expert joint generation: we combine control-label supervision, physical-time alignment, and directed cross-chain access without adding action parameters, while retaining host visibility constraints. (3) Empirical evidence on two hosts: JAC improves LIBERO success for FastWAM and LeapBot-WA to 98.3 , and improves their LIBERO-Plus totals by 16.9 and 4.2 percentage points, respectively. Three FastWAM ablations characterize sensitivity to access direction, reference supervision, and temporal coverage. Related Work Action sequences and hierarchical control. ACT improves fine manipulation through sequence generation and temporal ensembling~ zhao2023act . Diffusion Policy represents multimodal action distributions with conditional diffusion and receding-horizon control~ chi2023diffusion . Play-LMP learns latent plans from play data for goal-conditioned behavior~ lynch2019play . Dense Policy progressively expands sparse action keyframes into a dense sequence~ su2025densepolicy . JAC instead retains simultaneous reference and execution roles at a fixed total token count. Hierarchical methods distinguish longer-term plans from local execution. CHD jointly diffuses high-level subgoals and low-level trajectories, allowing low-level feedback to refine subgoals~ hao2025chd . JAC allocates reference and execution roles inside one existing action expert; its directionality is evaluated as an architectural choice. World modeling and action generation. Motus combines multiple experts and modality schedules for different conditional generation modes~ bi2025motus . LingBot-VA jointly models video and control with causal blocks and history updates~ li2026lingbotva . Fast-WAM separates video co-training from test-time future generation~ yuan2026fastwam , while LeapBot-WA explores world anchoring in predictive semantic space~ liu2026leapbotwa . JAC preserves a host's world objective and sampling process while changing targets and visibility within its action budget. Beyond joint action generators, DINO-WM optimizes actions through predicted visual features~ zhou2024dinowm , and V-JEPA 2-AC uses an action-conditioned latent world model for planning~ assran2025vjepa2 . Intermediate representations and action reasoning. UniPi synthesizes text-conditioned video plans and extracts controls from them~ du2023unipi ; CoTDiffusion generates visual subgoals to guide a low-level policy~ ni2024cotdiffusion . These differ from JAC's directly supervised control references. ECoT generates embodied reasoning about objects, end-effector states, and subtasks before actions~ zawalski2024ecot . LAWA learns codebook-based transition targets from action-free video, jointly denoises separate latent-action and executable-action experts, and omits the future video branch at inference~ li2026lawa . Its online latent intent evolves in a continuous embedding space. JAC shares the idea that execution can use evolving intent, but differs in supervision, taken directly from robot controls without a new video-action tokenizer; parameters and budget, reallocating a fixed token count inside an existing expert; and host integration, retaining the host world process while changing action-target organization and direct cross-chain access. Spatial, semantic, and historical conditions. Robust-WAM aligns action-stream queries with future semantic features and their physical times~ yan2026robustwam . MaskWAM combines object-mask prompting and prediction~ yu2026maskwam , and MemoryWAM studies persistent history~ yang2026memorywam . These mechanisms address semantic, spatial, and historical conditioning. JAC complements these mechanisms by supervising intermediate robot controls. Noise schedules and sequence generation. Diffusion Forcing assigns independent noise levels to sequence tokens~ chen2024diffusionforcing . JAC instead uses independent noise realizations at a common action noise level.
