title: Evo-World: A Lightweight Vision-Language-Action Model with Future Motion Prediction via Optical-Flow Supervision
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for visual understanding, language grounding, and robot control, yet anticipating how the scene will evolve beyond the current observation can provide additional information for control. Action supervision alone does not explicitly encourage such anticipation, while future-image prediction entangles task-relevant motion with largely static appearance. To address these limitations, we introduce Evo-World, a lightweight VLA model that augments policy learning with future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision, thereby providing a task-relevant predictive signal focused on motion rather than appearance. We further design the training procedure to preserve these predictive representations during policy learning, regulating representation diversity while decoupling representation learning from action optimization. Across simulation benchmarks, Evo-World demonstrates strong performance, achieving a tier-averaged success rate of 91.1% on Meta-World MT50 , with a 13.0% relative improvement over the non-predictive baseline. On real-world AgileX robots, Evo-World outperforms the evaluated baselines across single-arm and bimanual manipulation tasks while using only 0.87B parameters and delivering lower GPU memory usage and higher inference efficiency. These results demonstrate that future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision provides an effective and lightweight approach to enhancing the predictive capabilities of VLA models.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments We evaluate the performance of manipulation on Meta-World MT50, RoboTwin, and three real-world tasks on an AgileX dual-arm robot. Meta-World and RoboTwin are reported together in a single simulation table (Table~ tab:1 ): Meta-World provides the main quantitative setting across four difficulty tiers, while RoboTwin tests the model in a separate training and deployment setting. Real-world experiments assess performance on a physical robot. Meta-World and Robotwin Experimental setup Evo-World is initialized from general-purpose pretrained encoders and trained on four NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs, without additional robot-policy pretraining. Detailed configurations are provided in Appendix Table~ tab:A1 . Optical-flow supervision. Figure~ fig:3 illustrates the optical-flow renderings used to supervise the motion representation module on both simulation benchmarks. Compared with the corresponding RGB observations, these renderings emphasize image-space displacement and suppress static scene appearance. They serve as training targets for latent motion prediction; no optical-flow estimator is required at inference. Baselines. For Meta-World we compare with Pi0 , SmolVLA SmolVLA , RoboTron-Mani RoboTronMani , Evo-1 Evo1 , Evo-Depth EvoDepth , LA4VLA LA4VLA , and FabriVLA FabriVLA . For RoboTwin we compare against DP DiffusionPolicy , ACT ACT , RDT rdt , DP3 dp3 , starVLA StarVLA , AHA-WAM aha , GalaxeaVLA GalaxeaVLA , and Xiaomi Robotics-0 XiaomiRobotics0 . Table~ tab:1 also lists parameter counts and whether large-scale robot-data pretraining was used. The comparison contextualizes performance. Meta-World and RoboTwin results Table~ tab:1 reports both simulation benchmarks. On Meta-World MT50, Evo-World reaches a tier-averaged success rate of 91.1 , which is 10.5 percentage points above the reported Evo-1 score of 80.6 and 1.1 points above FabriVLA's 90.0 . Evo-World obtains the best score on the Hard tier and on the tier average, and the second-best score on the other three tiers, so the four tier scores are consistently high rather than driven by a single difficulty level. On RoboTwin, Evo-World achieves a Clean success rate of 67.1 and a Random success rate of 16.5 . Averaged across the Clean and Random settings, Evo-World achieves the highest overall success rate of 41.8 among the compared methods. Notably, Evo-World uses about 0.87B parameters and no robot-data pretraining, yet exceeds larger and robot-pretrained baselines such as (3.5B) and LA4VLA (1.0B) on the Meta-World average. Example episode trajectories from the simulation benchmarks are provided in the Appendix~ app:benchmark-examples . Real-world experiments We evaluate Evo-World on an AgileX dual-arm robot in three tasks covering both single-arm manipulation and bimanual collaboration (Figure~ fig:4 ). Floral arrangement is a single-arm task in which one arm inserts a flower stem into a vase. Mug hanging and microwave placement are bimanual collaboration tasks: the two arms work together to hang mugs on a rack or to open a microwave door, put the plate inside, and close the door, respectively. Appendix~ app:real-world-setup describes the hardware setup, demonstration collection, and supervised fine-tuning protocol. We compare Evo-World with OpenVLA-OFT openvlaoft and Pi0 . Each model is evaluated for 20 trials per task, and we report task success rates and their unweighted mean. All three models run on the same NVIDIA H20 GPU in BF16 precision. We also report parameter count, GPU memory usage, and measured inference frequency for each deployment configuration. Evo-World achieves the highest success rate on all three tasks: 55.0 for floral arrangement, 70.0 for mug hanging, and 65.0 for microwave placement. Its average success rate is 63.3 , compared with 51.7 for and 23.3 for OpenVLA-OFT. The gains over are 15.0, 15.0, and 5.0 percentage points, respectively, covering both single-arm manipulation and bimanual collaboration. With 0.87B parameters, Evo-World uses 2.54\,GB of GPU memory and achieves a measured inference frequency of 6.16\,Hz, giving the lowest memory usage and highest inference frequency among the evaluated models. Relative to , it uses 62.0 less GPU memory and has a 13.7 higher inference frequency under the tested deployment settings. These measurements support the practical efficiency of the compact policy alongside its higher task success rates.

title: JoyInside-VLM-Agent: Product-Conditioned Multimodal Policy Learning for Embodied Agents
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables; includes references and appendices
summary: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy's parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.
full_text: Introduction Embodied agents deployed on robotic platforms and smart hardware must translate multimodal observations and user instructions into executable behavior. Across products ranging from bipedal, quadruped, and wheeled robots to AI-enabled plush toys, the appropriate response to a given request depends on the agent's role, capabilities, and operating constraints. Changes in user goals, new visual evidence, and execution failures can further invalidate earlier plans. We study how to train a shared multimodal policy that adapts to product specifications and revises its decisions as interactions unfold. Figure~ fig:teaser presents the training framework and deployment examples. Multimodal training has demonstrated positive transfer across tasks and robotic embodiments driess2023palme,oxe2023 , while context-aware systems use user intent and environmental feedback to guide interaction king2024sasha,chang2024worldscribe . However, reported failures include actions beyond device capabilities and descriptions that no longer match the user's current scene or intent king2024sasha,chang2024worldscribe . These observations motivate training policies that combine transferable capabilities with adherence to product constraints and sustained alignment with the user's current goal. This objective imposes two requirements on training. The data must cover diverse product configurations, goal revisions, and failure recovery while preserving the correspondence between actions and observations. The learning signal must reflect reasoning quality, compliance with product constraints, and progress toward the current goal. Trajectory-level rewards summarize these criteria but do not specify how to distribute credit across tokens. Using additional evidence during training therefore requires selecting an appropriate source for each token and controlling how that evidence affects policy updates. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned data construction and staged policy learning. Our pipeline combines product roles, workflows, and constraints with available tools and skills to build executable environments. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories, which undergo execution checks and semantic validation. Multi-source supervised fine-tuning establishes behavior consistent with product specifications, while multi-expert on-policy distillation integrates complementary language and visual capabilities. Reinforcement learning then refines the policy using interaction-specific rewards. To guide reinforcement learning, we combine process-quality scores from a Generative Process Reward Model (GPRM), multi-judge rankings of the same candidate trajectories, and task-queue assessments of goal alignment and cross-turn continuity. For token-level policy optimization, we introduce DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing), building on RLSD's sign-preserving advantage modulation yang2026selfdistilledrlvr and DOPD's dual-source routing yu2026dopd . A frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy's parameters score tokens along the same student-generated trajectory. DPER selects evidence based on their disagreement and support for each sampled token. The selected evidence rescales token-level advantages while preserving their reward-derived signs. Privileged information is used only during training. We evaluate JoyInside-VLM-Agent on public tool-use benchmarks and the proprietary JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics datasets. The model achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, outperforming the evaluated baselines. Case studies on a physical quadruped robot provide qualitative evidence of visually grounded search, replanning in response to execution feedback, and honest failure reporting. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=1.5em,label= ] Product-conditioned trajectory construction. We compose executable product configurations and generate verified multimodal trajectories covering product variation, goal revisions, and failure recovery. DPER for policy optimization. We route token-level evidence between two privileged sources to scale token advantages while preserving their reward-derived signs. Multi-source interaction rewards. We combine process evaluation, multi-model rankings, and task-queue consistency into a learning signal for reasoning quality, adherence to product constraints, and alignment with evolving goals. JoyInside-VLM-Agent and its evaluation. We integrate these components into a unified training framework and assess the resulting model through public benchmarks and proprietary evaluation sets and qualitative quadruped case studies. Related Work Embodied and Context-Aware Interaction PaLM-E learns shared representations for robotic and vision-language tasks driess2023palme , while Open X-Embodiment studies cross-platform transfer using pooled interaction data oxe2023 . Context-aware assistants address how observations and user intent guide behavior: Sasha grounds smart-home requests in available devices and user feedback king2024sasha ; GazePointAR combines gaze, pointing, and dialogue history to resolve references lee2024gazepointar ; and WorldScribe adapts visual descriptions to intent and environmental changes chang2024worldscribe . Together, these lines connect shared capabilities with decisions grounded in the current interaction. Interactive benchmarks further make behavioral constraints explicit. -bench evaluates conversations under domain policies yao2024taubench , while -Bench considers user--agent coordination in a shared environment barres2025tau2bench . WildToolBench covers intentions distributed across turns and transitions among tool use, conversation, and clarification yu2026wildtoolbench . These settings motivate evaluating whether behavior respects constraints and follows the current goal. Our work addresses the corresponding training problem across robotic platforms and smart hardware, conditioning a shared policy on each product's role, capabilities, constraints, and interaction state. Multimodal Trajectory Construction Synthetic data methods expand agent training beyond available interaction logs. ToolACE constructs diverse function-calling dialogues with rule- and model-based verification liu2024toolace , and T3-Agent generates and verifies multimodal queries and tool-use trajectories gao2025mmagent . Their focus on coverage and validity provides a basis for learning tool interaction. Training for dynamic tasks additionally requires representing the consequences of intermediate actions and the decisions that follow unexpected feedback. Agent-R constructs revision trajectories through search and model-guided critique, connecting erroneous behavior to successful continuations yuan2025agentr . Agent World Model builds executable, stateful environments for interaction and reinforcement learning wang2026agentworldmodel . These approaches expose learners to recovery behavior or environmental transitions. Our pipeline couples such execution feedback with compositional product specifications and visual observations, covering both recovery toward an existing goal and adaptation after the user changes it. We jointly vary product roles, workflows, constraints, and capabilities within executable environments. Post-Training and Reward-Guided Optimization AgentTuning and Agent-FLAN study how instruction tuning develops agent behavior from demonstrations zeng2024agenttuning,chen2024agentflan . Generalized knowledge distillation obtains teacher feedback on student-generated sequences, addressing the mismatch between fixed demonstrations and the learner's behavior agarwal2024gkd . H-OPD combines vision-language and text-only teachers through visual-description transfer and token-level arbitration yin2026hopd . Agents-A1 integrates domain expertise through staged training and multi-teacher on-policy distillation agentsa12026scaling . RL Starts before RL studies OPD as preparation for reinforcement learning, reporting higher post-RL averages than direct RL and SFT-initialized RL in text and vision-language reasoning dong2026rlstartsbeforerl . These methods inform capability acquisition and consolidation; our training additionally conditions expert transfer on product specifications and refines the resulting policy against interaction-specific rewards. Reward modeling determines which behavior to encourage. Process supervision evaluates intermediate reasoning lightman2023verify , generative verifiers produce correctness judgments zhang2025genverifier , and PoLL aggregates assessments from multiple models verga2024poll . Aggregation can retain shared errors eisenstein2024herding ; evaluation criteria must still be defined for the target behavior. Using these assessments in optimization is a separate question. RLSD uses privileged evidence to scale token advantages while preserving their reward-derived signs yang2026selfdistilledrlvr . DOPD routes supervision between privileged teacher and student policies to address differences in token-level supervision yu2026dopd . DPER combines these mechanisms: it extends RLSD's magnitude modulation to dual-source evidence selected through DOPD's routing principle. Our multi-source rewards separately assess reasoning, product constraints, and goal consistency. Product-Conditioned Multimodal Data Construction sec:data-construction We construct multimodal interaction trajectories to learn a shared policy across heterogeneous robotic platforms---including bipedal, quadruped, and wheeled robots---and smart hardware. Our construction couples compositional product specifications with executable constraints and visual feedback consistent with the resulting state. This produces interactions that cover both recovery from execution failures and adaptation to revised user goals under the same product rules. Figure~ fig:data-pipeline connects product composition and environment initialization (steps 1--2), closed-loop interaction (step 3), and trajectory validation and reuse (step 4). Product and Environment Construction We use developer configurations, product descriptions, device images or interface screenshots, tool APIs, operational rules, and domain skills as source materials. JoyAI-VL performs product decomposition, code generation, trajectory generation, user simulation, and semantic auditing throughout this pipeline. It decomposes existing products into reusable modules and generates variants that preserve field restrictions and component semantics, following self-instructed data generation wang2022selfinstruct . Each product specification is a tuple : defines identity, embodiment, and interaction style; defines task strategies and workflows, including decision branches and recovery rules; specifies permissions, confirmation requirements, and operating constraints; and specifies tools, domain skills, and perceptual and action capabilities. Each component has a corresponding typed module library. A code-generation agent implements simulated tool and device backends from the resource interfaces. These programs validate arguments and preconditions, execute state transitions, and return results or errors, with branches for success, invalid arguments, insufficient permission, timeout, and partial execution. Calls and state changes are logged. Before admission to a library, modules undergo interface, state-access, and failure-branch tests, together with checks that backend outputs agree with the resulting states and observations. The composer selects modules from the four libraries and assembles compatible product configurations. Compatibility checks resolve dependencies and conflicts, ensure that workflows use installed resources and obey constraints, and require action arguments to be obtainable from user input, observations, prior results, or clarification. title: CeDR-Nav: Cross-Embodiment Mapless Navigation via Offline Demonstration Recasting
summary: Learning-based methods have demonstrated strong performance in mapless robot navigation. However, a learned policy remains restricted to the embodiment on which it was trained. Many cross-embodiment navigation methods require time-consuming online training and can still underperform target-specific policies. In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for deriving a policy for each target embodiment, but the embodiment mismatch prevents these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target. In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a cross-embodiment demonstration recasting framework that trains a dedicated navigation policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online data collection. Geometry-consistent scaling with per-demonstration validity assessment converts the source demonstrations into target training data, and a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy generates feasible avoidance maneuvers for each target embodiment. Extensive quantitative simulations and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CeDR-Nav, with an average success-rate gain of 13.8 percentage points over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations and target-specific policy training completed within seconds.

Many cross-embodiment navigation methods require time-consuming online training and can still underperform target-specific policies. In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for deriving a policy for each target embodiment, but the embodiment mismatch prevents these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target. In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a cross-embodiment demonstration recasting framework that trains a dedicated navigation policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online data collection. Geometry-consistent scaling with per-demonstration validity assessment converts the source demonstrations into target training data, and a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy generates feasible avoidance maneuvers for each target embodiment. Extensive quantitative simulations and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CeDR-Nav, with an average success-rate gain of 13.8 percentage points over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations and target-specific policy training completed within seconds. Introduction Autonomous navigation is a fundamental capability for mobile robots. In recent years, learning-based methods have emerged as effective approaches to mapless navigation in complex and cluttered environments xiao2022motion,xie2023drl,pfeiffer2017perception . However, a learned navigation policy is commonly restricted to the embodiment on which it was trained. In practice, the physical dimensions and sensor configurations of mobile robots not only vary across platforms, but also change within a single platform due to task requirements. When the robot's embodiment changes, the original policy can suffer substantial performance degradation and may cause dangerous collisions. Whether learning from collected demonstrations or from agent--environment interaction, obtaining a navigation policy demands significant effort for every new embodiment argall2009survey,osa2018algorithmic . Existing methods address this challenge by adapting trained policies at deployment zhang2025dimension , training universal policies across embodiment configurations zhang2025drl,putta2024embodiment,dezons2026multimodal,zhang2026ea , or learning from multi-platform navigation experience shah2023gnm,shah2023vint,sridhar2024nomad,yang2024pushing,hirose2023exaug,doshi24-crossformer . However, the conservative enclosure used by DVST can restrict passage through otherwise traversable gaps when the target and reference robots differ substantially in shape~ zhang2025dimension . Training universal policies across configurations, such as DRL-DCLP zhang2025drl , requires time-consuming online training with carefully designed environments, while the resulting policy can underperform a dedicated target-specific policy. These data-driven approaches rely on multi-platform datasets or scene-geometry estimation for experience augmentation shah2023gnm,shah2023vint,sridhar2024nomad,yang2024pushing,hirose2023exaug,doshi24-crossformer . In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for each target embodiment. However, the geometric dimensions and velocity limits of the source embodiment prevent these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target embodiment kim2020domain,hudson2022skeletal,he2026demojepajointembeddingpredictivearchitecture . This raises the central question of this work: can source demonstrations be converted into valid target supervision without new demonstration collection, so that a dedicated navigation policy can be obtained for each target embodiment without additional online interaction? In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a Cross-Embodiment Demonstration Recasting framework that obtains a dedicated policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online RL training. Specifically, CeDR-Nav first recasts source demonstrations into valid training data for the target embodiment through geometry-consistent scaling and validity assessment, ensuring that the recast trajectories remain geometrically consistent with the target embodiment. Subsequently, CeDR-Nav trains a target-specific policy using a Gaussian mixture model bishop1994mixture to capture the multimodal action distribution in the recast demonstrations. Extensive cross-embodiment simulations and quantitative real-world experiments on multiple robot platforms demonstrate that CeDR-Nav derives effective navigation policies for diverse target embodiments from source demonstrations. The main contributions of this article are summarized as follows. We introduce CeDR-Nav, an offline demonstration recasting framework for cross-embodiment mapless navigation that replaces target-specific online RL with offline learning from existing source demonstrations. It learns a navigation policy dedicated to each target embodiment, without requiring target-specific training-environment design. We develop a geometry-consistent recasting method that produces valid training data for the target embodiment. Target-specific policy learning is then adopted to support effective obstacle avoidance on the target embodiment. Extensive quantitative experiments in simulators and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms and navigation tasks validate the effectiveness of CeDR-Nav. Related Work Recent research has increasingly focused on cross-embodiment mapless navigation. Existing works address the embodiment mismatch from two different perspectives. From the policy perspective, on the one hand, some works attempt to reuse trained policies across robot configurations through perceptual representations and deployment-time transformations. Early works developed range-based representations to accommodate differences in sensing and robot configuration zhang2021learn,xie2023drl . Beyond perception, DVST adapts a trained policy to robots with different dimensions through transformations of both observations and actions at deployment, without retraining zhang2025dimension . However, the conservative enclosure used by DVST can lead to suboptimal behaviors when the target and reference robots differ substantially in shape. On the other hand, other works train a universal policy that accommodates multiple embodiments. These methods either incorporate embodiment information into the observation representation zhang2025drl,dezons2026multimodal,zhang2026ea or randomize embodiment parameters during training putta2024embodiment . Despite their applicability to multiple embodiments, reinforcement-learning-based methods such as DRL-DCLP require carefully designed environments and extensive agent--environment interaction zhang2025drl . Moreover, performance may degrade on robot configurations outside the training distribution~ eftekhar2024one . Other approaches, such as CE-Nav, learn target-specific policies through offline pretraining followed by online reinforcement-learning refinement~ yang2026nav , which still requires online agent--environment interaction for each target embodiment. From the data perspective, current methods address the embodiment mismatch by learning from multi-platform navigation experience. Specifically, navigation policies have been learned from data aggregated across multiple robot platforms~ shah2023gnm,shah2023vint,sridhar2024nomad,yang2024pushing,doshi24-crossformer . In addition, robot-conditioned policies have been obtained by augmenting visual navigation data with reconstructed scene geometry~ hirose2023exaug . However, these data-driven methods rely on multi-platform datasets or scene-geometry estimation for experience augmentation~ shah2023gnm,shah2023vint,sridhar2024nomad, yang2024pushing,hirose2023exaug,doshi24-crossformer . In summary, existing approaches to cross-embodiment mapless navigation can be limited by conservative policy transfer, training coverage, or the cost of policy learning and multi-embodiment data preparation. CeDR-Nav focuses on learning a dedicated policy for each target embodiment from existing demonstrations without additional online interaction. title: Failure-Resilient Multi-Robot Coordination with $k$-Connectivity Constrained Submodular Maximization
summary: Multi-robot coordination is essential in applications such as coverage, target tracking, and information gathering, where robots must jointly select actions to maximize team performance. Submodular maximization provides an effective framework for such coordination, and resilient variants further account for robot failures or adversarial removals. However, existing methods typically overlook the impact of robot loss on the communication network, which may disconnect the surviving team and prevent continued coordination. To address this issue, we introduce Resilient $k$-Connected Submodular Maximization, which jointly considers task performance, resilience, and communication connectivity. The resulting feasible family is not a matroid, preventing the direct application of classical curvature-greedy guarantees. We overcome this challenge through a Menger-based connectivity reduction, a connectivity-aware greedy algorithm with a feasibility-preserving fallback, and a new curvature-based analysis that captures the cost of enforcing connectivity through a single factor $ρ$. Our method achieves a worst-case post-failure objective within a factor of $[\max(1-ν_f(\mathcal{I}),h(N,β))]^2 ρ\frac{1}{κ_f}(1-e^{-κ_f})$ of the optimal connectivity-respecting resilient assignment, while recovering the classical unconstrained guarantee in the appropriate limits. Experiments on multi-robot target tracking validate the proposed method and characterize the practical impact of connectivity constraints.

Our method achieves a worst-case post-failure objective within a factor of the optimal connectivity-respecting resilient assignment, while recovering the classical unconstrained guarantee in the appropriate limits. Experiments on multi-robot target tracking validate the proposed method and characterize the practical impact of connectivity constraints. Introduction sec:intro Multi-robot systems provide scalable solutions to applications such as environmental monitoring, target tracking, search and rescue, and collaborative exploration~ marques2015critical, robin2016, queralta2020, burgard2005 . In many of these settings, the robots must coordinate their sensing or motion decisions to maximize a common team objective~ krausegolovin2014 . Submodular set functions provide a natural mathematical framework for such coordination by capturing the principle of diminishing returns: the marginal benefit of adding an additional robot decreases as more robots are already selected. Many commonly used objectives, including mutual information~ krause2008robust , area coverage~ shi2021 , number of observed targets~ zhou2019 , and sensor-measurement entropy~ dames2017 are monotone submodular~ nemhauser1978 . This structure enables computationally efficient greedy algorithms with well-established constant-factor performance guarantees, as reviewed in Section~ sec:rel . Classical submodular maximization, however, typically assumes that the selected robots remain available throughout execution. In practice, robots may be lost due to hardware failures, communication interference, denial-of-service attacks, or other adverse events. This has motivated resilient submodular maximization, where the team is selected so that the objective remains large even after a bounded number of robots are removed~ zhou2019, tzoumas2017, orlin2018 . Existing resilient formulations primarily focus on preserving submodular objective performance after such removals. Yet, critically, robot loss can disrupt the communication network among surviving robots. A team might therefore retain high sensing or coverage capacity after failures while becoming disconnected and rendered unable to continue coordinated operation. Communication connectivity and resilience have both been studied extensively, but largely as separate requirements. In this work, we consider them jointly and ask how to select robot actions so that the team achieves a high submodular objective while remaining connected even after adversarial robot removals. We refer to this problem as Resilient \(k\)-Connected Submodular Maximization (see Fig.~ fig:goal ). The joint treatment is substantially more challenging than simply combining two existing constraints. Resilience requires accounting for the worst-case subset of removed robots, while connectivity is a global property whose feasibility depends on which robots survive. This interaction also breaks key structures used in existing approximation analysis. In the resilient maximization framework of Tzoumas et al.~ tzoumas2017 , robustness is achieved by constructing a sacrificial ``bait'' set of \( \) high-value robots together with a greedily selected remainder. Under a connectivity requirement, however, the adversary determines which robots are removed, and the worst-case removal need not coincide with the bait set. Consequently, enforcing connectivity only on the non-bait robots does not guarantee that the surviving team remains connected. Moreover, the constraint of selecting one trajectory per robot together with a global vertex-connectivity requirement does not form a matroid. As a result, classical curvature-based greedy guarantees cannot be applied directly and must be re-established for the connectivity-constrained resilient setting. We make the following contributions: We formulate resilient submodular maximization under a -vertex-connectivity constraint and show that the family of partial, connectivity-feasible selections is not a matroid (Proposition~ prop:nonmatroid ), identifying precisely why the classical greedy analysis fails to transfer. We introduce a connectivity filter with a rigid-shift fallback across both bait and greedy stages, show it guarantees a feasible, -connected output that survives any removal of size at most regardless of composition (Proposition~ prop:connectivity ), and re-derive the curvature-greedy bound against a connectivity-respecting benchmark (Lemma~ lem:greedy ), isolating the filter's entire cost into a single interpretable constant . We prove a resilient, connectivity-preserving approximation guarantee (Theorem~ thm:main ) and empirically corroborate the algorithm's feasibility, the price of connectivity, and the squared resilience factor (Section~ sec:experiments ). Related Work sec:rel Our problem sits at the intersection of three literatures, summarized in Table~ tab:related . Submodular maximization and curvature. The classical greedy guarantee~ nemhauser1978 was sharpened via curvature~ conforti1984, iyer2013 and extended to matroid and knapsack constraints~ calinescu2011, chekuri2011 . None impose a structural -connectivity requirement on the selected elements. Connected submodular maximization. Connected maximum coverage was introduced by Vandin et al.~ vandin2011 and improved by Hochbaum and Rao~ hochbaum2020 , with follow-up work giving a -approximation in the geometric setting~ huang2019 , an bound~ kuo2014 , and a two-stage heuristic for -connectivity~ shi2021 . None provide a provable guarantee for , with or without an adversary. Resilient submodular maximization. Maximizing against an adversary removing elements was introduced and shown NP-hard by Orlin et al.~ orlin2018 ( guarantee, ). Tzoumas et al.~ tzoumas2017 remove this restriction for any , and Zhou et al.~ zhou2019 extend it to the matroid-constrained multi-robot setting~ krause2008robust . None impose a structural requirement on the surviving graph. No prior work imposes -connectivity as a constraint that holds simultaneously with adversarial resilience, and this is the gap we address. title: ReAT: Residual Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Robot Policies
summary: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.
full_text: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization ( ), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans. Introduction Autoregressive robot policies generate future actions by predicting discrete tokens one at a time~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla . To connect this prediction process to continuous motion, action tokenizers encode future action chunks into token sequences and decode the predicted tokens back into executable actions~ mete2024quest,pertsch2025fast . The encoded sequences provide the policy's training targets, so the tokenizer determines how action information is distributed across tokens and how each token depends on its predecessors~ liu2026oat,dong2026actioncodec . The question is then how to structure these targets so that each token has a clear role in reconstructing the action chunk. Learned action tokenizers use reconstruction objectives to compress action chunks into discrete sequences for policy learning~ lee2024vqbet,mete2024quest . Recent work further shows that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient to characterize these representations, as token organization also affects downstream policy learning~ dong2026actioncodec . Ordering constraints and prefix supervision provide additional structure by encouraging earlier tokens to preserve essential action information and later tokens to add detail~ liu2026oat . However, these objectives do not by themselves explicitly define each token's contribution relative to the actions already reconstructed. That contribution can remain implicit in the learned encoder--decoder mapping, leaving an opportunity to ground successive tokens in the action information still missing from the current reconstruction. The residual between a target action chunk and its current reconstruction provides a concrete description of this missing information. Because it is measured in the reconstructed actions, it reflects what preceding tokens have actually recovered, including the effects of quantization and decoding. Encoding this residual gives the next token an explicit target tied to the reconstruction produced so far. This motivates Residual Action Tokenization ( ), which structures action sequences as successive corrections to an evolving action draft. implements this formulation through explicit reconstruction feedback. During tokenizer training, the encoder maps the remaining reconstruction error to a discrete token, and the decoder uses that token together with the current action draft to produce a learned correction (Figure~ fig:overview ). The updated draft then provides the basis for constructing the next token. Each additional token thus represents a correction to the existing action draft, with Figure~ fig:libero-arms illustrating how reconstruction improves as tokens are added. The resulting residual tokens provide structured prediction targets for observation-conditioned autoregressive policies. We evaluate on 19 manipulation tasks spanning LIBERO, MetaWorld, RoboCasa, and real-world bucket stacking. With 8 tokens, outperforms the evaluated action-tokenization and diffusion-policy baselines in task success on all three simulation benchmarks and the real-world task. On LIBERO, it surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines using only 4 tokens. LIBERO ablations further support the contribution of explicit reconstruction feedback to policy performance and show that prefix supervision enables effective control with shorter token sequences. In summary, our contributions are: We introduce , an action tokenizer that constructs each successive token from the residual left by the decoded prefix, explicitly incorporating quantization and decoding effects into token construction. We combine a draft-conditioned recurrent decoder with prefix reconstruction supervision to turn residual tokens into successive action corrections. Each nonempty prefix reconstructs a complete action chunk, allowing a single autoregressive policy to use different token budgets without retraining. Experiments across three simulation benchmarks and real-world bucket stacking show that 8-token outperforms the evaluated action-tokenization and diffusion-policy baselines in task success. On LIBERO, 4-token also surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines, while mechanism ablations support the contributions of reconstruction feedback and prefix supervision. Related Work Generative robot policies. Robot policies generate actions through continuous representations or discrete token sequences. Continuous approaches include variational action-chunk prediction~ zhao2023act , diffusion-based generation~ chi2023diffusion , and flow-matching action experts~ black2024pi0,nvidia2025groot . Discrete autoregressive policies predict action symbols sequentially~ kim2024openvla , while recent extensions explore parallel continuous-chunk decoding~ kim2025oft and discrete-action pretraining followed by flow-matching post-training~ physicalintelligence2025pi05 . HiFlow further combines scale-wise autoregressive generation with flow matching in continuous action space~ yashima2026hiflow . These approaches primarily advance the mechanisms for generating actions, while leaving open how discrete action targets should be structured to support progressive correction. addresses this representation question by making residual correction the organizing principle of action tokenization, providing autoregressive policies with corrective prediction targets. Action tokenization and ordered prefixes. Learned action tokenizers compress action chunks into quantized representations for policy learning~ lee2024vqbet,mete2024quest,wang2025vqvla , while FAST exploits temporal regularity through frequency-domain coding and byte-pair encoding~ pertsch2025fast . Beyond compression, CARP organizes action representations into scales for next-scale prediction~ gong2025carp , and ActionCodec examines how token structure affects downstream policy optimization~ dong2026actioncodec . Ordered tokenizers use nested dropout to prioritize information in early prefixes~ rippel2014nested , enabling flexible-length reconstruction in image and action domains~ bachmann2025flextok,liu2026oat . Compact representations and ordered prefixes improve the usability of action tokens, but do not by themselves make the remaining action reconstruction error an explicit basis for subsequent token construction. introduces this connection, giving successive tokens a correction target defined by what earlier tokens have actually reconstructed. Residual coding and reconstruction feedback. Residual quantization successively approximates latent features, with applications in image generation~ lee2022rq , neural audio compression~ zeghidour2021soundstream,defossez2022encodec , and action tokenization~ lee2024vqbet,wang2025vqvla,gong2025carp . However, latent approximation error does not directly characterize the error remaining in decoded actions. Recurrent image codecs address the analogous distinction by feeding decoded-output errors back into progressive compression~ toderici2016compression,toderici2016fullresolution . brings this reconstruction-feedback perspective to action tokenization, constructing corrective representations for autoregressive policy learning. title: Forward Dynamics Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) have advanced robotic policy learning by building on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs), respectively. Yet VLAs learn without explicit supervision from future world states, while WAMs that condition actions on predicted futures incur extra inference cost and let visual prediction errors propagate into actions. We present Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models that couples action and future world-state prediction through an action-to-future paradigm. Future prediction is conditioned on action features, never the reverse: end-to-end training lets ground-truth future states supervise the policy through these features, while prediction errors cannot propagate into actions. At inference, FDM skips future generation entirely, avoiding its computational cost. The paradigm is backbone-agnostic, and we instantiate it with both VLM and VGM backbones. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate the effectiveness of FDM across both backbone families, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13% over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.

Yet VLAs learn without explicit supervision from future world states, while WAMs that condition actions on predicted futures incur extra inference cost and let visual prediction errors propagate into actions. We present (FDM), a family of robotic action models that couples action and future world-state prediction through an action-to-future paradigm. Future prediction is conditioned on action features, never the reverse: end-to-end training lets ground-truth future states supervise the policy through these features, while prediction errors cannot propagate into actions. At inference, FDM skips future generation entirely, avoiding its computational cost. The paradigm is backbone-agnostic, and we instantiate it with both VLM and VGM backbones. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate the effectiveness of FDM across both backbone families, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.4 average success rate on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13 over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks. Introduction Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs) offer two complementary foundations for robotic action learning. Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt VLMs to map current observations and task instructions directly to actions~ kim24openvla, intelligence2025pi_, yu2026wall, GR00T , following the action-imitation paradigm~ Diffusionpolicy, zhao2023act ( (a) ). While effective, this paradigm learns what to do without explicit supervision on what happens next, leaving the rich signal in future world states unused. World action models (WAMs) instead build on video backbones to model visual dynamics alongside actions~ hu2024video, feng2025vidar, pai2025mimic, bi2026motus . A prevalent design first predicts future world states and then infers actions from them in an inverse-dynamics manner~ li2026wall, zhao2025cot, ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot, ma2026internvla, agibot2026geact2, tian2024seer ( (b) ). However, future prediction is inherently error-prone, since every visual detail matters across both space and time. Placing it before action prediction means its errors accumulate and amplify into the actions, and future generation also adds substantial inference overhead. Other works predict future frames and actions jointly or in parallel~ ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot, wang2025unified , align policy features with future embeddings~ zheng2025flare , or train an action model and an action-conditioned world model side by side~ cen2025worldvla . These designs motivate studying the specific contribution of future supervision through action features, beyond supervision through shared context. We investigate whether a policy can benefit from future supervision without ever depending on predicted futures. To this end, we introduce Forward Dynamics Models ( ), a family of robotic action models built on an action-to-future learning paradigm. Borrowing the classical notion of forward dynamics~ jordan1992forward, agrawal2016poke , the mapping from state and action to the next state, connects action learning with future world state prediction: given the current world state and task instruction, jointly predicts actions and future world states with asymmetric conditioning. Future prediction reads action features, while action prediction cannot access future information. The model is trained end to end, so the future-prediction loss backpropagates through these action features into the policy. Action-to-future specifies this one-way information dependency within joint prediction. r 0.50 1bp ! Our contributions are threefold: (i) We introduce , a novel family of robotic action models that learns in an action-to-future manner during training, with future supervision flowing into the policy through its action features, and requires no future prediction at inference; (ii) We build VLM- and VGM-based instantiations of , demonstrating its backbone flexibility; (iii) Experiments in simulation and on real robots show that achieves strong or competitive performance across VLM- and VGM-based settings, and analysis shows that it avoids the error propagation of future-conditioned designs. Related work Vision-language-action models. VLA models adapt pretrained vision-language models to predict robot actions~ wang2026qwen, yuan2026qwen, ye2026starvla, black2024pi_0, yang2026abot, liu2026streampi, yu2026affordancevla, zhang2026onevla, zheng2026x, qu2025spatialvla, internvlam1, internvla_a1, shukor2025smolvla, wang2025vlaadapter . Recent approaches also predict future observations or their latent representations~ cen2025worldvla, ma2026internvla, cheang2024gr, cen2025rynnvla, lv2025f1, zhang2026uam, hu2026bagelvla, kang2026xtokenizer, yang2025mantis, zhang2025upvla , using future prediction as a learning objective or an input to action generation, as in visual chain-of-thought policies~ zhao2025cot . Our builds on and conditions future prediction on action features and the current context, establishing an action-to-future dependency. World action models. Video models provide visual dynamics representations for robot control~ hacohen2024ltx, ali2025world, wan2025wan . WAMs use these representations to condition action decoding~ hu2024video, pai2025mimic, ma2026dit4dit or jointly predict video and actions~ bi2026motus, ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot, lingbot-va2026, wang2026openwam, zhou2026zerowam, tian2026vtwam, zhu2025uwm . Extensions combine predicted outcomes with value estimates for planning~ bi2026motus2, kim2026cosmos, chen2026mvwam , while asynchronous designs improve efficiency through different denoising budgets or prediction horizons~ guo2026xwam, cai2026aha . Our places future prediction downstream of action features, keeping the action path independent of predicted video. Deployment therefore omits future-video computation while retaining current-observation processing. Joint predictive models use visual supervision for action learning~ wang2025unified, ma2026geosem, ye2026gigaworld, xu2026nextforcing, wu2023gr1, zheng2025flare, won2025dust . UVA and Fast-WAM also enable action-only deployment via separate video--action decoders and structured attention, respectively~ li2503unified, yuan2026fastwam . FDM conditions future prediction on action features and backpropagates prediction errors into them. Our context-only and stop-gradient controls isolate action conditioning and backward supervision, respectively. title: What Visual Representations Do World Action Models Need?
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) inherit powerful priors from pretrained video generation models, but their variational autoencoder (VAE) representations are optimized for visual reconstruction rather than manipulation. External visual representations can improve manipulation, but existing methods couple representation choices with different integration mechanisms, obscuring their individual effects. We systematically compare visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations under controlled settings. Our study yields three main findings. First, strong general-purpose visual representations provide broader robustness gains and can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities. Second, channel-wise joint prediction achieves the highest average success rate; further analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and the action expert's effective use of added visual information contribute to its gains. Third, additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they contribute beyond existing representations, as the same source can help one combination but harm another. However, even the best evaluated composition provides a smaller additional gain than the initial improvement from adding a strong general-purpose representation to the VAE-only baseline. We instantiate the resulting Representation Recipe as R$^2$-WAM. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop with an 84.7% success rate and reaches 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over the VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Taken together, these findings suggest that future work should prioritize stronger general-purpose visual representations and more effective mechanisms for integrating them into WAMs, with feature composition serving as a supplementary route to improvement.

Introduction World Action Models (WAMs) adapt pretrained video generation models to robot control by jointly predicting future video and actions. This allows robot policies to draw on the visual structure and temporal dynamics learned through large-scale video pretraining, as demonstrated by DreamZero~ dreamzero , LingBot-VA~ lingbotva , and Fast-WAM~ fastwam . Along with these priors, WAMs inherit the latent space of their variational autoencoders (VAEs). The inherited VAE is optimized for visual reconstruction~ wan , but how well its representations support robot manipulation remains unclear. Its reconstruction objective does not explicitly prioritize manipulation-relevant information, such as object semantics and spatial relationships. Recent studies augment WAMs with external visual features and report improvements in manipulation performance and robustness~ agra,robustwam,geosemwam . However, these methods select different representations based on prior assumptions about which visual capabilities WAMs lack. Systematic comparisons across representation types remain limited, leaving unclear which visual representations best support robot manipulation in WAMs. Beyond representation choice, WAM performance also depends on the mechanism used to integrate external features into the model~ fourdwam . A further question is whether combining more representations leads to continued performance gains. External features can be integrated through representation alignment~ repa,agra , action conditioning~ stwam , or joint prediction~ flexpi . Existing studies often couple selected representations with specific integration designs~ agra,flexpi,mecowam , making the effects of representation choice and integration mechanism difficult to disentangle across methods. Besides, the diverse demands of manipulation---including semantics, geometry, object extent, motion, and interaction---suggest that different representations may be needed. Yet additional sources may also introduce redundant information or interference during optimization. Whether and when different feature combinations improve WAM performance therefore remains an empirical question. To address these questions, we systematically study visual representations in WAMs, focusing on capabilities, integration mechanisms, and composition. Using a common WAM backbone built on a pretrained video generation model, we compare diverse visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and multiple source combinations under a shared training protocol. Our study addresses three research questions (RQs): 0pt 0pt Which visual representations improve WAM performance? Which feature injection mechanism yields the greatest performance gains from external features? Does combining more feature sources consistently improve WAM performance? Our controlled comparisons yield three findings that guide the selection, integration, and composition of external visual representations for WAMs. (1) General-purpose visual representations should be the default choice for augmenting WAMs. They can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities---even under perturbations relevant to those capabilities---while providing broader robustness gains. (2) Channel-wise joint prediction yields the largest average gains across matched sources. Our analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and effective use of the added visual information by the action expert contribute to these gains and should guide future integration designs. (3) Additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they add beyond the existing representations. The same source can improve one combination but provide little benefit or even reduce performance in another. Although feature composition can provide further gains, these are limited compared with the initial improvement. Feature composition should therefore serve as a supplementary route to improvement. Our contributions are threefold: 0pt 0pt A controlled study of visual representations in WAMs. We systematically compare representation sources, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations within a common WAM backbone and shared training protocol, enabling controlled comparisons of their effects on manipulation performance and robustness. Empirical guidance for WAM representation design. We derive practical recommendations for selecting, integrating, and combining external visual representations. These findings motivate future research on stronger general-purpose visual foundation models and more efficient and effective mechanisms for integrating their representations into WAMs. R -WAM and validation beyond the controlled study. We instantiate these findings as a Representation Recipe for WAMs, termed R -WAM. We validate the effectiveness of the recipe across different WAM formulations on LIBERO-Plus, and further demonstrate improvements over the corresponding VAE-only baselines on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop and RoboTwin~2.0, as well as in real-world robot experiments. Related Work World Action Models. WAMs learn action prediction alongside future visual dynamics. DreamZero~ dreamzero transfers a pretrained video diffusion backbone to joint video--action generation, and LingBot-VA~ lingbotva combines autoregressive diffusion with closed-loop visual feedback. Fast-WAM~ fastwam shows that video co-training can benefit control even when future video generation is omitted at inference. Other studies modify the visual prediction space or its supervision. LDA-1B~ lda1b learns dynamics in DINO feature space, while LaWAM~ lawam conditions action generation on predicted latent visual subgoals. RepWAM~ repwam and LingBot-VA~2.0~ lingbotva2 learn semantically aligned visual--action tokenizers. ST-WAM~ stwam diagnoses failures under visual shifts and combines DINO future prediction and history retrieval with VAE dynamics. Robust-WAM~ robustwam aligns queries in the action stream with future semantic features while retaining the VAE generation pathway. Flex- ~ flexpi jointly denoises RGB latents, 3D pointmaps, DINO features, and actions, supporting different combinations of input and prediction streams at deployment. These studies demonstrate the effectiveness of specific visual representations within their respective WAM designs, but systematic comparisons are still needed to identify which features complement the capabilities that WAMs inherit from pretrained video generators. Visual Representations. Pretraining objectives shape the information captured by visual representations. Visual self-supervision has produced encoders such as DINOv3~ dinov3 , VC-1~ vc1 , LingBot-Vision~ lingbotvision , VideoMAE~V2~ videomaev2 , and V-JEPA~2.1~ vjepa21 . Language-associated approaches include image--text models such as CLIP~ clip and SigLIP~2~ siglip2 , as well as multimodal language models such as Qwen3.5~ qwen35 . Other pretraining objectives target segmentation with SAM~3~ sam3 , geometry with VGGT- ~ vggtomega , and interaction-related information with HRP~ hrp and DynaFLIP~ dynaflip . UniTok~ unitok and C-RADIOv4~ cradiov4 further combine multiple learning objectives or teacher models within a single representation. These approaches provide different but overlapping visual capabilities, but how their pretraining emphases translate into manipulation gains in WAMs remains an empirical question. Study Design Base WAM Architecture sec:study-setting Given RGB observations, a language instruction, and the current robot state, the base WAM jointly predicts future-video latents and an action chunk . The model comprises a video expert initialized from Wan~2.2~ wan and a separate action expert. The experts interact through joint attention with an asymmetric mask: action tokens attend to both video and action tokens, whereas video tokens attend only to video tokens. Both experts attend to T5-encoded language features~ t5 through cross-attention and are additionally conditioned on the robot state and flow time. Throughout, denotes the current observation, indexes the future sequence, and denotes flow time. Thus denotes current-frame VAE latents, and denotes future-video latents at flow time . We train the model with a weighted sum of video and action flow-matching losses~ flowmatching : where denotes the modality-specific mean-squared error between predicted and target flow velocities, and weights the action loss. At inference, future-video latents and actions are initialized from noise and jointly denoised. Visual Representations sec:feature-sources We compare thirteen pretrained visual encoders, using their pretraining objectives as an initial indication of the information their representations capture and the visual capabilities they may support. All encoders remain frozen during WAM training and extract representations from the RGB observations available to the base WAM. We consider six pretraining emphases: Visual self-supervision: VC-1~ vc1 and VideoMAE~V2~ videomaev2 learn visual structure through masked image or video reconstruction. V-JEPA~2.1~ vjepa21 predicts visual features to learn spatial and temporal relationships; DINOv3~ dinov3 uses self-distillation to learn semantic and dense spatial features; and LingBot-Vision~ lingbotvision emphasizes fine spatial structure through masked boundary modeling. Language-associated pretraining: SigLIP~2~ siglip2 combines image--text alignment with captioning and self-supervised objectives to learn semantic and dense visual features. title: Human2Dex: Dexterous Robot Learning from Wrist-Centric Human Demonstrations
summary: Collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations for each robot hand requires repeated task-specific data acquisition. We ask whether one shared corpus of natural human demonstrations can instead serve as a reusable data interface for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot. We present Human2Dex, a wrist-centric human demonstration interface that separates shared human observation and motion semantics from embodiment-specific execution. It aligns observations through local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation with consistent structural semantics across human and robot observations. It constructs executable supervision by retargeting fused human hand motion to each target hand, and introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation (GPIR) to express tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket. The corpus is converted into separate training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, while action labels, normalization, training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain hand-specific. Across six real-world tasks, Human2Dex achieves 109/120 (90.8%) successes on Linker O6 and 97/120 (80.8%) on Wuji. Across both hands, Human-Raw achieves 63/240 (26.3%) successes, whereas the complete Human2Dex configuration achieves 206/240 (85.8%). These results support the use of wrist-centric human demonstrations as a reusable interface across calibrated dexterous hands while retaining embodiment-specific policy learning. The project website is publicly available at https://human2dex.pages.dev/.

Introduction Dexterous manipulation policies require demonstrations that jointly capture arm motion, high-DoF hand configuration, and contact-rich task progress. Acquiring such demonstrations separately for each target hand is costly and difficult to scale. Many existing systems make data collection more compatible with robot deployment through instrumented motion capture, robot-like interfaces, or wearable hardware~ dexcap,umi,legato,dexumi,realdexumi,dexop . These interfaces can reduce the correspondence burden during transfer, but they often establish robot compatibility partly through the acquisition setup, control interface, or embodiment-aware mapping. When the target embodiment changes, the corresponding conversion or embodiment-specific setup must still be established for the new hand. This motivates a higher-level question: how can a reusable human demonstration interface convert the same human manipulation episodes into executable training data for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot? We study this question from a wrist-centric perspective. Head-mounted egocentric video provides scalable human data and broad scene context~ egomimic,egodex,humanego,vividex,unidex , whereas a wrist-mounted camera provides local hand--object observations that more closely correspond to the eye-in-hand views used for close-range dexterous control. This similarity in observation arrangement makes wrist-centric acquisition a natural starting point for demonstration reuse. However, matching the observation arrangement does not by itself establish correspondence between human and robot data. The two settings can still differ in hand appearance, articulated structure, kinematics, command spaces, and grasp-related geometry. Even under wrist-to-eye-in-hand alignment, three linked mismatches remain. First, human and robot hands differ in appearance and articulated structure, so the same visual content does not automatically provide the same structural semantics. Prior work has addressed this issue through appearance adaptation, robot-hand rendering, and structured hand representations~ mirage,dexumi,dexpilot,anyteleop . Second, human motion is not itself an executable command for a target hand: Linker O6 and Wuji have different kinematic structures, degrees of freedom, joint limits, and native action spaces. Human-to-robot retargeting and embodiment-aware motion mapping therefore remain necessary for constructing target-specific supervision~ dexcap,dexpilot,dexh2r,mocaprobot . Third, even after observation semantics are aligned and executable supervision is constructed, a policy must infer how the task object is positioned relative to the hand's current grasp configuration. Image-centered object coordinates indicate where an object appears, but do not directly express its relation to the closing hand. Existing work has explored hand--object and functional grasp representations for grasp synthesis, contact modeling, and perception~ functionalgrasp,drograsp,humanego,contactpose,hot3d . Thus, structural correspondence supports observation interpretation, executable supervision supports target-hand policy learning, and an explicit object--hand relation can provide a more direct interaction cue, particularly when grasp alignment matters. We present , a reusable wrist-centric human demonstration interface that shares human demonstrations and their observation and motion semantics across embodiments while retaining target-hand-specific executable supervision and policy learning. To align observations, combines mask-guided local hand-appearance adaptation with a shared 21-point hand representation, establishing consistent structural semantics for human and robot observations. To construct executable supervision, fused human hand motion is retargeted separately to each calibrated target hand, producing native action labels for Linker O6 and Wuji. To represent interaction geometry, introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation ( ), which expresses tracked task objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket defined by the thumb--index grasp center. The same human demonstration corpus is therefore converted into separate training sets for the two target hands, while action labels, normalization statistics, policy training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain specific to each hand--task pair. No task demonstrations are collected with the target robot hands. We evaluate whether this interface supports human-data reuse across embodiments under real-world dexterous manipulation. A matched Linker O6--Croissant study examines wrist- versus head-centric observation, while the main evaluation covers Linker O6 and Wuji across six real-world tasks. Additional reference-frame and task-wise analyses examine selected design choices and the task dependence of interaction grounding. Our contributions are: A reusable human demonstration interface for multiple dexterous embodiments. Human2Dex converts one wrist-centric human demonstration corpus into separate hand-specific training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, allowing each hand to learn an independent policy without collecting task demonstrations on the target robots. A grasp-centered interaction representation for policy conditioning. The Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation expresses tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket, complementing structural observation alignment and target-specific action supervision with an explicit object--hand relation. A two-hand, six-task physical evaluation with targeted design analyses. We evaluate the complete interface on two calibrated dexterous hands and six real-world tasks, complemented by controlled comparisons of observation viewpoint and object-reference coordinates and task-wise analysis of interaction-grounding behavior. Related Work Learning Robot Policies from Human Demonstrations Human-data interfaces differ in where compatibility between human demonstrations and robot execution is established. Portable robot-like tools, motion-capture systems, teleoperation platforms, and wearable interfaces introduce deployment-relevant visual, kinematic, or contact signals during collection~ mimicplay,umi,legato,dexcap,holodex,anyteleop,opentelevision,dexumi,realdexumi,dexop,dexvitac . Recent UMI-style systems extend demonstration interfaces toward richer physical sensing and broader motion coordination. OmniUMI~ omniumi integrates visual, tactile, and force-related sensing within a handheld interface for contact-rich manipulation. BifrostUMI~ bifrostumi combines lightweight VR tracking with UMI-inspired grippers to collect robot-free demonstrations, from which a policy predicts human keypoint trajectories that are retargeted for humanoid whole-body execution. Other approaches preserve more natural human behavior through egocentric video, human play, or human--robot co-training, while some convert human data through simulation or limited robot data~ egomimic,egodex,humanego,motiontrans,vividex,unidex,dexwild,robotictelekinesis,dextransfer,dexmimicgen . Among the closest interface-based approaches, UMI establishes deployment-compatible observations and actions through a portable robot-like gripper, while DexUMI~ dexumi further reduces the human--robot kinematic gap using a wearable hand exoskeleton together with robot-hand visual adaptation. RealDexUMI~ realdexumi instead shares the dexterous end-effector and sensing modules between demonstration collection and deployment, thereby minimizing end-effector mismatch. HumanEgo~ humanego follows a different route by lifting egocentric human video into an explicit entity-level hand--object interaction representation. Human2Dex studies a complementary setting: the source remains wrist-centric bare-hand manipulation, and embodiment adaptation is performed after collection to construct native action supervision and separate policies for dexterous hands with different kinematics and action spaces. Visual and Kinematic Cross-Embodiment Alignment Cross-embodiment alignment involves both visual identity and articulated motion. Visual adaptation methods reduce differences between source and target hands through cross-painting, robot-hand rendering, or fine-grained hand--object segmentation~ mirage,dexumi,egohos . Hand estimators and teleoperation systems provide structured landmarks or mappings for transferring human motion under different morphologies and kinematic constraints~ mediapipe,hamer,dexpilot,anyteleop,dexh2r,mocaprobot,crossdex . Human2Dex uses a 21-point hand representation as an intermediate interface for shared observation semantics and motion fusion, while retaining embodiment-specific retargeting, action labels, and policy checkpoints for each target hand. Thus, the shared representation defines data semantics rather than a common robot action space. Object-Centric and Functional Grasp Representations Object-centric representations provide relational information beyond isolated hand or object states. FunctionalGrasp and D(R,O) Grasp use semantic hand--object structure or robot--object descriptions for grasp generation, while ContactPose and HOT3D support contact modeling and egocentric hand--object tracking~ functionalgrasp,drograsp,contactpose,hot3d . Human2Dex uses the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation ( ) for a narrower purpose: sequential wrist-view policy control. GPIR expresses tracked task objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket and retains object scale and tracking reliability. It is therefore a low-dimensional grasp-relative interaction cue, rather than a general object reconstruction, universal grasp representation, or complete contact model. title: Grounded-Dreamer: Robot Learning from World Model Synthetic Data with Physical Grounding
summary: Scaling robot manipulation policies requires large amounts of diverse, action-labeled data, yet collecting such data in the real world remains expensive and difficult to scale. Existing methods either depend on human teleoperation, rely on simulation with limited visual realism, or use human videos that lack embodiment-specific annotations. In this paper, we introduce Grounded-Dreamer, a framework for synthesizing physically grounded robot manipulation data with video world models while avoiding human teleoperation demonstrations. Grounded-Dreamer combines the visual realism of generative video models with simulator physics engines. Starting from a small set of real images depicting robot task initial states, our method automatically reconstructs task-relevant objects and camera geometry, aligns them in simulation, and collects physically valid trajectories. These trajectories are used to post-train both a video world model and an inverse dynamics model, enabling the generation of visually realistic robot manipulation videos and corresponding robot actions from real images. To filter physically implausible rollouts, Grounded-Dreamer replays generated trajectories in the reconstructed simulation and retains only those that successfully complete the tasks. The real-world robot policies are trained solely on the grounded synthetic trajectories without any human demonstrations. Empirical results in real-world tasks demonstrate that Grounded-Dreamer can synthesize physically grounded data and substantially facilitate policy learning without requiring human teleoperation effort.
