Project Page: . Introduction Intro Building general-purpose robot policies capable of performing diverse manipulation tasks across varied environments requires large-scale, high-quality data. However, robot data is difficult to scale, and existing sources present a challenging trade-off between quality and quantity. Real-world teleoperation provides high-fidelity demonstrations but is limited by intensive human labor. While UMI data collection~ chi2024universal, xu2025dexumi improves efficiency, there remains a need for manual operations. Conversely, simulation data offers inexpensive, action-labeled trajectories but is hindered by the sim-to-real visual gap. Human-centric videos are abundant and diverse, yet they lack the robot action annotations essential for direct policy training. Consequently, the field remains trapped between costly manual collection and the limitations of imperfect proxy data. This dilemma motivates the pursuit of scalable robot data synthesis. Prior efforts such as DemoGen~ xue2025demogen and MimicGen~ mandlekar2023mimicgen have attempted to augment existing datasets by diversifying robot demonstrations; however, these methods still rely on human-collected trajectories as initial seeds. Other approaches, including RoboGen~ wang2023robogen and GenSim~ wang2023gensim,hua2024gensim2 , leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) and simulators to automate task generation and trajectory collection. While these frameworks significantly reduce human intervention, the resulting data remains confined to simulation, leaving the visual sim-to-real discrepancy unresolved. Generative video world models offer a potential alternative. Trained on internet-scale data, these models capture rich visual and world dynamics priors, enabling the generation of manipulation rollouts. When paired with an Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM), such videos can be converted into action-labeled trajectories. However, pretrained models like Cosmos~ agarwal2025cosmos are primarily trained on human-centric videos. Directly applying them to robotic tasks often results in "hallucinated" physics, such as inconsistent object motions or non-physical contacts. In this work, we introduce Grounded-Dreamer, a framework that synthesizes high-fidelity robot manipulation data without a single human teleoperation demonstration. Our core insight is to link the visual realism of generative world models with the grounding of physics simulators. We first build an automatic real-to-sim pipeline that calibrates camera poses, reconstructs task-relevant objects, and aligns them with the scene. Within this reconstructed simulator, we automatically collect diverse trajectories by leveraging the simulator's ground-truth states. These grounded trajectories serve as the foundation for post-training both the video world model and the IDM. During data synthesis, the post-trained world model generates visually realistic manipulation videos from real-world initial images, while the IDM extracts the corresponding robot actions. To guarantee physical validity, we implement a closed-loop verification step: replaying the inferred trajectories within the reconstructed simulation. This process filters out physically inconsistent generations, ensuring that only successful, grounded trajectories are used for further policy training. We evaluate Grounded-Dreamer across seven diverse real-world manipulation tasks, spanning short-to-long horizon sequences and sophisticated tool use. Our empirical results demonstrate that policies trained exclusively on grounded synthetic data achieve performance competitive with those trained on real-world human demonstrations. Furthermore, owing to the inherent visual diversity and our targeted augmentation strategies, Grounded-Dreamer significantly outperforms real-data policies in out-of-distribution scenarios, showcasing robust zero-shot generalization across novel scenarios. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose Grounded-Dreamer, a data synthesis framework that eliminates the need for human demonstrations by linking video world models with simulator physics engines. We introduce an automated real-to-sim reconstruction and collection pipeline, enabling data synthesis that maintains both high visual fidelity and strict physical grounding. We demonstrate through extensive real-world experiments that our grounded synthetic data effectively facilitates policy learning, achieving robust performance across diverse scenarios through purely autonomous data generation. Related Work Robot Data Synthesis Simulation has been widely used to generate diverse conditions for robot data. Early sim-to-real work relied on visual or dynamics randomization tobin2017domain,peng2018sim . Later environments extended this idea to broader robot-learning settings: RLBench standardizes manipulation tasks james2020rlbench , robosuite and SAPIEN provide modular robot-object simulation platforms zhu2020robosuite,xiang2020sapien , and Isaac Gym and RoboCasa emphasize scalable physics or household manipulation makoviychuk2021isaacgym,nasiriany2024robocasa . Recent generative frameworks, such as GenSim, GenSim2, and RoboGen, use language or foundation models to generate tasks, scenes, demonstrations, or supervision wang2023gensim,hua2024gensim2,wang2023robogen . Their data quality, however, still depends on generated task programs, planners, solvers, or simulator assumptions. For manipulation, local grounding outweighs global visual realism. Incorrect object pose, axis, or camera frame can make a plausible trajectory physically misleading. 6D pose estimation and reconstruction recover task-relevant structure from real observations hodan2018bop,wen2024foundationpose , while structure-from-motion, NeRF, and 3D Gaussian Splatting facilitate view-consistent geometry or appearance schoenberger2016sfm,mildenhall2020nerf,kerbl2023gaussian . Another route reuses collected trajectories. A series of studies adapt human demonstrations to new object configurations mandlekar2023mimicgen , corrective interventions~ hoque2024intervengen , long-horizon skills~ garrett2024skillmimicgen , and bimanual dexterous manipulation jiang2024dexmimicgen . DemoGen further adapts one demonstration and edits the 3D scene to synthesize new observations xue2025demogen . DROID and Open X-Embodiment instead scale real robot data directly, but require substantial collection effort khazatsky2024droid,oneill2024openx . Grounded-Dreamer lies between these directions: it grounds synthetic data in real scene-object inputs, preserves physical structure through simulation, and expands the distribution with world-model rollouts. World Models for Robot Learning World models were originally developed as learned dynamics models for predicting future states before acting ha2018worldmodels,hafner2019dreamer,hafner2023dreamerv3 . In robotics, visual foresight leveraged video prediction for model-based control by selecting actions whose predicted futures match a goal finn2017visualforesight . More recently, diffusion-based video models have enabled realistic rollout generation from images or text ho2022videodiffusion , while systems such as UniSim and Genie move toward controllable visual worlds yang2023unisim,bruce2024genie . However, visually plausible videos are not directly usable robot training trajectories, as they often lack actions, embodiment constraints, and physically reliable interactions. DreamGen adapts video world models to robot learning by recovering pseudo actions through latent action or inverse dynamics models jang2025dreamgen , while GigaBrain-0 further scales world-model-generated data for VLA training gigabrain2025 . Prior works have also explored inverse dynamics models to bridge observations and actions agrawal2016learning,pathak2018zeroshot . Once converted into action-conditioned trajectories, such generated data can train policies including Diffusion Policy, RT-2, and chi2023diffusion,zitkovich2023rt2,black2024pi0 . Grounded-Dreamer builds on this line of work by coupling world-model rollouts with reconstructed scene inputs and simulation-based grounding to ensure both visual realism and physical consistency before policy learning. Methodology sec:method We introduce Grounded-Dreamer, an autonomous pipeline designed to generate verifiable, high-fidelity synthetic data for scalable robot policy learning without the need for human-collected real-world trajectories. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:pipeline , starting from a small set of reference images captured in the real world, Grounded-Dreamer synthesizes massive, validated datasets through an automated workflow, which consists of four core stages: (i) Task-Oriented Simulation Reconstruction, where we reconstruct physically consistent simulation scenes and task-relevant objects; (ii) Sim Data Collection and Interaction-Aware Masking, where simulation data is automatically collected to fine-tune Cosmos-Predict 2.5 and the IDM with interaction-aware masking; (iii) Initial Frame Synthesis, where the Nano Banana-based pipeline aligns real-sim composites and generates augmented initial images to enhance diversity and visual fidelity; (iv) Data Synthesis and Closed-Loop Verification, where synthetic trajectories are generated from real-world initial frames and validated via simulation verification. Task-Oriented Simulation Reconstruction subsec:reconstruction Scene Reconstruction. Our framework is built upon the Lehome simulation environment~ li2025lehome . Given the workspace boundaries and the relative pose of the robot base, we construct a lightweight simulation scene containing the robotic arm and workspace table. To align the simulated and real-world viewpoints, we perform extrinsic calibration using the FEEPE framework~ wu2025foundation and directly adopt the intrinsic parameters of the physical camera. This process ensures consistent fields of view (FOVs) between simulation and reality, providing a reliable geometric foundation for data grounding. For efficiency, we reuse off-the-shelf Lehome assets for tabletop textures and environmental backgrounds, since pixel-level fidelity in task-irrelevant regions is unnecessary for our pipeline. title: Prediction-Informed Landing Window Planning for UAV Landing on USV in High Sea States
summary: Autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) on unmanned surface vehicle (USV) is difficult in high sea states. Existing hierarchical landing methods often infer future USV motion only implicitly from short observation histories, which limits their ability to adapt to severe and rapidly changing sea conditions. This paper presents a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework. A pretrained model is developed to explicitly predict the USV attitude during high-level landing decisions. The prediction helps identify suitable landing windows and choose the right touchdown time, while a conventional low-level flight controller maintains UAV stability and tracks motion commands. To evaluate the framework under realistic disturbances, a real-sim validation setup is constructed in which USV-motion data collected in real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo USV. The experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using explicit attitude prediction to improve landing-window selection and support timing-aware UAV landing planning in rapidly varying marine environments.

Existing hierarchical landing methods often infer future USV motion only implicitly from short observation histories, which limits their ability to adapt to severe and rapidly changing sea conditions. This paper presents a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework. A pretrained model is developed to explicitly predict the USV attitude during high-level landing decisions. The prediction helps identify suitable landing windows and choose the right touchdown time, while a conventional low-level flight controller maintains UAV stability and tracks motion commands. To evaluate the framework under realistic disturbances, a real-sim validation setup is constructed in which USV-motion data collected in real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo USV. The experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using explicit attitude prediction to improve landing-window selection and support timing-aware UAV landing planning in rapidly varying marine environments. UAV landing, UAV-USV, high sea states, attitude prediction, hierarchical control, real-sim Introduction Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and unmanned surface vehicle (USV) are increasingly used as a complementary robotic team in search and rescue, offshore inspection, environmental monitoring, and maritime surveillance. UAV provide rapid aerial observation and wide-area coverage, whereas USV provide endurance and direct access to the water surface. Reliable autonomous landing is therefore essential for sustained UAV-USV operation because it enables UAV recovery, recharging, and redeployment without continuous human intervention. Landing a UAV on a moving USV is particularly challenging in high sea states gupta2023landing . Wave-induced heave, roll, and pitch continuously change the relative pose and velocity between the vehicle and the deck. During the final descent, USV attitude can vary substantially within the time required for the UAV to reach the deck, so a touchdown condition that is safe at the current instant may become unfavorable before contact. Wind, sensing uncertainty, and control delay further reduce the available touchdown margin. The landing problem therefore involves not only stabilizing the vehicle and tracking the USV, but also choosing a touchdown time that is consistent with the future motion of the deck. This temporal decision becomes more difficult as sea conditions become more dynamic. A controller that reacts only to the current USV attitude may begin to descend when the platform is temporarily favorable but fail to anticipate the rapid closure of the corresponding landing window. Conversely, an overly conservative controller may miss short favorable intervals and increase the recovery time. These observations motivate a landing architecture that preserves reliable low-level flight control while providing the high-level decision layer with explicit information about future platform attitude. In this paper, we develop a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework for UAV landing on USV in high sea states. A pretrained temporal model forecasts the short-term evolution of USV attitude, and the predicted attitude is used to evaluate feasible touchdown windows and guide the high-level landing decision. A conventional low-level flight controller remains responsible for vehicle stabilization and motion tracking. The framework is evaluated in a real-to-simulation setting, where USV-motion data collected under real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo landing platform. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: A prediction-informed hierarchical landing framework is developed by coupling explicit platform-attitude forecasting with high-level landing-window planning and conventional low-level flight control. A pretrained temporal prediction model is introduced to provide future attitude information for touchdown-window assessment under rapidly varying sea states. A real-to-simulation validation setup is established by replaying platform-motion data collected in real sea conditions on a MuJoCo platform, enabling evaluation under realistic disturbance patterns. Related Work Learning-based methods have been investigated to improve the adaptability of UAV landing under uncertain platform motion. Compared with controllers that depend on an accurate analytical model, such as NMPC-based cooperative UAV-USV tracking and landing li2023nmpc and synchronized-motion-based cooperative landing li2022synchronized , reinforcement learning (RL) can learn a feedback policy from repeated interaction with a simulator or physical system. Polvara et al. explored end-to-end UAV landing through deep reinforcement learning, mapping visual observations to landing actions polvara2018toward . Rodriguez-Ramos et al. extended deep RL to landing on moving platforms, demonstrating that a learned policy can adapt its control behavior to platform motion rodriguez2019deep . Subsequent work considered autonomous multi-rotor landing and vision-based ship landing under disturbance, further showing the potential of learning-based policies in dynamic landing scenarios goldschmid2024reinforcement , saj2022robust . Despite this adaptability, fully end-to-end learning is difficult to deploy in safety-critical flight systems. High-dimensional visual inputs, the simultaneous learning of stabilization and landing decisions, and the absence of an explicit temporal representation can increase training complexity and reduce interpretability. These limitations have motivated hierarchical formulations, in which a learned policy makes high-level landing decisions while a conventional flight controller maintains attitude stability and tracks motion commands. WaveLander is representative of this direction: its recurrent RL policy uses a compact platform-relative observation and outputs a scalar vertical-velocity reference, while the low-level controller handles stabilization and tracking li2026wavelander . The main limitation of current hierarchical learning-based landing methods is their limited awareness of future landing windows. In WaveLander, timing-aware behavior is learned from short observation histories, recurrent hidden states, and attitude-aware reward shaping. The policy can therefore slow down, hold, or retreat when the current platform condition is unfavorable, but its prediction of future platform motion remains implicit. Under rapidly changing high-sea-state conditions, this reactive mechanism may identify an unfavorable touchdown condition only after a safe landing interval has started to close. The policy is consequently required to infer both the platform trend and the appropriate touchdown timing from limited short-term evidence. Explicit platform-motion prediction provides a complementary solution to this limitation. Li et al. used recurrent prediction to estimate USV attitude and exploit favorable motion phases during cooperative landing li2022synchronized . Such methods demonstrate that future attitude information can support temporal coordination, but the prediction module is commonly coupled to a specific synchronization or tracking controller. The predicted motion is not necessarily exposed as a general landing-window interface for a hierarchical planner. In contrast, the present work treats attitude prediction as an independent high-level information source: the predicted attitude evolution is used to assess candidate touchdown windows and guide the descent decision, while the conventional low-level flight-control stack is retained. This formulation separates prediction, landing-window planning, and stabilization, and is intended to improve temporal awareness without requiring the learned component to directly control UAV actuators. Methodology System Overview As shown in Fig.~ fig:architecture , the system adopts a prediction-informed hierarchical control architecture. USV motion data collected under real sea conditions are used to pretrain a model that predicts short-term future attitude changes. The motion is then loaded into the MuJoCo environment to drive the dynamic platform. The current deck tilt, tilt rate, UAV relative height, relative vertical velocity, and predicted attitude are combined to form the observation input to the PPO policy. PPO outputs a continuous vertical-velocity command, while the low-level controller allocates the motor thrusts. The reward function jointly considers horizontal alignment, descent progress, touchdown safety, and platform attitude, guiding the UAV to select an appropriate landing time. Pretrained Module The prediction module is an encoder-decoder LSTM trained before RL optimization. It uses real USV motion data sampled at 0.1~s. A history of 20 samples is used to predict the next 10 samples, providing a 1.0~s forecast: The LSTM has 256 hidden units and a linear output layer. Each input window is normalized independently and restored after prediction. The model is trained with MSE loss, while MAE is used for monitoring. Adam, weight decay, learning-rate scheduling, and early stopping are adopted. During online inference, the forecast is updated every 0.1~s and sent to the RL environment. Prediction-Informed Model The observation combines the current landing state with the predicted deck motion: The first four elements describe the current relative height, relative vertical velocity, platform tilt, and tilt rate. The remaining ten elements provide the predicted roll sequence. The PPO policy maps this observation to a continuous relative vertical-velocity command: The predicted sequence improves awareness of future landing windows and contributes to reward evaluation, but it does not directly replace the policy action. As the high-level decision layer, the PPO policy outputs only the vertical velocity reference. The controller then computes the desired acceleration and thrust direction, generates the desired attitude and moments, and allocates the resulting wrench to the four motors. Reward Design The reward is implemented as an additive multi-component function: The progress term tracks a height-dependent target descent velocity. The target is faster at high altitude and gradually approaches zero near the contact height: The touchdown term is activated when ~m and ~m. title: Beyond Actions: Learning Future Operation Targets for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Actions specify what a robot should execute, but do not describe what those commands will achieve. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies nevertheless learn primarily by predicting action chunks from images, language, and state. We introduce Action--Future Coupled Effect Learning (AFCE), which makes a future-grounded physical Effect the policy's primary prediction target. An offline tokenizer constructs temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions. Reconstruction objectives encourage the representation to retain executable detail and observed physical change. A flow-matching VLA predicts Effects from current images, instruction, and robot state, while a state-conditioned decoder converts them into action chunks. Embodiment-specific interfaces allow single- and dual-arm tasks to share the Effect model. On DexJoCo, AFCE achieves $50.97\%$ overall success, improving over $π_{0.5}$ and UVT by 11.82 and 15.21 percentage points, respectively. It leads on all five bimanual tasks, highlighting the value of Effect supervision for coordinated dexterous manipulation. The project page is available at https://afceproject.github.io/AFCE-Web/.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made substantial progress toward generalist robot control by mapping images, language, and robot state to continuous actions zitkovich2023rt2,octo2024,kim2025openvla,black2024pi0,black2025pi05 . Yet the target used to train this mapping usually describes what the robot commanded, not what the command changed. An action sequence specifies motor behavior, but leaves its effects on the robot and environment implicit. In dexterous manipulation, this gap matters: contact, hand configuration, and object pose can turn similar commands into different outcomes, while different motions can achieve the same task-relevant change. The challenge is to make physical progress part of the policy's prediction target without sacrificing the detail needed to execute an action. Predicting the future offers one way to expose such progress. World and world-action models use future observations or latent dynamics to support control wu2024gr1,cen2025worldvla,zhang2025dreamvla,ye2026dreamzero . However, a complete visual future contains changes due to appearance, occlusion, and camera motion that need not determine the next control command. Conversely, a scene change alone may leave out the contact timing, finger coordination, and robot motion required to produce it. Latent-action and future-informed visuomotor methods provide more compact targets ye2024lapa,bu2025univla,chen2025villax,luo2026jala, liu2026lara,xu2026futurevla,luo2026beingh07 , but compactness alone does not resolve whether a target is both predictable from the current observation and sufficient for precise action decoding. We therefore seek a target that connects three requirements: it must be predictable before acting, retain task-relevant information about the resulting physical transition, and support recovery of executable continuous actions. We introduce AFCE (Action--Future Coupled Effect Learning), which learns a temporal Effect from synchronized demonstrations of executed actions, realized robot-state changes, and sparse world changes. Rather than specifying the Effect through hand-designed semantic labels, we let these sources interact and constrain a shared representation through joint reconstruction. The action objective retains control detail, while the robot-response and world-change objectives ground that detail in observed consequences. Figure~ fig:framework illustrates the resulting training interface. An offline tokenizer constructs Effect targets from recorded trajectories, where future evidence is available. The VLA then learns to predict these targets using only the current images, language instruction, and robot state. At deployment, a decoder maps the predicted Effect and current state to an action chunk. Thus, future observations shape the supervision without becoming inputs to the deployed policy. The central test of this interface is whether the Effect remains useful after prediction. Accurate reconstruction from a ground-truth Effect does not ensure that the VLA can predict that Effect, nor that decoded actions succeed under closed-loop control. We evaluate these questions separately: reconstruction tests what the representation retains; ground-truth-Effect replay tests whether it supports execution; and predicted-Effect rollout tests the complete policy against direct action supervision under the same evaluation protocol. In mixed single- and dual-arm training, AFCE improves aggregate task success, particularly on dual-arm tasks, while some fine-control tasks remain challenging. Our contributions are: We formulate VLA target learning around three coupled requirements: predictability from current observations, information about task-relevant future changes, and continuous-action executability. We introduce AFCE, a temporal Effect learned by jointly reconstructing executed actions, realized robot response, and sparse world change from a shared representation. We evaluate the representation and the complete policy through reconstruction, ground-truth-Effect replay, and predicted-Effect closed-loop control, showing aggregate gains under mixed single- and dual-arm training while identifying remaining fine-control limitations. Related Work sec:related-work VLA Policies and Action Supervision Vision-language-action (VLA) models have established a powerful interface between semantic understanding and robot control. RT-2 casts discretized actions as language-like tokens, while Octo and OpenVLA learn generalist policies from heterogeneous robot data zitkovich2023rt2,octo2024,kim2025openvla . and further combine pretrained visual-language representations with a flow-matching action expert for continuous control black2024pi0,black2025pi05 . Complementary advances such as ACT, Diffusion Policy, and FAST improve action prediction through chunking, expressive generative modeling, and efficient tokenization zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion,pertsch2025fast . Together, these methods provide increasingly capable ways to generate robot commands. They also motivate a closer examination of what the policy is asked to predict: an action records the commanded motion, whereas the resulting robot and scene changes carry additional information about the intended manipulation. Building on these advances, AFCE preserves the VLA observation interface and continuous action execution while introducing a physical Effect as the policy's intermediate supervision target. World Models and Future-Informed Control Future-aware learning offers a complementary route to stronger visuomotor policies. GR-1 and VidMan use video dynamics to inform manipulation, while WorldVLA and DreamZero connect predictions about the evolving world to action generation wu2024gr1,wen2024vidman,cen2025worldvla,ye2026dreamzero . FutureVLA and Being-H0.7 further show how future-informed representations can guide policies that act from current observations xu2026futurevla,luo2026beingh07 . Collectively, these studies establish future information as a valuable training signal for control. AFCE asks how that signal can be organized into a target that is both informative about physical change and directly useful for producing actions. Demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions jointly specify the Effect during training; at deployment, the policy predicts it from the current context and a state-conditioned decoder converts it into robot commands. This formulation explicitly links future-grounded supervision to the action interface used for closed-loop execution. Latent Actions and Transferable Policy Targets Latent-action learning provides intermediate targets that capture structure beyond individual action coordinates. LAPA derives latent actions from visual transitions, while UniVLA and villa-X develop representations for learning from robot and video data ye2024lapa,bu2025univla,chen2025villax . JALA and LARA connect transition-derived features to actions and policy learning luo2026jala,liu2026lara . UVT combines demonstrated action chunks with discrete visual dynamics codes into a decodable policy target feng2026unifiedvisuomotortargetssupervising . AFCE develops this direction by constructing a temporal Effect from demonstrated commands, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions. Its action and response branches relate observed scene changes to both the issued commands and the motion actually realized. Realized responses are particularly informative in dexterous manipulation, where contact and hand configuration can make similar commands produce different outcomes. Temporal Effect tokens preserve the progression from initial contact to subsequent object interaction. A state-conditioned decoder maps the Effect to native actions, making the learned target useful for continuous control. Embodiment-specific adapters accommodate different native state and action dimensions while retaining a common Effect shape. The action encoder uses group-specific projections for position, rotation, and finger commands before combining them into step-level features. The response encoder represents realized palm translation, relative orientation, fingertip displacement, and finger-joint change in the reference frame of the prediction window. Its features are computed from observed states and forward kinematics and aligned with future action steps; both arms are retained for dual-arm demonstrations. title: Dual-Stream Memory for Vision-Language-Action Policies
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Evaluated on 16 RoboMME tasks and 4 real-world robotic manipulation tasks
summary: Memory-dependent manipulation requires a policy to track execution state and recover visual evidence that is no longer observable. We propose dual-stream memory for vision-language-action policies, assigning these requirements to complementary representations. A task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet compresses history into one temporal token, supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. A task-conditioned retriever retains frames above a fixed relevance threshold; linear multi-scale fusion encodes each frame into sixteen spatial tokens. We then freeze the temporal compressor and jointly optimize retrieval and policy learning. Across sixteen RoboMME tasks, the complete model achieves 49.22% mean success versus 44.51% for the published FrameSamp+Modul reference, improving fourteen tasks and all four suite means. On four real-robot tasks, mean success reaches 62.5% versus 37.5%, with the largest gains on repeated actions requiring execution-stage discrimination. These results support combining execution context with selective visual access, while failures under cup swaps expose persistent identity tracking as an unresolved requirement.

INTRODUCTION Long-horizon manipulation can produce perceptually similar observations that require different actions, depending on prior execution or earlier visual evidence. Repeated actions require execution-stage information, whereas occlusion and target reidentification require distinguishing visual detail that may no longer be observable. These requirements motivate separate representations for evolving execution context and accessible historical evidence (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and instructions to robot actions~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,ghosh2024octo,black2025pi0,black2025pi05 . Large-scale robot data, action chunking, and generative action models broaden their capabilities~ brohan2022rt1,oxe2023,chi2023diffusion,zhao2023act . However, they do not determine which episodic information a policy should retain. Recent memory-augmented policies preserve perceptual observations, cognitive summaries, or representations at several temporal scales~ shi2026memoryvla,torne2026mem,wang2026nativemem . Which historical information should be compressed, and which should remain directly accessible? Recurrent compression summarizes execution history, but a compact state need not preserve detail for later target identification. Storing historical features preserves access, but uniform sampling may miss brief evidence, and spatial pooling may discard distinguishing detail. We therefore distinguish execution context, frame relevance, and within-frame detail. Our design combines recurrent temporal memory with selected spatial evidence (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ). We make three contributions: 0pt ) We introduce a task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet (GDN) compressor supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. These objectives encourage execution context and reconstructable visual history in one temporal token. We formulate task-conditioned evidence access as threshold retrieval with shared temporal and spatial supervision. The retained-frame count adapts to the available evidence. We introduce linear multi-scale fusion to combine coarse context and fine spatial detail within sixteen tokens per retained frame. RELATED WORK Memory for robot policies Robot memory research distinguishes sequencing skills from retaining information within an episode. CALVIN and LIBERO study sequential manipulation and knowledge transfer~ mees2022calvin,liu2023libero ; RoboMME targets Counting, Permanence, Reference, and Imitation~ dai2026robomme . Its FrameSamp+Modul baseline exposes sampled historical features to a VLA policy. Beyond sampled observations, memory interfaces compress and organize history. Latent bottlenecks and cross-attention provide mechanisms for reading visual context~ jaegle2021perceiver,alayrac2022flamingo . MemoryVLA combines perceptual and cognitive memory, MEM organizes video and text at multiple temporal scales, and NativeMEM learns policy-aligned memory tokens~ shi2026memoryvla,torne2026mem,wang2026nativemem . Our design separates recurrent state from retrieved evidence, with distinct operations for execution context, frame selection, and spatial detail. Recurrent compression and selective access Content-based attention reads stored representations~ vaswani2017attention ; Transformer-XL, Compressive Transformer, and Recurrent Memory Transformer extend historical access through recurrence or compression~ dai2019transformerxl,rae2019compressive,bulatov2022rmt . Linear attention and state-space models instead maintain recurrent states~ katharopoulos2020linear,gu2023mamba,dao2024mamba2 . DeltaNet introduces delta-rule updates, while GDN adds data-dependent forgetting~ yang2024deltanet,yang2025gateddelta . Test-Time Training and RoboTTT further explore expressive recurrent states and robot-policy context~ sun2024ttt,jiang2026robottt . We build on GDN by supervising execution progress and reconstructable visual history, with a separate spatial memory bank for direct evidence access. Spatial representations for memory Patch encoders provide spatial features~ dosovitskiy2020vit : DINO learns self-supervised visual structure~ caron2021dino,oquab2023dinov2,simeoni2025dinov3 , whereas CLIP and SigLIP learn image--text correspondence~ radford2021clip,zhai2023siglip . Feature pyramids, hierarchical Transformers, and mixed-resolution tokenization preserve information across spatial scales~ lin2016fpn,liu2021swin,ronen2023mixedres ; PerAct emphasizes spatial structure for manipulation~ shridhar2022peract . We use DINOv3 for temporal compression and frozen SigLIP for retrieval and spatial memory. Our fusion aligns coarse, base, and fine features within sixteen slots, enriching retained frames without enlarging their token budget. title: Robust Vision-Language Navigation with Awareness of Instruction-Execution Progress
summary: In Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) tasks involving multi-step instructions as guidance, an agent must associate its observations with the relevant instruction content at each decision point. Most graph-based methods commonly match candidate trajectories with the entire instruction, allowing already executed content to interfere with subsequent decisions. Although instruction-execution progress provides a direct cue for separating executed and pending content, existing progress estimation approaches often rely on explicit progress supervision, sophisticated progress-learning stages, or costly online reasoning with LLMs. In this paper, we propose a robust VLN framework with Awareness of Instruction-Execution Progress (VLN-AIEP), which couples progress estimation with navigation decision-making. VLN-AIEP associates the visited trajectory with the instruction to suppress embeddings corresponding to executed content, and then matches candidate locations with the pending content. This coupling makes correct navigation decisions depend on accurate progress estimation, allowing the progress estimator to learn directly from navigation decision labels without explicit progress annotations. To support progress estimation, we construct a landmark-anchored trajectory representation that encodes the semantic labels and viewpoint-relative geometry of instruction-referred landmarks. These landmarks serve as spatial references for associating the visited trajectory with executed instruction content. Extensive experiments on R2R, RxR, CVDN, and R2R-CE demonstrate that the proposed method achieves favorable performance across multiple metrics.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language Navigation (VLN)~ anderson2018vision,li2024human,lin2025navcot,zhang2024navid,chen2024mapgpt aims to empower an agent with visual sensors to navigate in a 3D environment following natural language instructions. For example, given an instruction like ``Walk towards the French doors and turn left. Walk past the kitchen area...'', the agent needs to comprehend this instruction, make movement decisions while perceiving its surroundings, and accurately halt at the destination. Recently, VLN has witnessed significant progress with the introduction of topological graphs~ chen2022think,lu2024pret . These graphs record all visited and navigable locations observed so far, thereby expanding the action space to the entire explored area and facilitating high-level planning over long horizons. Despite these advances, following detailed multi-step instructions remains challenging, as the agent needs to accurately associate its observation with the relevant instruction to take an appropriate action at each critical decision point. Representative graph-based methods~ chen2022think,an2022bevbert,lu2024pret typically construct candidate trajectories by appending candidate locations to the historical trajectory. Subsequently, they match the entire candidate trajectory with the entire instruction, i.e.,~global coarse matching, to determine the next movement. Such global coarse matching allows parts of the instruction that have already been executed to continue influencing the current decision. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:1 (a), this interference can mislead the agent into executing ``turn left'' twice. Intuitively, a multi-step instruction should be followed like a checklist: once a step is completed, subsequent decisions should be guided by the remaining instruction steps. Accordingly, once the agent has turned left in Figure~ fig:1 (b), it should shift its focus to locating the ``kitchen area'' in subsequent navigation. Robust navigation therefore requires the agent to estimate instruction-execution progress, namely, how much of the instruction has been completed. Several existing approaches~ ma2019self,ma2019regretful,hong2020sub,he2021landmark,cui2026fca,guo2026aware,wang2026progressthink,long2024discuss,qiao2025open have taken steps toward equipping agents with the ability to estimate instruction-execution progress. Traditional progress monitors~ ma2019self,ma2019regretful use normalized distance to the goal as supervision. However, this geometric progress signal can be inconsistent with actual instruction completion. To reduce this mismatch, some methods~ hong2020sub,he2021landmark,cui2026fca,guo2026aware introduce additional supervision to learn fine-grained instruction-trajectory alignment or progress awareness. However, whether manually annotated~ hong2020sub,he2021landmark or automatically generated~ cui2026fca,guo2026aware , such supervision requires additional annotation or a data-generation pipeline. Recently, Progress-Think~ wang2026progressthink circumvents the need for explicit progress annotations, but still requires dedicated progress-learning stages within a three-stage training procedure. Alternatively, LLM-based methods infer progress online from instructions and visual navigation context, but require repeated, costly inference~ long2024discuss,qiao2025open . Together, these trade-offs motivate us to learn progress estimation directly from navigation decision labels. Beyond supervision, accurate progress estimation requires associating trajectory states with instruction steps. Instruction-referred landmarks provide semantic and spatial cues that help establish this association. However, the use of such landmarks as spatial references for navigation progress estimation remains underexplored. In this paper, we propose a robust VLN framework with Awareness of Instruction-Execution Progress (VLN-AIEP). To learn to estimate instruction-execution progress directly from navigation decision labels, VLN-AIEP is designed to couple progress estimation with navigation decision-making, making accurate progress estimation a prerequisite for correct navigation decisions. Specifically, it first associates the visited trajectory with the instruction to estimate execution progress and suppresses embeddings associated with executed content. It then matches candidate locations with the pending instruction content to make a navigation decision, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:1 (b). This coupling allows navigation decision labels to supervise progress estimation without explicit progress annotations, while focusing on pending content mitigates interference from executed instruction content. To further facilitate progress estimation, we construct a landmark-anchored trajectory representation that encodes the semantic labels and viewpoint-relative geometry of instruction-referred landmarks. These landmarks serve as spatial references for associating the visited trajectory with executed instruction content. We evaluate our method on R2R~ anderson2018vision , RxR~ ku2020room , and CVDN~ thomason2020vision , and further validate its effectiveness in the continuous R2R-CE environment~ krantz2020beyond . VLN-AIEP performs competitively with state-of-the-art approaches in quantitative evaluations. In addition, qualitative analyses show that VLN-AIEP estimates navigation progress accurately. Our contributions can be summarized as: We propose VLN-AIEP, which couples progress estimation with navigation decision-making to focus on pending instruction content and learn to estimate progress from navigation labels without explicit progress supervision. We construct a landmark-anchored trajectory representation that encodes semantic labels and viewpoint-relative geometry, allowing instruction-referred landmarks to serve as spatial references for progress estimation. Extensive experiments on R2R, RxR, CVDN, and R2R-CE demonstrate favorable performance of VLN-AIEP against state-of-the-art approaches. Related Work sec:formatting 1mm VLN methods have evolved from sequence-based cross-modal learning to structured long-horizon reasoning. Early agents improved instruction-observation alignment through data augmentation and auxiliary objectives~ fried2018speaker,wang2019reinforced,tan2019learning . Transformer-based methods subsequently strengthened temporal modeling through multimodal pretraining and explicit history encoding~ hao2020towards,qiao2022hop,chen2021history,lin2022multimodal,wang2023gridmm . Building on these advances, graph-based methods explicitly represent the explored environment~ chen2022think,an2022bevbert,lu2024pret,an2024etpnav . These representations support local grounding and long-range planning. Continuous-environment methods further relax the assumption of a predefined navigation graph~ krantz2020beyond,krantz2022sim,hong2022bridging . More recently, rapid advances in foundation models have led to their growing adoption in VLN. These methods generally follow two paradigms: online reasoning and task adaptation. Online agents invoke foundation models during navigation. They reason over textualized observations, maps, or multiple experts~ zhou2024navgpt,chen2024mapgpt,long2024instructnav,long2024discuss,qiao2025open,xue2026profocus,dai2026history . This enables flexible zero-shot decision-making but requires repeated inference. Adaptation-based systems instead train navigation policies or reasoning modules. They use video trajectories, generated supervision, or multi-task data~ zhang2024navid,lin2025navcot,guo2026aware,Wei2025StreamVLNSV,zhang2026navfom,jiang2026m3e . This reduces reliance on explicit online prompting but requires additional data and training. Unlike representative graph-based methods that match complete candidate trajectories against the entire instruction, VLN-AIEP uses the visited trajectory to attenuate instruction embeddings associated with likely executed content. It then matches candidate-location embeddings with the resulting progress-aware instruction embeddings, which emphasize the pending instruction content. This progress-aware matching reduces the influence of previously executed instruction steps on the current decision. Existing methods obtain instruction-related progress information from geometric targets, fine-grained supervision, dedicated progress learning, or online reasoning. Early progress monitors use normalized goal distance to supervise progress estimation, and the Regretful Agent further uses the estimated progress for backtracking~ ma2019self,ma2019regretful . However, geometric progress may not reflect instruction completion because different instruction segments can cover unequal distances. To better reflect instruction completion, fine-grained methods use human-annotated correspondences between instruction parts and navigation states. These annotations associate sub-instructions or landmarks with positions along the trajectory~ hong2020sub,he2021landmark , but are costly to collect. LAW similarly introduces language-aligned waypoint supervision~ raychaudhuri2021law , which requires a dedicated target-construction process. To reduce manual annotation, FCA-NIG and AwareVLN automatically construct alignment or progress-aware reasoning supervision before policy training~ cui2026fca,guo2026aware . Similarly, ATD uses a powerful LLM to generate progress-related state estimates for training its state-estimation branch~ zhang2025cross . Although more scalable, they still require a separate data-generation pipeline. Progress-Think avoids explicit progress annotations through self-alignment~ wang2026progressthink . However, it employs a dedicated progress module, progress-specific objectives, and a three-stage training procedure. Another line of work relies on online foundation-model reasoning to infer progress or subgoal completion. DiscussNav and Open-Nav reason over the instruction and navigation context, while SkillNav and Fast-SmartWay track the current subgoal~ long2024discuss,qiao20

title: GuidedNav: Shaping Vision-Language Navigation Representations through Pre-action Attention and Spatial Guidance
summary: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to track progress through an extended instruction, identify landmarks relevant to its current objective, and understand the surrounding spatial structure to act. End-to-end navigation policies typically rely on action supervision to implicitly learn these capabilities. Without explicit guidance on the evidence underlying each decision, however, policies can overfit to correlations predictive of training actions rather than learn the task-relevant grounding and geometry needed for generalization. Our insight is to guide the representations that connect instructions to actions: identifying what remains to be done determines which visual evidence matters, while understanding the geometry around that evidence informs how to move. We introduce GuidedNav, a unified framework that explicitly shapes these representations through training-time guidance. Subtask and landmark guidance steer native pre-action attention toward the active instruction segment and relevant visual regions, grounding action prediction in the current objective. Spatial guidance aligns the policy's internal representations with geometric features that capture long-horizon context and local spatial structure. Together, these objectives strengthen navigation capabilities while avoiding the inference overhead of intermediate textual reasoning and online geometric encoding. We also introduce Guided-R2R and Guided-RxR, two annotation-enriched navigation datasets that support more interpretable VLN research. GuidedNav establishes state-of-the-art performance among the compared monocular RGB policies, improving success rates by 8.1% and 13.1% relative to the strongest prior results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen, respectively, while achieving faster inference. Extensive experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness and real-world transferability of our approach.

Introduction sec:introduction Consider the instruction ``Walk towards the yellow chair, then walk past the dining table, and enter the room'' (Figure~ fig:concept_overview ). Moving forward may be appropriate at each stage, although the active instruction span and relevant landmark differ. The action label alone therefore does not specify which evidence should support a decision. This ambiguity matters in vision-and-language navigation (VLN), where an agent follows extended instructions through changing visual observations~ anderson2018vln,ku2020rxr . Recent vision-language policies predict actions directly from instructions and RGB video~ zhang2024navid,zhang2025uninavid,cheng2025navila , but their behavioral supervision only indirectly constrains the task and visual information used to act. Grounding the current objective is only part of the problem: the policy must also relate 2D observations to the 3D layout through which it moves. Historical views provide broader spatial context, while nearby observations reveal local structure relevant to the next movement. Existing work strengthens these capabilities through progress reasoning, region-level grounding, and geometric memory~ wang2026progressthink,guo2026awarevln,li2023kerm,zeng2026janusvln . Intermediate text generation and online geometric encoding can, however, add inference cost. Auxiliary reasoning and future-state prediction provide additional training signals~ wang2025auxthink,zhang2026futurenav , motivating a complementary question: at the moment of action generation, does the policy attend to the active instruction span and its visual referents, and encode the spatial information needed to proceed? We introduce GuidedNav, a unified framework that strengthens navigation representations through training-time auxiliary guidance. The position immediately preceding the first action token provides a natural supervision point: its hidden state predicts the action sequence's beginning, while its native attention gathers evidence from instructions and observations. Subtask and landmark guidance direct this attention toward the active instruction span and associated image regions, grounding action prediction in the current objective. Spatial guidance aligns current-frame representations with long-horizon geometric targets and supervises local temporal fusion with geometric information from nearby views. At inference, the policy retains the learned fusion but discards the geometric teacher and auxiliary projectors, enabling faster, direct action prediction without intermediate reasoning. We introduce Guided-R2R and Guided-RxR, two annotation-enriched datasets linking navigation steps to active subtask spans and landmark masks. GuidedNav improves success rates by 8.1 and 13.1 relative to the strongest prior models on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, respectively, while achieving a per-action inference speedup. Our contributions are threefold: We propose GuidedNav, a unified framework that explicitly guides navigation representations through subtask attention, landmark grounding, and spatial supervision, strengthening direct action prediction without intermediate reasoning or an online geometric encoder. We introduce Guided-R2R and Guided-RxR through a landmark-centric data engine, linking navigation steps to active subtask spans and landmark masks to support representation learning and more interpretable VLN research. We achieve state-of-the-art navigation performance with faster inference. Extensive benchmark evaluations, component ablations, representation analyses, and real-robot experiments validate the effectiveness of our guidance and its transfer to real-world environments. title: Reflect-VLA: Internalizing Reflective Guidance via Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation for Autonomous Driving
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) substantially improves planning performance in autonomous-driving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar trajectory rewards that measure overall quality but fail to identify specific planning errors or provide actionable correction signals. In long-tail scenarios, errors in scene understanding, behavior selection, and trajectory execution are compressed into a single score. We observe that Reflective Guidance turns trajectory evaluation into explicit diagnoses and corrective instructions, substantially improving planning accuracy. Yet such guidance requires an initial prediction and its evaluation results, making it unavailable for direct single-pass inference. We propose Reflect-VLA, which treats Reflective Guidance as training-time privileged information and internalizes its planning benefits through Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation (Dual-OPSD). Unlike scalar-reward optimization, Dual-OPSD uses the driving score only to route student-generated trajectories. It distills dense token-level corrective distributions from the teacher for risky trajectories while applying self-imitation to preserve reliable ones. To provide reliable corrective distributions on student rollouts, the teacher is progressively constructed through Driving-Knowledge Pretraining, Planning-and-Refinement SFT, and Self-Refinement Rejection Sampling. At inference time, Reflect-VLA generates trajectories in a single pass without explicit guidance or iterative refinement. Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 and Bench2Drive demonstrate competitive planning performance while reducing training time by over 90% compared with RL.

Introduction Autonomous driving is shifting from conventional modular pipelines toward end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems~ vlasurvey . Unlike modular systems~ hu2023planning,jiang2023vad,e2esurvey that coordinate perception, prediction, and planning through handcrafted interfaces, VLA models integrate visual observations, language instructions and action generation within a unified architecture. Recent driving VLA methods commonly adopt a multi-stage training paradigm~ li2025recogdrive,zhou2025autovla,adathinkdrive,luo2026last,lu2026xiaomi . They first acquire domain knowledge from large-scale driving question-answering data, then learn trajectory generation through supervised fine-tuning, and finally improve the policy using reinforcement learning or planning-oriented objectives. Despite progress, VLA models struggle to learn from planning failures, especially in complex and long-tail scenarios. A scalar planning score can identify a poor trajectory but cannot reveal whether the error arises from scene understanding, behavior selection, or trajectory execution, nor indicate how to correct it. Trajectory-level rewards collapse these heterogeneous failure modes into a single value, leaving the model without a direction for improvement. ELF-VLA~ luo2026unleashing alleviates this problem by introducing structured failure information, showing that detailed feedback can guide the correction of failed trajectories. However, how to convert feedback-assisted correction into an intrinsic single-pass planning capability remains underexplored. We begin with a key observation: Reflective Guidance provides substantial planning gains. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:intro , a VLA model may produce an incorrect trajectory during direct inference, yet generate a markedly better trajectory when provided with evaluation-derived diagnoses and corrective suggestions~ yang2026judge,he2026drivever,chen2026vilta . Constructing the guidance requires both an initial trajectory and its evaluation results, whereas an autonomous driving system must produce an executable plan before acting. The central challenge is therefore not to perform iterative refinement at inference time, but to transfer the planning preferences induced by Reflective Guidance into the model's direct trajectory-generation policy. To this end, we propose Reflect-VLA, a training framework that treats Reflective Guidance as privileged information and internalizes its planning benefits through Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation (Dual-OPSD). Starting from the same VLA checkpoint, the model supplied with Reflective Guidance acts as the frozen teacher, while the model receiving standard inputs acts as the student. The student first generates trajectories from the input available at deployment. A planning score then routes each trajectory to one of two learning paths. For risky or suboptimal trajectories, the teacher provides dense token-level distributions that encode corrective planning preferences. For reliable trajectories, a self-imitation objective preserves the student's existing decisions. The scalar score is therefore used only for trajectory-quality-aware routing, while the teacher distribution supplies the fine-grained supervision required for correction. Effective self-distillation requires a teacher that can refine trajectories drawn from the student's rollout distribution. We construct this teacher using a progressive strategy comprising Driving-Knowledge Pretraining, Planning-and-Refinement SFT, and Self-Refinement Rejection Sampling. The first two stages establish driving knowledge, direct trajectory generation, and guidance-assisted refinement. The final stage exposes the teacher to student-generated failures and retains verified refinements, reducing the distribution gap between offline refinement data and on-policy trajectories. After Dual-OPSD, Reflect-VLA performs single-pass trajectory generation without Reflective Guidance, an online planning evaluator, or an iterative correction procedure. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=*] We construct Reflective Guidance that converts trajectory evaluation results into structured, trajectory-specific diagnoses and corrective suggestions, and use it as privileged information available only during training. We propose Dual-OPSD, a trajectory-quality-aware self-distillation method that transfers corrective distributions for risky trajectories while preserving reliable planning. We develop a progressive teacher-construction strategy that combines driving-knowledge pretraining, planning-and-refinement supervision, and self-refinement rejection sampling to support stable guidance internalization and efficient single-pass planning. Related Work VLA models for autonomous driving VLMs and VLA models have been increasingly studied for autonomous driving, with applications ranging from scene understanding~ jiang2024senna,jiang2025alphadrive,marcu2024lingoqa to direct trajectory prediction~ xing2025openemma,zhao2025sce2drivex,liu2025reasonplan,fu2025orion . To improve interpretability and planning accuracy, several methods introduce explicit intermediate reasoning, such as Chain-of-Thought reasoning~ liu2025reasonplan,zhao2025sce2drivex,mtrdrive . Their training pipelines typically begin with supervised fine-tuning on driving data and subsequently apply reinforcement learning, including Group Relative Policy Optimization, to improve planning performance~ adathinkdrive,zhou2025autovla . Although scalar planning rewards provide a direct measure of trajectory quality, they offer limited supervision when diverse failure causes receive similarly low scores~ chen2026drivereward . This issue is especially pronounced in long-tail scenarios, where repeated low-reward rollouts can make policy optimization inefficient. ELF-VLA~ luo2026unleashing addresses this limitation by using teacher-generated feedback to diagnose planning failures and construct improved training samples. Our work instead focuses on internalizing the benefit of such structured guidance so that it is no longer required during inference. On-Policy Distillation and On-Policy Self-Distillation On-policy distillation (OPD) and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) are post-training approaches that supervise a student on trajectories sampled from its own policy~ agarwal2024onpolicy,opsd . Unlike off-policy distillation, this formulation queries a teacher with student-generated prefixes, thereby providing token-level supervision over the distribution encountered during training. OPD commonly relies on a separately trained teacher, whereas OPSD can derive the teacher from the same model by conditioning it on privileged information~ ye2026onpolicycontextdistill,sang2026crisp , such as ground-truth answers, additional instructions, or preference information. Recent work has combined dense token-level signals from OPD with reinforcement learning for VLA post-training~ zhong2026vlaopd , but its application to autonomous-driving planning remains limited. We formulate Reflective Guidance as privileged information and use it to obtain corrective teacher distributions on student-generated trajectories. Dual-OPSD further accounts for trajectory quality by distilling corrections only when needed and preserving decisions that are already reliable. title: Measurable Semantic 3D Gaussian Splatting with Joint Region and Depth Supervision for Interactive Building Inspection
summary: Image-based 3D reconstruction provides a scalable representation for building inspection and maintenance. However, photorealistic reconstruction alone does not fully provide the geometric measurability, semantic structure, and interactive information access required for engineering applications. This study proposes a measurable semantic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework with region and depth supervision for interactive building inspection from multi-view imagery. Mask-based region supervision suppresses irrelevant backgrounds and focuses optimization on target regions. Point-wise depth supervision guides Gaussian centers toward physical surfaces using reference geometry derived from multi-view stereo (MVS) point clouds, providing geometric anchors for measuring physical dimensions and areas. A semantic Gaussian field associates learnable class features with individual Gaussian primitives, enabling semantic rendering and component-level inspection. These capabilities are operationalized through AEC-SplatTwin, an interactive building inspection platform supporting real-time visualization, semantic analysis, quantitative measurement, and multimodal large language model (MLLM)-assisted interaction. On the synthetic UAV-inspection QuakeCity and smartphone-captured HKUPB datasets, the framework reduces Gaussian-center depth MAE by 58.1% and 86.8%, while its semantic field achieves mIoU values of 0.8529 and 0.8642. On HKUPB, the mean relative errors for height, width, and area measurements are 0.33%, 1.07%, and 0.60%. These results show that the proposed framework extends 3DGS beyond visual reconstruction into a measurable, semantically structured, and interactive engineering representation for building inspection.

title: RESCUE: Is This Alarm Worth Acting On? Counterfactual Evaluation of VLA Runtime Monitors
summary: Runtime failure monitors for robot policies are typically evaluated by how accurately they distinguish failed from successful executions. Yet an accurate alarm may arrive too late for recovery, while an unnecessary intervention may disrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed. We introduce RESCUE, a counterfactual framework for evaluating whether a monitor's alarms enable useful interventions. By restoring simulator and policy states at execution checkpoints, RESCUE compares alternative actions, identifies the latest checkpoint satisfying a specified recovery criterion, and evaluates whether acting on alarms reduces expected task-completion cost. We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and $π_{0.5}$ over LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus using 128,340 counterfactual branches. Recoverability depends on the state--intervention pair rather than on robot state alone: at $τ=0.5$, 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, compared with 34 of 66 under continuation or scripted recovery, while recovery reduces recoverability in other conditions. On the primary strong-policy conditions, favourable detection scores do not establish lower intervention cost. Under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, even an idealised detector can afford only a 2.0--3.3% false-alarm rate before unnecessary resets outweigh the savings from stopping failures early. These results show that monitor value depends jointly on the intervention available and the workload in which it is deployed.

We find that recoverability isn't a function of robot state alone but rather depends on the state--intervention pair. For example, compared with continuation, scripted recovery more than doubles the number of recoverable failures in one setting, but reduces it in others. The reason is structural rather than a shortcoming of these particular monitors: even an idealised detector can afford only a 2.0–3.3 false-alarm rate before the cost of needless resets exceeds everything early stopping saves.
