INTRODUCTION Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly capable of executing diverse robotic manipulation tasks from visual observations and language instructions~ kim2025openvlaoft,physicalintelligence2025pi05 . Despite this progress, long-horizon execution remains vulnerable to compounding errors, environmental perturbations, and out-of-distribution conditions. Runtime monitors therefore aim to detect impending or ongoing failures from policy representations, observations, or predictive world models so that execution can be stopped, recovered, replanned, or escalated~ gu2025safe,seligmann2026vlafail,liu2026checkvla,zhang2026foresight . These monitors are commonly selected using discrimination, calibration, or timing-aware detection metrics. However, predicting failure and deciding whether to intervene are different problems. A monitor may accurately distinguish failed from successful executions while still providing a poor intervention rule: an alarm may arrive after useful recovery has disappeared, or a false alarm may interrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed. Conversely, an imperfect predictor may still be useful if it alarms while an effective and inexpensive intervention remains available. Related agent studies similarly show that better failure prediction or calibration need not improve outcomes under intervention~ vasudev2026failure,zhang2026calibration . In robotics, this distinction is particularly important because interventions alter physical state and may incur reset, delay, or damage costs. Timing-aware evaluation addresses part of this problem, but elapsed time alone is insufficient. VLA-FAIL~ seligmann2026vlafail incorporates detection time into monitor evaluation, PREFAIL~ shangguan2026prefail identifies an actionable intervention window for lift-and-place failures, and CheckVLA~ liu2026checkvla defines an intervention-relative irreversibility time by testing whether a fixed set of repairs can still restore success. CheckVLA establishes that actionability depends on available repairs, but leaves open how intervention value changes across the trajectory and whether acting remains preferable once false alarms and intervention costs are included~ liu2026checkvla . The same robot-policy state can therefore have different value under continuation, recovery, or stop-and-reset. We introduce RESCUE (Recoverability Evaluation of Stopping Criteria Under Execution), a counterfactual framework for evaluating existing runtime monitors as intervention rules. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:rescue_overview , RESCUE restores simulator and policy states at action-chunk boundaries and evaluates alternative interventions, estimating action-conditioned task success under a declared intervention repertoire , execution model , and remaining task budget . Evaluating these outcomes across the trajectory yields a recoverability horizon: the latest checkpoint at which the declared repertoire satisfies a specified recovery criterion. The horizon therefore depends explicitly on the available interventions, execution model, and task budget. Recoverability establishes what can still succeed, but not whether intervention is worthwhile. Stopping a failed execution can save time, whereas an unnecessary stop incurs a reset and another attempt. RESCUE therefore evaluates interventions in a common cost-to-completion space incorporating failure prevalence, alarm timing, false alarms, and intervention cost. For stop-and-reset, this yields a closed-form break-even false-alarm rate computable from ordinary execution logs, allowing a monitor's realised operating point to be compared directly with never intervening. We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and on LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus~ liu2023libero,fei2025liberoplus , comprising 1,562 trunk episodes and 128,340 counterfactual branches. At , only 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, while 34 of 66 clear under continuation or scripted recovery. Under stop-and-reset, even an idealised detector that identifies every failure immediately can afford only a 2.78--3.32 false-alarm rate under the evaluated cost model. A steps-since-progress monitor tuned to a nominal 5 operating point instead costs reset-equivalents per completed task relative to never intervening. Across matched evaluation sets, conventional detection and timing metrics admit the real monitors in 61 of 75 verdicts, whereas decision value admits none of 15 against never intervening. These results show that failure-prediction quality alone does not establish intervention value. Our contributions are: We formulate runtime-monitor evaluation over state--intervention pairs and introduce a counterfactual branching protocol that estimates intervention success along robot-policy trajectories, yielding a recoverability horizon conditional on the intervention repertoire, execution model, and remaining task budget. We complement recoverability with a decision-value formulation accounting for failure prevalence, alarm timing, false alarms, and intervention cost, and derive a closed-form break-even false-alarm criterion for stop-and-reset from standard execution logs. We evaluate the framework at scale across two VLA policies and show that recoverability changes substantially with the available intervention, while monitors favoured by conventional detection and timing metrics can remain decision-negative when evaluated against the intervention they trigger. RELATED WORK sec:related_work Runtime Failure Monitoring for Robot Policies. Runtime monitors detect execution failures using policy representations, action consistency, and predictive world models. Sentinel~ agia2025sentinel pairs temporal action consistency with VLM-based task-progress reasoning. FIPER~ romer2025fiper combines embedding-space out-of-distribution detection with action-chunk uncertainty, conformally calibrating both scores on successful rollouts. For VLA policies, SAFE~ gu2025safe predicts failures from policy representations, VLA-FAIL~ seligmann2026vlafail introduces AUCPDT to assess detection accuracy and timing, and Foresight~ zhang2026foresight uses action-conditioned world-model latents to detect long-horizon manipulation failures. These works primarily evaluate how reliably and how early failures are identified. CheckVLA~ liu2026checkvla couples detection to repair by evaluating suffix rewrites from restored simulator states. It defines an irreversibility time beyond which none of its tested repairs restores success, and reports rescue, harm, and task success. RESCUE instead compares alternative interventions throughout execution and evaluates whether acting on alarms lowers expected task-completion cost under the workload's failure prevalence and intervention costs. Failure Recovery and Intervention Timing. Recovery methods address how a robot should respond when execution goes wrong. AEGIS~ chen2026aegis selectively escalates to a stronger policy, B2FF~ shin2026b2ff selects a pre-imagined familiar future as a recovery goal, and Rewind-IL~ zheng2026rewind returns the robot toward a previously verified safe state. PREFAIL~ shangguan2026prefail identifies the latest actionable intervention time for lift-and-place failures, assessing whether predictions arrive early enough to prevent failure. These works focus on designing recovery behaviour or assessing whether intervention occurs within an actionable window. RESCUE instead evaluates declared branchable interventions from every saved action-chunk boundary, allowing recovery opportunities to be measured throughout execution rather than only at a single trigger point. The recoverability estimate is conditional on the intervention repertoire, execution model, and remaining task budget. RESCUE therefore defines the recoverability horizon as the latest checkpoint satisfying the recovery criterion, without assuming that recoverability decreases monotonically with execution time. From Prediction Quality to Decision Value. Predictive accuracy does not guarantee beneficial decisions, a distinction reflected in cost-sensitive learning~ elkan2001foundations and critiques of aggregate evaluation measures~ vickers2006decision,drummond2006cost,hand2009auc . ThriftyDAgger~ hoque2021thriftydagger studies intervention budgets in interactive imitation learning. For LLM agents, Vasudev et al.~ vasudev2026failure show that interventions can both rescue failed executions and disrupt successful ones. Zhang et al.~ zhang2026calibration measure intervention advantage by branching alternative actions from the same execution prefix, showing that better risk calibration need not reduce control regret. RESCUE brings this decision-oriented view to robot manipulation, where interventions alter physical state and resets require another attempt. It evaluates existing monitors by comparing counterfactual interventions from restored robot-policy states and measuring expected cost per complet

title: Beyond Successful Robot Demonstrations: Learning from Human Interactions and Modeling Failure Dynamics
summary: Action-conditioned world models offer a promising foundation for generalist robotic intelligence by predicting the consequences of actions. However, existing robotic datasets provide limited coverage of the diverse interaction dynamics required for generalizable world modeling. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer complementary interaction experience, yet the embodiment gap between human hands and robotic manipulators hinders effective cross-embodiment learning. Meanwhile, the predominance of successful demonstrations leaves failure dynamics substantially underrepresented, limiting the ability of world models to anticipate unsuccessful executions. To address these limitations, we introduce HF-WM, an action-conditioned world model that combines Human interaction learning with Failure-aware post-training. To bridge the embodiment gap, we develop a dual-branch framework that couples video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction, using stabilized pointflow as a unified motion representation across human and robot interactions while suppressing egocentric camera motion. To improve failure modeling, we further perform Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training on perturbed actions derived from successful demonstrations, guided by action alignment and physical plausibility rewards, enabling the model to learn plausible failure dynamics without paired ground-truth videos. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HF-WM achieves state-of-the-art performance in action-conditioned video generation and exhibits strong utility for policy evaluation in downstream robotic tasks.
full_text: Introduction With the rapid advancement of video generation models wan, cosmos3 , world models have witnessed significant breakthroughs and are increasingly regarded as a promising pathway toward generalist robotics dreamzero, fastwam . In particular, action-conditioned world models take robot action sequences as input and model the resulting state transitions to predict future states irasim . This predictive capability supports scalable data generation, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning in generated environments EVA, pilworld, sc3 , thereby closing the loop between imagination, evaluation, and policy improvement. This paradigm has emerged as a key foundation for learning and improving robot action planning systems. Despite these advances, action-conditioned world models still struggle to accurately capture interaction dynamics and execution outcomes, largely due to the limited scale and coverage of high-quality embodied data~ videoembody . To alleviate this limitation, recent studies have turned to large scale egocentric human object interaction datasets dreamdojo,oscar , leveraging human demonstrations to enhance model performance. 1) However, a substantial domain gap persists between human and robotic manipulation, and egocentric recordings are often affected by camera jitter and unstable viewpoints, which can obscure interaction-relevant regions and hinder the learning of physically meaningful representations. Consequently, effectively exploiting human egocentric data for embodied world model learning remains an open challenge videoembody . 2) In addition, existing embodied datasets are heavily biased toward successful demonstrations, with limited coverage of failure cases and off-target interactions mirabench . Yet world models for embodied scenarios require not only modeling successful trajectories, but also capturing failure dynamics and counterfactual outcomes induced by erroneous or suboptimal actions pilworld . In the absence of failure demonstrations, how to effectively synthesize failure scenarios to improve physical reasoning remains an important open problem. Related Work To this end, as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser , we propose a set of key insights to address the aforementioned challenges. 1) Firstly, we introduce a skeleton grounded action representation that bridges human and robotic action spaces through a shared spatial formulation oscar , mitigating the cross embodiment gap. To better exploit egocentric human interaction data, we introduce pointflow supervision as a motion constraint that tracks point trajectories, capturing interaction driven dynamics pointworld, tracegen . We further apply a stabilization procedure on pointflows to suppress camera induced motion, ensuring that point trajectories primarily reflect interaction driven dynamics rather than viewpoint variations. This allows the model to better focus on physically meaningful motion signals and improves the effective utilization of egocentric human interaction data. The primary challenge in introducing failure cases is the lack of real failure video supervision, which limits direct learning under failure scenarios. 2) To address this, we propose a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) based reinforcement learning framework flowgrpo for post-training, enabling better modeling of failure dynamics using reward signals without requiring ground-truth failure video supervision. Specifically, we construct pseudo failure actions by perturbing successful action trajectories, thereby inducing counterfactual action conditions. These perturbed actions are then used as conditions for video generation, where the model is optimized via reward-based feedback under GRPO. The reward function consists of two complementary terms: a skeleton-based action following score that measures the consistency between the generated motion and the given action condition abot , and a physical plausibility score that evaluates whether the predicted dynamics remain physically consistent. Both rewards are computable without paired ground-truth videos, enabling GRPO post-training on perturbed actions to strengthen failure-aware dynamics modeling without direct supervision of the corresponding outcomes. In summary, our main contributions are: [leftmargin=*, nosep] We present HF-WM, an action-conditioned world model that learns from egocentric human interactions and counterfactual action perturbations for embodied dynamics modeling. We introduce a dual-branch framework with auxiliary pointflow supervision, establishing a shared motion representation across human and robot interactions that enables embodied world models to learn more effectively from egocentric human data. We present a GRPO based post-training framework that enables failure aware optimization without paired failure video supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HF-WM achieves state-of-the-art performance in action-conditioned video generation, and further validate its effectiveness as a policy evaluator for downstream robotic tasks. video generation. Controllable video generation as an important extension of video foundation models, aims to introduce diverse external control signals beyond text conditioning to enable fine-grained control over generated content. Recent work on controllable generation incorporates a variety of conditioning signals into existing video foundation models, including spatial structural information (e.g., human poses egosim , depth maps gta , and skeletons oscar ), temporal dynamics (e.g., optical flow orthophys , motion trajectories irasim , and camera parameters tu2026embody4d ), as well as multimodal inputs such as reference images or audio. These methods typically inject external control signals into pretrained video diffusion models through dedicated condition encoders tesseract , cross-attention mechanisms trajectorycrafter , or ControlNet architectures yang2026neoverse , thereby constraining and guiding the generation process. -conditioned world models. Recent advances have positioned action-conditioned world models as a key interface between generative video modeling, action-conditioned dynamics prediction, and policy evaluation in embodied intelligence abot . IRASim irasim incorporates robotic trajectories into the video generation process, demonstrating the feasibility of synthesizing future visual states under explicit action conditions. Ctrl-World ctrl extends this paradigm to multi-view embodied generation, where three-view synthesis improves the spatial coverage of generated environments and yields practical gains in real-robot deployment. SC3-Eval sc3 further closes the loop by leveraging world models as offline policy evaluators, enabling policies to be assessed without costly physical rollouts. Despite recent progress, existing action-conditioned world models remain constrained by limited embodied data and failure coverage dreamdojo, oscar , motivating us to study how human object interaction data and counterfactual failure samples can improve the modeling of action consequences and physical dynamics. Learning Across Embodiments: From Human to Robot human Introducing human egocentric interaction data into action-conditioned world models first requires addressing the representational mismatch between human hand actions and robot arm actions. These two action forms differ naturally in degrees of freedom, dimensionality, and motion structure, making it difficult to share a common action conditioning space directly. Thanks to the Cosmos 3 foundation model cosmos3 , which has been pretrained on both human interaction data and embodied manipulation data, the model already possesses certain cross embodiment interaction priors, thereby partially reducing the domain gap between human hands and robot arms. Building on this prior, we adopt the 2D skeleton representation from OSCAR oscar , mapping human hand and robot arm actions into a shared spatial action space, thereby avoiding direct alignment between heterogeneous action vectors. With this unified action representation, human egocentric interaction data can be incorporated as effective augmentation data for training action-conditioned world models. Furthermore, we develop a dual-branch learning framework that couples video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction pointworld , where pointflow supervision guides the video branch to focus on motion regions that are truly relevant to physical interactions, enabling human interaction data to provide more effective supervision for embodied world model learning. By suppressing motion caused by viewpoint changes, the stabilized pointflow enables the model to better learn interaction dynamics from human demonstration data. title: RARA: Robust Policy Fine-Tuning through Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Pre-trained robot policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, provide a strong foundation for generalist robotic manipulation, but adapting them to new tasks with only a few demonstrations remains challenging. Directly fine-tuning a pre-trained policy often achieves strong in-distribution performance, yet it can distort the representations learned during pre-training and weaken the model's generalization ability under out-of-distribution shifts. We propose Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment (RARA), a two-stage adaptation method, to address this issue. First, RARA retrieves representation features from pretraining with similar task intent and motion, and aligns the policy's representations of the target demonstrations with the pre-trained representations of the retrieved demonstrations. Second, RARA fine-tunes the policy on the target demonstrations while limiting how much its representations of the retrieved demonstrations change during fine-tuning. By reducing the representation mismatch before action learning and preserving pre-trained knowledge during adaptation, RARA limits unnecessary representation drift during fine-tuning. Experiments with Diffusion Policy and GR00T on 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot show that RARA improves the average success of fine-tuning by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, and outperforms all compared baselines. Project page: https://shua-kang.github.io/RARA_robot/

title: CompactSplat: Spatially Adaptive Gaussian Distribution for Feedforward Scene Reconstruction
summary: Reconstructing 3D scenes from sparse views without per-scene optimization remains highly challenging, especially for recovering accurate geometry and fine textures. While recent feedforward approaches leverage generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for scene generation, they typically assign one or multiple Gaussians to each pixel. Such uniform allocation not only produces highly redundant representations by wasting primitives in homogeneous areas, but also fails to exploit the inherent geometric priors of planar surfaces, often resulting in sub-optimal structural modeling. To address these limitations, we present CompactSplat, a novel feedforward framework that enables a content-aware allocation of 3D Gaussians. By integrating texture-guided spatial partitioning with hierarchical sampling, CompactSplat adaptively distributes primitives - concentrating dense Gaussians in complex regions while tiling flat areas with expanded, scale-modulated primitives. Moreover, our framework inherently supports dynamic sparsity control at inference time, enabling seamless trade-offs between rendering fidelity and memory footprint without requiring network retraining. Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K, DL3DV, and ScanNet demonstrate that CompactSplat consistently outperforms prior methods on both standard metrics and high-resolution rendering consistency, achieving high-fidelity reconstructions with significantly fewer primitives.
full_text: CompactSplat is a highly efficient feed-forward network that predicts 3D scene representations from sparse input images. While previous methods typically allocate one or more Gaussians per pixel—leading to excessive primitives and spatially redundant representations, CompactSplat adaptively allocates primitives based on regional complexity. It concentrates dense Gaussians in texturally rich areas while deploying expanded, scale-modulated primitives in flat regions. This paradigm enables high-fidelity reconstruction with substantially fewer primitives. Crucially, it inherently supports dynamic sparsity control at inference time, allowing seamless trade-offs between visual fidelity and memory footprint across diverse deployment constraints. teaser para:abstract Reconstructing 3D scenes from sparse views without per-scene optimization remains highly challenging, especially for recovering accurate geometry and fine textures. Such uniform allocation not only produces highly redundant representations by wasting primitives in homogeneous areas, but also fails to exploit the inherent geometric priors of planar surfaces, often resulting in sub-optimal structural modeling. To address these limitations, we present CompactSplat, a novel feedforward framework that enables a content-aware allocation of 3D Gaussians. By integrating texture-guided spatial partitioning with hierarchical sampling, CompactSplat adaptively distributes primitives — concentrating dense Gaussians in complex regions while tiling flat areas with expanded, scale-modulated primitives. Moreover, our framework inherently supports dynamic sparsity control at inference time, enabling seamless trade-offs between rendering fidelity and memory footprint without requiring network retraining. Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K, DL3DV, and ScanNet demonstrate that CompactSplat consistently outperforms prior methods on both standard metrics and high-resolution rendering consistency, achieving high-fidelity reconstructions with significantly fewer primitives. Introduction Recovering geometrically accurate and visually consistent 3D scenes from sparse views is a fundamental problem for immersive VR, gaming, and digital content creation. The recent success of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d has significantly advanced this field by representing scenes as collections of 3D Gaussians, enabling real-time rendering with high visual fidelity. Existing methods for constructing such representations generally follow two paradigms. Traditional approaches rely on dense multi-view captures and COLMAP-based~ schoenberger2016sfm point cloud initialization, followed by computationally expensive per-scene optimization. To avoid this bottleneck, feed-forward approaches have recently gained increasing attention. By leveraging pretrained models, they directly predict 3D Gaussians from sparse inputs in a single forward pass, eliminating per-scene optimization and enabling fast, scalable 3D reconstruction. Despite their rapid inference, many existing feed-forward methods remain inefficient in their primitive allocation. Natural scenes exhibit substantial spatial variation in texture and geometric complexity, yet prior methods typically adopt a rigid pixel-wise prediction paradigm, assigning one~ chen2024mvsplat,xu2024depthsplat,he2026surfsplat or multiple~ charatan2024pixelsplat,tang2024hisplat Gaussians to every pixel. This uniform allocation forces the network to populate large, textureless regions with thousands of primitives. Consequently, the generated 3D representations can suffer from substantial spatial redundancy. This redundancy increases representation storage costs and motivates more compact 3D priors for downstream tasks. To address this issue, we introduce CompactSplat, a novel feed-forward framework for high-fidelity 3D reconstruction with content-aware Gaussian allocation. Instead of retaining a primitive at every pixel, CompactSplat allocates Gaussians according to image texture, using sparse primitives in homogeneous regions while concentrating denser predictions in areas with rich texture. To achieve this adaptive allocation, we decouple the primitive generation process into two complementary components. First, a Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP) analyzes the input views to estimate regional texture complexity and partition each image with a quadtree. Second, a Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS) uses this guidance to sample explicit Gaussian attributes from a pooled multi-resolution attribute pyramid. Together, these components enable CompactSplat to adapt its primitive density to the input texture, reducing spatial redundancy while retaining strong reconstruction quality. Crucially, CompactSplat provides a unified paradigm for controllable inference. Owing to the scale-aware synergy between TAP and HPS, our framework naturally supports dynamic sparsity control at inference time. By modulating a single partition threshold, the model can select different trade-offs between rendering fidelity and primitive count---without requiring any network retraining or auxiliary modules. This intrinsic adaptability provides an on-the-fly mechanism to select different representation sizes using a single set of pretrained weights. Ultimately, CompactSplat establishes a more compact paradigm for 3D representation. By replacing rigid pixel-wise allocation with texture-driven primitive allocation, our approach adapts to spatial variations in image content. In our experiments, it delivers high-fidelity reconstructions with fewer primitives. This allocation transforms dense, redundant outputs into compact 3D representations with a tunable primitive count. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We propose CompactSplat, a feed-forward framework for compact sparse-view 3D reconstruction. By combining a Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP) with a Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS), our method adaptively allocates 3D Gaussians based on image texture, significantly reducing spatial redundancy. We introduce a controllable inference paradigm for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. With a single partition threshold, CompactSplat supports dynamic, on-the-fly sparsity control. This capability enables seamless trade-offs between visual fidelity and primitive count using a single set of network weights, completely eliminating the need for sparsity-specific retraining. Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K and ACID demonstrate that CompactSplat achieves competitive quality with fewer primitives. It retains strong performance on both standard metrics and high-resolution rendering consistency, while cross-dataset evaluation on DTU, DL3DV, and ScanNet reveals quality--compactness trade-offs. Related Works 3D Gaussian Splatting Since the advent of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2021nerf , novel view synthesis has advanced rapidly, evolving from implicit MLPs to grid-based~ muller2022instant,fridovich2022plenoxels and anti-aliased~ barron2021mip,barron2022mip representations. To further accelerate rendering, recent paradigms shifted towards explicit point-based architectures. Notably, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d revolutionized the field by modeling scenes with semi-transparent, anisotropic ellipsoids, enabling photorealistic, real-time rendering via differentiable rasterization. Consequently, a proliferation of extensions has emerged to refine 3DGS. These include optimizations for training stability~ cheng2024gaussianpro,zhang2024fregs,radl2024stopthepop,diolatzis2024n , anti-aliasing techniques~ yan2024multi,yu2024mip,song2024sa,liang2024analytic , and adaptations for dynamic scenes~ luiten2023dynamic,wu20234d,wan2024superpoint,huang2023sc,he2024s4d . Additionally, several works focus on compressing these representations to reduce storage and accelerate inference~ girish2024eagles,navaneet2024compgs,niedermayr2024compressed,lee2024compact,fan2024lightgaussian,chen2024hac . Generalizable 3D Reconstruction To bypass the computationally expensive per-scene optimization of traditional 3DGS, recent literature has explored feedforward models that directly predict Gaussian attributes from sparse inputs. Splatter Image~ szymanowicz2024splatter pioneered the translation of 2D images into Gaussian parameter maps. Subsequent frameworks integrated geometric priors to enhance spatial understanding; for instance, pixelSplat~ charatan2024pixelsplat utilized epipolar geometry, while MVSplat~ chen2024mvsplat and DepthSplat~ xu2024depthsplat leveraged cost volumes and cross-task depth interactions. Further advancements addressed specific challenges, such as expanding synthesis ranges~ wang2024freesplat , improving geometric surfaces via 2DGS~ he2026surfsplat , and handling unposed inputs~ kang2025selfsplat,jiang2025anysplat . VGGT~ wang2025vggt and MV-DUSt3R~ tang2025mv likewise reconstruct uncalibrated views, while CompactSplat assumes known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Other pipelines introduced triplane representations~ zou2024triplane,xu2024agg and canonical space generation~ ye2024no for feedforward 3D reconstruction and generation. SplatFormer~ chen2024splatformer instead uses a point transformer to refine an already optimized Gaussian scene for novel-view extrapolation. Pixel-wise prediction strategies, including multi-layered approaches like HiSplat~ tang2024hisplat , can generate redundant primitives in homogeneous regions. Recent methods explore alternatives: TokenGS~ ren2026tokengs uses learnable queries to decouple Gaussian count from image resolution and view count, while C3G~ an2025c3g predicts a compact Gaussian set from unposed multi-view images using learned queries. VolSplat~ wang2026volsplat lifts features using predicted depth and decodes Gaussians from occupied voxels. Off The Grid~ moreau2026off detects subpixel primitive positions and adapts patch density using image entropy. CompactSplat adopts a content-aware allocation paradigm based on an image-space quadtree. TAP concentrates finer partitions in textured regions, while HPS samples pooled Gaussian attributes and modulates primitive scales according to block footprints. This spatial hierarchy supports inference-time quality--compactness control with one checkpoint, reducing per-view redundancy while preserving detail at the selected operating point. Method Model Architecture Building upon the robust feature extraction paradigms established in recent feed-forward models~ he2026surfsplat,xu2024depthsplat , CompactSplat employs a dual-path encoder to capture both multi-view correspondences and single-view geometric priors. For the single-view branch, we utilize a pretrained monocular depth backbone (e.g., Depth Anything V2~ yang2024depth ) to extract structural and semantic cues, which are particularly beneficial for ill-posed regions lacking cross-view overlaps. Concurrently, the multi-view branch processes the inputs through self- and cross-attention mechanisms~ vaswani2017attention,liu2021swin to construct plane-sweep cost volumes~ chen2024mvsplat,collins1996space , enforcing strict multi-view consistency. The complementary features from both branches are then concatenated to form a unified volumetric representation. This fused feature volume is subsequently fed into a multi-scale 2D U-Net~ ronneberger2015u architecture. Unlike prior works that deterministically upsample all features into a single, full-resolution map for pixel-wise Gaussian prediction, our architecture decouples primitive generation to eliminate spatial redundancy, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:model . Specifically, we introduce the Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP), which analyzes spatial frequency and regional complexity from the inputs to produce a set of hierarchical partition masks. title: JitterVLA: A Replay Benchmark for Motion Quality in VLA-Driven Human-Robot Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies issue sparse targets whose arrival at the robot controller is delayed and irregular, so a reasonable predicted action can still produce abrupt motion near people. Remedies are evaluated on different streams, delays and metrics. JitterVLA replays identical commands and arrival traces through alternative controllers, isolating the controller's effect. We apply it to synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, three open VLA pipelines (838 episodes) and a physical UR3. Interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk for every source, by 83% (615 to 106 m/s^3) on human motion with 200 ms delay, at a 2.0 cm tracking cost, and the effect replicated on 598 new episodes; jerk-limited generation lowered jerk further at a larger cost. Entropy-discontinuity associations had opposite, replicated signs in two pipelines, and entropy gating helped in one but not the other. On the UR3, interpolation lowered accelerometer-derived jerk by 3.0-14.0% in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not resolve the contrast. JitterVLA supports screening before human-centred studies; code and data will be released.

Introduction A person hands a manipulator an object, guides its target, or works beside it. The high-level policy produces a sensible action, but its targets arrive sparsely and at irregular times, so the low-level controller receives discontinuous goals. What the person experiences is not the predicted action but the motion the robot executes. VLA policies such as OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla run at a few hertz, one to two orders of magnitude below the robot's control loop~ jiang2026fast , and remote or shared inference adds network delay. Human-robot interaction (HRI) research links onset latency to teleoperation performance~ rakita2020onset,khalil2026nonlinear and robot motion to observers' responses and perceived safety~ kulic2007physiological,rubagotti2022perceived . Timing is not only latency. A constant delay shifts every command, whereas timing jitter (variation in delay and arrival spacing, including bunching) changes which targets the controller sees and when. Remedies exist at several layers: action chunking and asynchronous execution~ zhao2023learning,black2026real,zhao2025vla,guo2026action,kim2025fine , interpolation and jerk-limited trajectory generation such as Ruckig~ berscheid2021jerk , geometry-guided jerk reduction in VLA execution~ yun2026groove , and stiffness adaptation~ ferraguti2013tank . Each paper evaluates its remedy with its own inputs, delays, plant and metrics, so the remedies cannot be compared fairly. JitterVLA addresses that comparison problem. It evaluates the middle of the chain (command stream, timing, controller, executed motion) before candidate behaviours are shown to people. It does not replace human studies. We ask four research questions (RQ1--RQ4). RQ1 (timing): how do timing irregularities change motion-quality proxies for identical command streams? RQ2 (control): how do stepped, interpolated, entropy-gated, constant-gain and jerk-limited strategies move the jerk--tracking trade-off? RQ3 (cross-source): do these relationships hold across synthetic, human and three VLA action representations, and on new episode draws? RQ4 (physical): are the contrasts observable on a real UR3 under a bounded protocol? Contributions. (1) A paired replay benchmark and protocol that holds the command source and delay realization fixed while varying the controller. (2) An evaluation that progresses from controlled synthetic reaches to 20-person human motion, three VLA pipelines with a planned replication on 598 new episodes, and measured network traces (Table~ tab:design ). (3) Findings: a consistent jerk--tracking trade-off for interpolation, representation-dependent uncertainty associations, and a failure of entropy gating on some inputs. (4) A bounded UR3 check, including a null result for the planned position-derived metric. Code, the transformed VLA streams, the human windows and the traces will be released. Terms. Latency is delay; jitter is its variation. Command discontinuity is the spatial jump between successive targets or chunks. Jerk is the benchmark plant's jerk proxy, or a sensor-derived estimate on the UR3. Tracking error is the root-mean-square error (RMSE) against the undelayed reference. Jerk, tracking error, log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) and spectral arc length (SPARC)~ balasubramanian2015smoothness are motion-quality proxies; comfort, preference and safety were not measured. Benchmark design Paired replay. Within a comparison, every controller receives the same source (episode, person or synthetic reach) and the same delay realization (seed or trace offset). Differences are therefore attributable to the controller rather than to different stochastic inputs. Statistics are paired over the source unit: episodes, people or seeds. Intervals are 95 unit bootstraps (5000 resamples), not time-sample intervals. Timing pipeline. For VLAs, measured inference service times from one RTX~5090 feed a single-worker first-in, first-out (FIFO) queue. A network delay is then added: zero, Gamma-distributed with mean 0--400\,ms (shape 2), or sequential samples from 12\,h of measured lab-path traces: local area network (LAN), internet round trip, and a cold HTTPS request. Delivery is in order, and the newest delivered target wins. Separating the mean delay from its spread lets RQ1 test jitter as well as latency. Plant and controllers. Delivered targets drive a generic three-axis point mass (3\,kg, critically damped impedance, 20\,ms force lag, 3000\,N/s force-rate cap, 1\,ms steps). It is not a UR3 model; absolute jerk values are not hardware predictions. Controllers: B0 holds each delivered target (stepped). B2 interpolates linearly over one command period. A2 adds entropy-gated stiffness to interpolation. B3 (Ruckig, jerk limit 25\,m/s ) is an explicit jerk-limited trajectory generator. Interpolation is the simple smoothing baseline; B3 tests whether gains survive a stronger motion-generation method. A constant-gain grid (8 fixed stiffness values, stepped and interpolated) asks whether gating beats the best attainable constant gain at no worse tracking, rather than an obviously stiff baseline. We report 99th-percentile (p99) and root-mean-square (RMS) jerk and tracking RMSE, plus LDLJ and SPARC. LDLJ and SPARC are established dimensionless movement-smoothness measures, and they check that the conclusions do not depend on p99 jerk alone. Evidence hierarchy. Protocols were frozen before data were seen: frozen analyses (v1.1, v1.3), a planned replication on new draws (v1.4), post-outcome robustness checks (v1.5: traces, LDLJ/SPARC, Ruckig, pi0.5~ intelligence2025pi_ ), and an exploratory hardware follow-up (v1.2a). We label results accordingly and never pool across these labels. Results R1: interpolation trades jerk for tracking on every source (RQ1--3; frozen, replicated). Interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk and raised tracking error for synthetic, human and all three VLA sources (Table~ tab:interp ). The effect held on the new episode draws. The reduction is not confined to synthetic or learned commands: it appears when replaying reaches from 20 people. Timing irregularity, not mean delay, drove stepped-goal jerk. In the frozen v1.0 sweep on synthetic reaches, pure fixed delays of 0, 200 and 400\,ms left stepped p99 jerk unchanged (535, 534 and 533\,m/s ), whereas a 200\,ms delay spread raised it to 623. Under the three measured traces, the B2 B0 direction held for every source; for example, pi0-FAST gave , and \,m/s for LAN, internet and HTTPS. LDLJ and SPARC favoured B2 in every tested cell, and no interval crossed zero (post-outcome). The generic plant's force-rate cap accentuates stepped-goal differences, so these magnitudes are not hardware predictions. R2: lower jerk is not free (RQ2). Figure~ fig:frontier shows the geometry on human input at 200\,ms mean delay. Stepped B0 averages 615\,m/s at 9.91\,cm tracking error. Interpolation (B2) moves to 106\,m/s at 11.87\,cm. Jerk-limited B3 reaches 23.5\,m/s , but at 14.79\,cm. Entropy-gated A2 (150\,m/s , 16.72\,cm) is worse than B2 on both axes for this input. The benchmark thus identifies a useful intervention, a costly one, and a plausible heuristic that fails. R3: uncertainty is representation-dependent (RQ3; frozen, replicated). In OpenVLA, mean translational-token entropy was weakly negatively associated with the successive goal step (mean within-episode Spearman [ , ]; new 200: [ , ]). In pi0-FAST, chunk-token entropy was positively associated with the chunk-boundary jump ( [ , ]; new 199: [ , ]) (Fig.~ fig:uncertainty ). Both directions replicated. Because the events and representations differ, the defensible conclusion is not that one model's uncertainty is better. Instead, whether uncertainty tracks downstream discontinuity depends on the pipeline, so uncertainty-based control needs pipeline-specific validation. Controller outcomes follow the same split. On pi0-FAST, A2 lowered p99 jerk against B2 by 208\,m/s (new draw: 199) for +0.18\,cm (+0.16) tracking. It also beat the best attainable constant gain on feasible subsets ( \,m/s on 66/80; on 162/199); feasibility was incomplete, and that audit was post hoc for the original set. On OpenVLA, A2 did not help: +2.3 [ , 5.2]; new draw +3.4 [1.9, 4.8]. Table~ tab:replication summarises what replicated: all pre-registered pi0-FAST contrasts (28/28) and 22/28 for OpenVLA, whose six misses were mostly cells near zero. R4: a bounded physical check (RQ4). The frozen v1.2 protocol replayed an author teleoperation trace in 30 small-amplitude runs on a UR3 CB3 at 125\,Hz. Position-derived p99 filtered jerk was 77.7--81.9\,m/s across conditions, and the planned contrast was not resolved at that logging resolution. That null result exposed a measurement limit, so an explicitly exploratory v1.2a session repeated the same motion plan while logging the robot's tool-flange accelerometer (Fig.~ fig:physical ). In direct mode, B0 exceeded B2 in all three paired repeats at each delay, by 3.07\,m/s on average without added delay and 5.79 with 200\,ms mean delay. B2 reductions were 3.0--14.0 , and plant-mode differences had mixed signs. The sensor read p99 3.79 when stationary and 43.05--51.52 during motion; its gain, bandwidth and the source of the moving signal were not established. The same session's position metric also showed positive direct contrasts, so the accelerometer is not the sole source of the direction. It does not validate the point-mass plant as a UR3 model, and it is not a calibrated tool-centre-point jerk or safety result. Code structure, usage and maintenance The Python code has four parts: core/ (command timing and FIFO delivery, the impedance plant, the paired stepped, interpolated and entropy-gated conditions and their metrics; NumPy and SciPy), benchmark/ (frozen protocols, experiment drivers, paired analysis, and the v1.5 add-ons: Ruckig jerk-limited controllers, LDLJ/SPARC and trace delays), jittervla/ (the command-line tool) and tests/ (34 unit tests); scripts/ holds the UR3 session and analysis tools. python -m jittervla replay - -csv my.csv replays one's own time-stamped targets and stream - -npz a stored VLA stream, each printing every condition under the same arrivals. The code will be released under Apache-2.0 after the review period, in a public repository with versioned releases and an archived snapshot linked from the pr

title: Cooperative Aerial Transportation of a Payload with a Sliding Cable Attachment
summary: This paper presents a dual-quadrotor hook- suspended transport system for cooperative aerial manipulation of a payload that is not rigidly attached to a fixed point along the cable. Two quadrotors are connected by a single inextensible cable that passes through a frictionless hook mounted on the payload, allowing the cable to slide between its two segments. This introduces a cable-distribution variable that couples the quadrotor motion, cable geometry, and payload dynamics. A feasible reference-generation framework is formulated using the desired payload pose, cable distribution, and system shape while satisfying the cable-length constraint and elliptical workspace. The quadrotors track the geometrically generated trajectories while maintaining positive cable tension and respecting actuator limits. The payload pose is estimated from the system geometry, and its measured position is used only to validate the desired trajectory. The approach is evaluated through experimental demonstrations.
full_text: Cooperative Aerial Transportation of a Payload with a Sliding Cable Attachment dept. Electrical and Computer Engineering \\ Oakland University\\ Rochester, MI, US \\ tilaguylez@oakland.edu This paper presents a dual-quadrotor hook-suspended transport system for cooperative aerial manipulation of a payload that is not rigidly attached to a fixed point along the cable. Two quadrotors are connected by a single inextensible cable that passes through a frictionless hook mounted on the payload, allowing the cable to slide between its two segments. This introduces a cable-distribution variable that couples the quadrotor motion, cable geometry, and payload dynamics. A feasible reference-generation framework is formulated using the desired payload pose, cable distribution, and system shape while satisfying the cable-length constraint and elliptical workspace. The quadrotors track the geometrically generated trajectories while maintaining positive cable tension and respecting actuator limits. The payload pose is estimated from the system geometry, and its measured position is used only to validate the desired trajectory. The approach is evaluated through experimental demonstrations. INTRODUCTION Cooperative aerial systems have expanded the capabilities of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) beyond surveillance and conventional logistics. Through distributed actuation and coordinated motion, multiple UAVs can perform tasks that exceed the physical limitations of a single platform, including heavy-payload transportation, infrastructure interaction, and emergency response Kardasz_2016,Garg_2023,Ostermann_2025 . Aerial logistics has therefore received increasing attention for rapid operation in remote or hard-to-reach environments, motivating scalable and autonomous multi-robot transportation strategies Moshref-Javadi_2021 . Cable-suspended transportation provides several advantages for aerial manipulation. By separating the payload from the aerial platform, the cable reduces the direct transmission of disturbances and allows the UAVs to maintain a safer distance from the transported object. It can also facilitate payload attachment and release while the aerial vehicles remain in flight Eskandaripour_2023,Pounds_2011 . Early studies primarily considered payloads suspended from a single UAV, which inherently limits the available lifting capacity and controllability of the payload. Cooperative multi-UAV systems address these limitations by distributing the payload weight among multiple aerial vehicles and coordinating the cable forces applied to the load Michael_2011 . Several approaches have addressed cooperative cable-suspended transportation through differential flatness, coordinated rotorcraft motion, inertial sensing, autonomous hook-based grasping, and nonlinear model predictive control Kotaru2017DifferentialFlatness,GarciaDeMarina2019Flexible,Xie2020CooperativeTransport,Antal2023HookBasedGrasping,Sun2023NonlinearMPC . These methods enable trajectory generation, cooperative transport, payload grasping, and constrained full-pose manipulation. However, they generally assume fixed cable attachment points and do not consider cable-length redistribution through a sliding payload-mounted hook. Cable-suspended aerial lifting is commonly divided into setup, pull, and raise stages Cruz_2015,Estevez_2024 . While the pull and raise stages have received significant attention, setup often requires manual cable attachment, reducing autonomy and limiting operation in hazardous or inaccessible environments. A catenary robot, formed by two aerial vehicles connected by a flexible cable, can manipulate the cable to interact with objects DAntonio_2021 . However, engaging a payload-mounted hook allows the cable to slide, coupling UAV motion, cable geometry, payload dynamics, and cable-length distribution. Motivated by this gap, this work introduces the Dual-Quadrotor Hook-Suspended Transport System (DQ-HSTS), shown in Fig.~ fig:mainfigure . Two quadrotors are connected by a single cable passing through a frictionless hook rigidly attached to the payload. Unlike conventional systems, the cable slides through the hook, redistributing its total length between the two cable segments. This paper addresses quadrotor coordination for payload-pose and cable-distribution control without fixed cable attachments. The contributions are threefold: i) the DQ-HSTS, in which a cable slides through a payload-mounted hook; ii) trajectory generation parameterized by payload pose, cable distribution , and system shape ; and iii) coordinated trajectory tracking under tension, geometric, and actuator constraints, validated in experiments. Sliding hook-payload sec:problem_statement Cooperative aerial transportation using cables traditionally assumes that the payload is rigidly attached to one or more aerial vehicles through fixed cable connections. In contrast, this work considers a Dual-Quadrotor Hook-Suspended Transport System (DQ-HSTS), where two quadrotors are connected by a single cable that passes through a frictionless hook rigidly attached to the payload (see Fig.~ fig:free-body ). Unlike conventional systems, the cable is allowed to slide freely through the hook. This dynamically changes the distribution of the cable length between the left and right segments while preserving the total cable length, heavily coupling the cable geometry, payload dynamics, and quadrotor motion. System Description and Kinematics [Dual-Quadrotor Hook-Suspended Transport System] The DQ-HSTS is a mechanical system composed of two quadrotors attached to the ends of a single ideal cable. The cable is assumed to be massless, inextensible, perfectly flexible, and taut. It passes through a frictionless hook, rigidly fixed at a constant distance from the payload, allowing the cable to slide while maintaining equal tension in both segments. title: SmolWAM: A Latent World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Robot Learning with World Models Workshop. Code: https://github.com/iitimii/SmolWAM Project: https://smolwam.vercel.app/
summary: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices. We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.
full_text: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices. We present , a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, succeeds in 95.5 of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57\,ms and 2.3\,TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4\,GiB of GPU memory, 11 faster than its teacher with 18.5 fewer FLOPs and 3.2 less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion. Code: github.com/iitimii/SmolWAM ; project page: smolwam.vercel.app . Introduction sec:intro World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's next actions together with the observations they should produce~ kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero,lu2026wamsurvey . ~ kim2026cosmospolicy builds one from the Cosmos-Predict2 video model~ nvidia2025cosmos by treating actions, future observations, and values as latent frames of a single denoising sequence, and reaches 98.5 success on LIBERO~ liu2023libero . Its inference stack, however, was built for video generation: a 4.8B-parameter T5-XXL text encoder~ raffel2020t5 , a VAE that encodes a 33-frame clip per query, and five denoising steps of a 2B-parameter transformer over 1,764 tokens, which cost 624\,ms, 42.6\,TFLOP, and 7.55\,GiB per 16-action chunk on an A100 even with cached text features. Efficient policies usually give up the world model or the video prior: compact vision-language-action (VLA) models such as SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvla and TurboVLA~ xie2026turbovla predict only actions, and Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam skips future prediction at test time. We ask whether a strong pretrained WAM can itself be made small while still predicting the future. We present (Fig.~ fig:overview ). Our premise is that much of the teacher's cost comes from an interface designed for video generation, not from what control requires. reuses the trunk's weights, token positions, and rectified-flow readout; it encodes single frames through a small adapter, replaces T5-XXL with cached BERT features~ devlin2019bert padded to preserve the trunk's attention sinks, keeps 12 of 28 blocks, and reads actions from 28 state-conditioned queries. Most changes break the trunk zero-shot, so a distillation curriculum recovers from pruning before compaction. We contribute (i)~ , which retains 97 of its teacher's success at 11 lower latency; (ii)~a method, with a diagnostic behind each step, for deriving compact WAMs from pretrained video WAMs (Sec.~ sec:method ), including three pitfalls (attention-sink padding, jointly fatal blocks, and chunks that cannot be cut short); and (iii)~findings that the compressed world head preserves motion forecasting, whereas latent-action cascades or visual-reward fine-tuning degrade control (Sec.~ sec:experiments ). Related Work sec:related Generalist VLAs bring pretraining to control~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,openx2024,octo2024,black2025pi0,pertsch2025fast , often with diffusion~ chi2023diffusionpolicy or chunked~ zhao2023act action heads; OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025openvlaoft , TinyVLA~ wen2025tinyvla , SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvla , and TurboVLA~ xie2026turbovla speed them up; borrows TurboVLA's principles but retains a world model. Latent world models learn dynamics in feature space~ zhou2025dinowm,assran2025vjepa2,zheng2025flare,maes2026leworldmodel,gao2026fastleworldmodel , and GR-1~ wu2024gr1 , PAD~ guo2024pad , and WorldVLA~ cen2025worldvla generate future images and actions jointly. Recent WAMs build on video models~ kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero and add action evaluation~ zhou2026tau0wm , modalities~ nvidia2026cosmos3 , object state~ liu2026oawam , geometry~ lopetegui2026sawam , or latent actions~ chen2026abotm05 ; Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam drops future prediction at test time and Light-WAM~ li2026lightwam decodes actions from a smaller video backbone, whereas reads future latents from its action pass. SmolWAM sec:method Teacher: Cosmos Policy On LIBERO, the video diffusion transformer (DiT)~ peebles2023dit of (28 blocks, 1.96B parameters) denoises nine latent frames of tokens (Fig.~ fig:overview ): a blank frame, the robot state , the wrist and third-person camera latents and , a chunk of actions, and, at time , the state , the camera latents and , and a value . Images are encoded by the Wan2.1 VAE~ wan2025 from 33-frame clips, and the instruction enters through cross-attention to 512 T5-XXL embeddings. The model is a rectified flow~ liu2023rectifiedflow,lipman2023flowmatching : for it predicts the velocity , which gives the closed-form clean estimate . Generated frames start at ( ); the released pipeline takes five steps. Deriving SmolWAM from the teacher sec:derivation Single-frame latents. encodes each camera image once, as a single frame, with the Wan2.1 encoder (54M parameters). Such latents raise the teacher's action error (normalized L1 of its one-step chunk to the demonstration) from 0.0089 to 0.038; a 0.5M-parameter adapter maps them to clip-mode latents and restores it to 0.0092. Cached text that keeps the attention sinks. We replace T5-XXL with cached BERT-base~ devlin2019bert features of the instruction, projected to the context width. The trunk's cross-attention has bias-free key and value projections, so T5's zero-padded positions contribute zero logits and values and act as an attention sink~ xiao2024streamingllm : truncating the context to 32 or 128 positions drops the teacher to 0/5 closed-loop successes, and restoring the removed softmax mass analytically returns it to 5/5, matching the padded attention to . thus zero-pads the BERT features to 512 positions; six zero-initialized vision-to-language layers from TurboVLA~ xie2026turbovla let the text attend to the images. Boundary-preserving pruning. Block influence ~ men2025shortgpt is highest for blocks 0, 1, and 25--27, while blocks 3--22 are individually close to the identity. Zero-shot screens (5 episodes each) show that removals do not compose: skipping block 1, 26, or 27 fails every episode, skipping block 7, 14, or 20 alone fails none, and skipping four near-identity blocks (12--15) together fails all. keeps blocks 0--2 and 19--27 (0.85B parameters). State-conditioned action queries. A zero-initialized MLP adds the robot state to 28 action queries that replace the 196-token action frame at its original positions. Beyond these queries we keep only the blank and image frames (1,008 tokens). Zero-shot, dropping the future-state and value frames barely changes the action error (0.009 to ), but dropping the blank (0.30) or state (0.058) frame or compacting the vector frames to 28 tokens (0.21) does, so the layout is learned. One-pass readout. evaluates its trunk once at with fixed noise and reads the action chunk and future latents from , so its actions never condition on a denoised future; as Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam also finds, acting does not need one, and the teacher solves all 60 screening episodes in one step (Table~ tab:main ). The future latents form its world head, supervised in training and never decoded. Distillation with a layout curriculum sec:training We train on 68,830 observations sampled every fourth step from the 1,700 successful LIBERO demonstrations released with , using the teacher's one-step predictions of the action chunk and future latents, and , cached at fixed noise (66 min on one A100). As in pruning and distillation of language models~ muralidharan2024minitron,hinton2015distilling , the loss matches the student's one-step estimates to both the demonstrations and the teacher, plus 0.1-weighted terms for the state and value frames while they exist. Pruning and compaction are separate distribution shifts, so the student, initialized from the kept teacher blocks, trains in the teacher's 1,764-token layout for the first 1,000 of 5,000 steps and in the compact layout afterward (AdamW; learning rate for inherited and for new weights; batch 32; bf16) in 3.6\,h on one A100 (App.~ app:training ). Experiments sec:experiments We ask (Q1) how much of the teacher's success retains, (Q2) where its savings come from, (Q3) whether it remains a world model, and (Q4) whether richer WAM components help. Setup. LIBERO~ liu2023libero has four suites of ten tasks; we use the teacher's observation pipeline (wrist and third-person images at 224\,px, proprioception, 16-action chunks executed open loop), seed 195, and 10 trials per task (400 episodes). A 60-episode screening set (3 tasks per suite, 5 trials each) includes the tasks an earlier pruned student failed most, so it scores below the full protocol. Latency is the wall-clock time from observation to action chunk on one A100-SXM4-40GB (batch 1, bf16), including preprocessing and VAE encoding, with text features cached for every model; FLOPs are counted with PyTorch's FlopCounterMode, attention included. Q1: retains most of the teacher's success. succeeds in 382/400 episodes (95.5 ; 95 Wilson interval 93.0--97.1) against the teacher's 393/400 (98.2 ; 96.4--99.1); App.~ app:rollouts shows both from the same initial states. We detect no difference on Spatial and Object; the deficit lies in the multi-step Goal (94 vs.\ 99) and Long (89 vs.\ 97) suites, where failed rollouts usually complete the first subgoal and stall on the second. An earlier student that removed only 8 blocks and recovered with LoRA~ hu2022lora distillation (19.7M trainable parameters, under an hour on one L4, no demonstrations) on 414 teacher-rollout observations reached 87.5 ; differs in distillation coverage, full fine-tuning, and the learned layout, effects we have not separated. title: Multi-Modal Graph Neural Network-Inspired Vessel Identification and Tracking for UAV-Based Maritime Surveillance
summary: The unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based maritime surveillance is becoming an important part of maritime Internet of Things (IoT) and intelligent transportation systems. It provides a flexible and cost-effective way to large-scale maritime traffic monitoring. However, achieving robust situational awareness remains challenging in practical maritime environments. The main challenges arise from heterogeneous sensing modalities, adverse imaging conditions, and spatial misalignment caused by UAV motion. To address these problems, this paper proposes an airborne multi-modal graph learning-driven framework, termed AMGT, for vessel identification and tracking in UAV-assisted maritime IoT. Specifically, visible and infrared images are first aligned and fused through a multi-parameter perspective transformation model. This improves visual perception under low visibility and complex illumination conditions. Automatic identification system (AIS) messages are then temporally synchronized using interpolation and linear prediction. To detect small and oriented vessels, we develop a mixed-modality MAir-YOLOv8-OBB detector, followed by the MAir-SORT algorithm for stable vessel tracking. We further design a graph learning-driven association network to model temporal dynamics and spatial dependencies among vessels and between vessels and UAVs. A motion-aware coordinate unification (MCU) strategy is also introduced to reduce nonlinear misalignment caused by UAV motion. Experiments on the MAP-M2UAV50 dataset show that AMGT achieves high accuracy and efficiency. The results demonstrate its potential for UAV-assisted maritime IoT applications, including vessel monitoring, traffic situational awareness, and intelligent maritime transportation services. The dataset and code will be available at https://github.com/MAPGroup/AMGT.
