The dataset and code will be available at https://github.com/MAPGroup/AMGT. Maritime Internet of Things (MIoT), maritime surveillance, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), multimodal sensor fusion, vessel identification and tracking. Introduction ith the development of the low-altitude economy, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are being increasingly integrated with terrestrial, coastal, and shipborne networks 11165289 . This integration forms an air-ground collaborative system and provides new infrastructure for maritime Internet of Things (IoT). In this system, UAVs can collect maritime traffic information from flexible viewpoints. Coastal and shipborne stations can support communication and data transmission. A central controller can further process the collected information and support decision-making. Therefore, UAV-assisted maritime IoT is becoming an important enabling technology for next-generation intelligent transportation systems (ITS), especially for large-scale maritime traffic monitoring and management. The low-altitude sensing, communication, computing, and control (SCCC) system provides a basic architecture for ITS-oriented maritime surveillance. The SCCC system in Fig. fig: sccc system consists of UAV platforms, coastal or shipborne base stations, and a central controller. These components work together to support real-time perception, information exchange, data processing, and decision-making. Different from traditional passive monitoring, maritime surveillance in IoT-enabled ITS is moving toward a closed-loop process. Such a closed-loop process requires continuous traffic sensing, multisource data transmission, vessel-state analysis, and adaptive control. These capabilities are important for trajectory analysis, traffic optimization, collision avoidance, and emergency response 10869306,wang2024deep . In this way, UAV-assisted SCCC systems can improve maritime traffic safety and efficiency, while also supporting the development of the low-altitude economy. Recent studies have explored system-level co-design and optimization for UAV-assisted intelligent systems, particularly the joint coordination of communication, computing, and control resources 10379519,tu2022resource,11142291 . These studies highlight the importance of cross-domain resource coordination for reliable UAV-enabled services. As illustrated in Fig. 1, reliable maritime situational awareness within such an SCCC system relies on continuous perception and effective processing of heterogeneous information collected from dynamic UAV platforms. Although UAV platforms provide flexible sensing capability, robust maritime situational awareness is still challenging. A single sensing modality is often insufficient for complex maritime environments. Visible cameras provide rich appearance information, but they are sensitive to illumination changes, weather degradation, and limited fields of view. Infrared (IR) cameras can capture object outlines under adverse conditions, such as nighttime, haze, and fog. IR cameras can therefore complement visible-light sensors. However, image-based observations alone cannot reliably provide vessel identity and navigation information such as MMSI, course, and speed. By contrast, the automatic identification system (AIS) provides important maritime information, such as maritime mobile service identity (MMSI), course, and speed. Nevertheless, AIS messages may suffer from low update rates and missing data and may be unavailable for small or non-cooperative vessels. Therefore, it is necessary to fuse visible, IR, AIS, and UAV flight data for accurate and complete maritime perception. UAV motion further increases the difficulty of multi-source data fusion sun2018robust . Existing vessel association methods 10159572,yang2022multi,qu2023improving,liu2026nav mainly focus on shore and ship-based surveillance systems. In contrast, UAVs continuously change their altitude and attitude, including pitch, yaw, and roll. These changes introduce nonlinear spatial discrepancies between image coordinates and geographic coordinates. The problem becomes more serious when data from cameras, AIS receivers, and UAV navigation sensors are collected asynchronously. Motion blur, unstable viewpoints, and inaccurate coordinate transformation can also degrade traditional methods based on fixed geometric assumptions. In addition, airborne maritime scenes often contain dense vessel traffic, partial occlusion, adverse weather, sea clutter, and distant small objects. These factors make vessel detection, identification, and tracking more difficult. Graph learning provides an effective means of modeling relational information in dynamic maritime scenes. Conventional association methods mainly rely on pairwise geometric distances or trajectory similarities, whose reliability can degrade under asynchronous observations, UAV-induced coordinate variations, and ambiguous vessel motion. In contrast, graph-based modeling represents vessels as nodes and their spatial-temporal relationships as edges, allowing association to exploit not only individual trajectories but also the relative topology among multiple vessels. Such relational structures tend to remain locally consistent even when individual observations are noisy or incomplete. Graph neural networks (GNNs) are therefore well suited to aggregate neighborhood information and learn spatial-temporal dependencies for robust visual–AIS association under dynamic UAV motion. To address the key challenges of adverse maritime imaging, unstable tracking under dynamic UAV motion, and spatial-temporal misalignment between heterogeneous visual and AIS observations, we propose an airborne multi-modal graph learning-driven framework, termed AMGT, for robust vessel identification and tracking. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We introduce MAP-M2UAV50 to address the lack of comprehensive multimodal data for UAV-based maritime surveillance, integrating visible/IR videos, AIS data, UAV flight data, and comprehensive vessel annotations. We develop a lightweight MAir-YOLOv8-OBB detector to improve small and oriented vessel detection under adverse maritime conditions. It enhances multi-scale feature fusion and uses mixed-modality training to achieve multi-modal perception. We propose MAir-SORT to improve vessel tracking under false detections, occlusions, and UAV motion. It combines angle-adaptive tracking, camera-motion compensation, and multi-cue association to reduce false tracks and identity switches. We develop a motion-aware coordinate unification and graph-based association method to address visual–AIS misalignment under dynamic UAV motion, combining motion-compensated spatial alignment with spatio-temporal graph learning for reliable vessel identification. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the recent research on object association. Section 3 analyzes the self-collected challenging multi-modal dataset. In Section 4 , a multi-modal graph learning-driven framework is proposed and detailed for robust multi-vessel identification and tracking. Section 5 conducts comprehensive experiments to demonstrate the superiority and efficiency of our method. Finally, Section 6 summarizes the main contributions and future perspectives of this work. Related Work 2 UAV-based maritime surveillance involves locating objects in aerial images, maintaining their identities across frames, and linking visual observations with AIS information. Related studies are reviewed according to these three tasks, namely object detection, object tracking, and visual--AIS vessel association. UAV-Based Maritime Object Detection Airborne maritime detection must localize small objects across changing scales, orientations, and imaging conditions. Existing approaches include two-stage detectors and single-stage models from the YOLO family. Zhao and Song zhao2024anchor optimized anchor boxes for two-stage detectors using the object-size characteristics of SeaDronesSee, improving the localization of difficult maritime search-and-rescue targets. For oriented detection, YOLOv8-OBB and YOLO11-OBB Jocher_Ultralytics_YOLO_2023 predict rotated boxes that describe object position, size, and orientation. This representation retains geometric information that is not explicitly encoded by horizontal boxes. In addition to model design, recent research considers the availability and diversity of maritime training data. Zhao et al. zhao2025construction constructed a virtual maritime search-and-rescue dataset with varied weather, lighting, waves, and UAV shooting modes. Such work complements detector adaptation by expanding the observation conditions represented in training data. Nevertheless, distant targets may occupy only a small number of pixels, while changing viewpoints and illumination affect their apparent shape and contrast. Reliable localization across these conditions remains a central difficulty in airborne maritime detection. UAV-Based Maritime Object Tracking Tracking-by-detection maintains object identities by associating observations across frames. SORT 7533003 combines Kalman prediction with Hungarian assignment, providing an efficient motion-based approach. However, discarding low-confidence detections can interrupt otherwise valid tracks. ByteTrack zhang2022bytetrack addresses this issue by additionally associating low-confidence detections with existing tracklets. BoT-SORT aharon2022bot further combines motion and appearance information with camera-motion compensation. These approaches address different sources of tracking error, including uncertain detections and changes in the camera viewpoint. For UAV-based maritime tracking, Yang et al. yang2024seayo

title: Noise Space Learning for VLA Adaptation
summary: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models encode broad manipulation priors, yet adapting them to specific tasks requires balancing limited robot interaction, computational resources, and safety constraints. Noise space learning (NSL) adapts flow-matching-based VLAs by learning a context-conditioned distribution over noise while keeping the pretrained VLA fixed. Building on prior noise-steering methods, we formulate NSL as an interface for VLA adaptation that accommodates different learning algorithms and instantiate it with PPO, SAC, and AWR. Theoretically, we provide an information-theoretic analysis of how NSL enables efficient adaptation. Empirically, we study these NSL algorithms on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and four real-robot manipulation tasks under interaction, computation, and execution constraints. Across these settings, we develop a suite of effective NSL variants and derive practical recommendations for choosing among them under different resource and deployment regimes.
full_text: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models encode broad manipulation priors, yet adapting them to specific tasks requires balancing limited robot interaction, computational resources, and safety constraints. Noise space learning (NSL) adapts flow-matching-based VLAs by learning a context-conditioned distribution over noise while keeping the pretrained VLA fixed. Building on prior noise-steering methods, we formulate NSL as an interface for VLA adaptation that accommodates different learning algorithms and instantiate it with PPO, SAC, and AWR. Theoretically, we provide an information-theoretic analysis of how NSL enables efficient adaptation. Empirically, we study these NSL algorithms on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and four real-robot manipulation tasks under interaction, computation, and execution constraints. Across these settings, we develop a suite of effective NSL variants and derive practical recommendations for choosing among them under different resource and deployment regimes. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly combine pretrained visual-language representations with continuous action generation. Early VLAs such as RT-2~ brohan2023_rt2 predict discretized actions as tokens. Octo~ octomodelteam2024_octo subsequently combines a generalist robot transformer with a diffusion action head to model continuous, multimodal behavior. More recent VLAs, including ~ black2024_pi0 and ~ physicalintelligence2025_pi05 , use flow matching to transform standard Gaussian noise into action chunks, with the flow generator conditioned on visual observations and language. This progression has made flow matching an increasingly prominent approach to continuous action generation. The broad manipulation priors of flow-matching-based VLAs provide a starting point for deployment, but precise alignment, contact handling, and dynamic manipulation still require adaptation to the target task. The central challenge in VLA adaptation is to acquire task-specific behavior efficiently while preserving useful pretrained priors. Full-parameter updates to a large VLA are costly and can disturb these priors when training is limited to narrow task experience. For example, low-data supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can leave a policy fixated on training objects or spatial targets, even when a new instruction specifies a different target~ huang2026_delock . A parameter-efficient alternative is low-rank adaptation (LoRA), which keeps the VLA backbone fixed and trains low-rank adapters. This approach can better preserve VLM-derived visual-semantic recognition than full-parameter fine-tuning~ zhang2025_vlminheritance , and retain earlier skills with substantially less forgetting in continual VLA adaptation~ hu2026_continualrl . These observations motivate efficient adaptation that freezes the VLA backbone and learns a small task-specific module. Keeping the VLA backbone fixed can help preserve pretrained priors and improve adaptation efficiency, but does not by itself ensure effectiveness. Different ways of adapting a fixed backbone face different limitations. Adapting only the action head can underfit task execution despite better preservation of visual-semantic knowledge~ zhang2025_vlminheritance . Inference-time candidate selection can improve task success, but seeking better actions through a broader search requires generating and scoring more candidates, increasing inference cost~ yang2025_taco . Residual adaptation learns action corrections, but keeping these corrections close to the base policy for stable learning can limit the behavioral changes it can achieve~ ankile2025_resfit . These trade-offs motivate a central question: To address this question, we study noise space learning (NSL) for flow-matching-based VLAs. NSL trains a lightweight noise actor to produce a context-conditioned distribution over the noise that initializes action generation while keeping the VLA backbone fixed. This formulation builds on learning a conditional noise actor in DSRL~ wagenmaker2025_dsrl and noise supervision obtained by inverting corrective actions in UniSteer~ lu2026_unisteer and FlowDAgger~ murray2026_flowdagger . NSL targets effective adaptation by favoring useful behaviors already represented by the generator, supports efficient learning through lightweight actor updates, and preserves the pretrained noise-to-action mapping. The practical challenge is how to optimize the noise actor to realize these benefits. We develop NSL variants based on three reinforcement learning paradigms: on-policy policy optimization with PPO~ schulman2017_ppo , off-policy actor--critic learning with SAC~ haarnoja2018_sac , and advantage-weighted regression (AWR)~ peng2019_awr that uses supervised learning as subroutines. We study how these variants are impacted by different implementation techniques such as noise limit, task balancing, and success/failure balancing. Based on these results, we conclude which algorithms are effective and which implementation choices yield strong performance, aiming to establish best practices for NSL under different resource and deployment constraints. We evaluate NSL on two simulation benchmarks, LIBERO~ liu2023_libero and RoboTwin~ chen2025_robotwin , and four real-robot manipulation tasks, cup stacking, toy fishing, sequential insertion, and bead placement, under the following constraints: The interaction constraint refers to the sample budget for adaptation, which differs between simulation and real-robot experiments and influences algorithm choice. The computation constraint refers to the computational effort allowed in adaptation and may limit the performance. The execution constraint concerns the safety of learned behavior on physical robots. We observe that noise distributions far from standard Gaussian can be tolerated in simulation but are associated with unsafe motions and safety interventions, such as emergency stops, on real robots. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate NSL as a VLA adaptation interface that maximizes success rate through a context-conditioned noise actor that steers action generation while keeping the VLA backbone fixed. Second, we analyze NSL's adaptation efficiency through an information-theoretic comparison with generator adaptation and residual adaptation. Third, we develop NSL variants based on PPO, SAC, and AWR through implementation refinements, and evaluate them on simulation and real robots. Our experiments show that NSL-SAC performs well in simulation with ample interaction budgets and requires more computation. However, its noise distribution can deviate from standard Gaussian, with associated unsafe motions and emergency-stop interventions on real robots. In contrast, NSL-AWR is better suited to interaction-limited real-robot adaptation, combining lower computational cost with safer execution. NSL-PPO also achieves competitive performance in simulation, benefiting from more rollouts while showing limited average gains from additional updates. Related Work Adapting pretrained VLAs. Supervised and parameter-efficient methods update the effective action generator through either full-model fine-tuning or parameter-efficient updates to a limited set of weights~ kim2024_openvla,kim2025_oft,hu2021_lora,jiang2026_vlagse . Reinforcement-learning methods instead optimize generative policies using denoising or flow-transition likelihoods, critic-derived targets, or policy gradients~ ren2024_dppo,zhang2025_reinflow,chen2025_pirl,shi2026_flowdpg . These approaches can expand or reshape the behaviors produced by the VLA, with retention and computational cost depending on the update recipe. In continual VLA adaptation, full-parameter RL can cause substantial forgetting of earlier skills, while LoRA-based updates can improve retention~ hu2026_continualrl . Residual methods such as ResFiT~ ankile2025_resfit leave the base policy intact and correct its output, whereas hybrid methods such as EXPO-FT~ dong2026_expoft combine generator fitting with action editing and selection. Inference-time methods instead alter integration or select among generated candidates~ ruan2026_qpilots,yang2025_taco,giridhar2026_qplanning . While prior designs aim to balance effectiveness, prior preservation, adaptation and inference efficiency, we argue that NSL provides a better option for this balance. Learning through noise. DSRL~ wagenmaker2025_dsrl uses a conditional noise actor for frozen diffusion policies and adopts an actor-critic variant. UniSteer~ lu2026_unisteer , FlowDAgger~ murray2026_flowdagger , and Flow Reversal Steering~ tang2026_frs use approximate inversion to convert action-level corrections into noise supervision. These methods share a noise-space interface and differ in feedback requirements and critic construction. Golden Ticket~ patil2026_goldenticket improves generative robot policies by searching for a single, context-independent noise vector. LP-DS~ simsir2026_lpds learns constrained noise perturbations for continuous control and robotic manipulation. LeaP~ dai2026_leap jointly learns a noise prior and generator for robotic imitation learning. Together, these studies establish noise-distribution design as a promising direction for improving generative robot policies. We build NSL upon these precedents and formulate it into a unified interface for adapting flow-matching-based VLAs. Then, we analyze different approaches for VLA adaptation from an information-theoretic perspective to demonstrate the effectiveness of NSL. Finally, we present different NSL variants that optimize the noise actor using PPO, SAC, and AWR, respectively. title: Splat2Act: From Captured Scenes to Personalized VLA Manipulation
summary: A user who brings a generalist manipulation policy into their home or office wants it to pick up their objects from their shelves, counters, and tables. Yet even a strong generalist like $π_{0.5}$ achieves 0% pickup success in our captured deployment scenes without adaptation, and collecting real demonstrations in every user's environment is prohibitively expensive. We present Splat2Act, an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that personalizes a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a specific scene and object set using only a handheld phone scan and images of the user's objects. Unlike prior real-to-sim work that reconstructs individual tabletops, Splat2Act operates on building-scale indoor environments: it builds a photorealistic digital twin with 3D Gaussian Splatting and collision geometry, automatically discovers tabletop and non-tabletop receptacles, constructs feasible pickup tasks, and generates successful demonstrations with a privileged simulation oracle, with only scene and object capture required from a human. Applied to 101 scanned campus environments with a median navigable area of 104.87 m$^2$ and 7 receptacles, the pipeline yields 852 receptacles and over 68,000 pickup demonstrations. We fine-tune $π_{0.5}$ in two stages: Stage 1 adapts to hundreds of public object assets, drawn either from the deployment scene alone or from all 101 scenes; Stage 2 personalizes to the user's own objects on the deployment scene's receptacles. Our strongest personalized policy reaches 62.5% aggregate pickup success in the target scene. Deployed on a real Stretch 3, the same policy achieves 63.9% success on a 12-task subset, closely tracking its 66.7% simulated success on those tasks. These results suggest that automated real-to-sim-to-real training can personalize VLA manipulation policies using only simulation-oracle data.

We find that is able to adapt to the target scene and objects from only simulation oracle data, suggesting an alternative way for personalizing VLA manipulation training using an automated real-to-sim-to-real approach. INTRODUCTION Consider a mobile manipulator deployed in a user's home. The user wants it to fetch a pill bottle from the shelf and a can of soup from the side table. Generalist VLAs promise this kind of open-world capability~ intelligence_ :_2025, ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot , but deployment exposes a gap: in our experiments, pretrained achieves 0.0 pickup success rate (SR) in two target scenes (Sec. result ). Closing this gap through fine-tuning is standard practice, but the required data has traditionally come from teleoperation, policy rollouts, or human intervention in the target environment~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1810-02890, intelligence2025pi06vlalearnsexperience , a cost that recurs for every new user, receptacle, object, or configuration. Simulation demonstrations and evaluation metrics help further improve generalist models, but they often rely on mesh-based rendering of generic scenes with simplified lighting conditions, matching deployment configurations marginally~ nasiriany_robocasa:_2024, feng_libero:_2023 . Current real-to-sim-to-real systems use scene reconstructions through 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to improve visual fidelity and close the sim-to-real gap through demonstration generation and evaluation with privileged information~ kim2026legs, jain_polaris:_2025, sato2026dreamdeploymenttimedemonstrationgeneration, jiang_gsworld:_2025 . However, these either still require human demonstration or annotation, or are often reconstructed at the level of individual tabletops, making it still laborious for deployment in a user's full environment. To address these challenges, we present , an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline for VLA manipulation training and evaluation within a large building-scale scene and custom objects. The pipeline combines 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) appearances with collision geometry from scenes scanned with a hand-held device. Target and distractor objects can be either chosen from publicly available 3D assets or generated using single images of real objects. The pipeline detects valid receptacles and uses a privileged-state geometric oracle to generate successful pickup demonstrations in simulation. The resulting environments also provide task resets and success predicates for policy evaluation. The only human input to is a 20-30 minute handheld scan of the scene plus one image and the dimensions of each target object; no robot, operator expertise, or per-task repetition is needed. The same half hour of teleoperation would yield demonstrations for only one receptacle and one object set, before accounting for robot setup and operator training. Our pipeline scales to 101 scanned indoor environments with a median of 104.87 m navigable area, from which we generate 68,021 successful pickup demonstrations across 852 automatically discovered receptacles. We will make this dataset publicly available upon acceptance. Using a selected subset of this data, we study different approaches to personalization across broad adaptation sources and conduct sim-to-real experiments in target scenes and out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We find that same-scene broad adaptation followed by personalization yields the strongest policy, improving over direct personalization by 17.5 percentage points on aggregate and reaching 63.9 real-world SR where it scores 66.7 in simulation, and a personalized policy fine-tuned from diverse multi-scene adaptation retains robustness to unseen receptacles Our contributions are: An automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that converts scene captures and real objects into feasible manipulation tasks and demonstrations with no human effort beyond scene and object scans. A large-scale simulation dataset generated from our pipeline, constructed from 101 building-scale indoor scenes with 852 diverse receptacles, with corresponding task metadata and demonstrations. An empirical study on how broad simulation adaptation and personalization affect pickup performance on a user's scene and objects, with controlled simulation and real-world evaluation. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models and Adaptation Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained visual and linguistic representations with robot demonstrations to support transferable manipulation policies. OpenVLA provides an open model that can be fine-tuned for new tasks and embodiments~ kim_openvla:_2024 ; introduces a VLM-backed flow-matching architecture for continuous control, and uses heterogeneous co-training to improve generalization to unfamiliar environments~ black_ :_2024, intelligence_ :_2025 . Even with broad heterogeneous pretraining, downstream adaptation remains important for policy improvement. OpenVLA-OFT studies action representations, parallel decoding, action chunking, and training objectives that improve fine-tuning efficiency and performance~ kim_fine-tuning_2025 . Personalization also has a perceptual dimension, as Visual Attentive Prompting grounds user-specific objects from reference images and guides frozen VLAs through visual highlighting and instruction rewriting~ lee2026bringcuppersonalizingvisionlanguageaction . Our setting couples personalized object assets with adaptation to the appearance, receptacles, and feasible pickup configurations of a captured deployment scene. Automated and Deployment-Specific Data Generation Large real-world datasets such as Open X-Embodiment and DROID provide diverse manipulation experience, but collecting demonstrations across robots and environments requires substantial human effort~ oneill_open_2024, khazatsky_droid:_2024 . MimicGen and DemoGen amplify limited human demonstrations by adapting trajectories and observations to new spatial configurations~ mandlekar_mimicgen:_2023, xue_demogen:_2025 . Generative simulation methods address a different source of scale: GenSim generates task programs and expert demonstrations, RoboGen generates tasks, scenes, and supervision, and RoboTwin 2.0 combines automated execution-code generation with structured domain randomization for bimanual manipulation~ wang_gensim:_2023, wang_robogen:_2023, chen2025robotwin . These approaches establish the value of automated data generation, but deployment personalization additionally requires grounding the generated experience in the environment where the policy will operate. Real-to-Sim-to-Real Manipulation Reconstructed environments support both policy improvement and controlled evaluation. RialTo uses scanned digital twins, inverse distillation of real demonstrations, and simulation RL to robustify manipulation policies~ torne_reconciling_2024 . EmbodiedSplat personalizes navigation policies in deployment environments reconstructed from mobile-device captures~ chhablani_embodiedsplat:_2025 ; our work builds on this paradigm for receptacle-local manipulation. For evaluation, SIMPLER studies how reducing visual and control discrepancies makes simulated policy performance predictive of real-world behavior, while PolaRiS constructs interactive environments from real-world captures for scalable policy evaluation~ li_evaluating_2024, jain_polaris:_2025 . Photorealistic rendering has emerged as an enabling component of real-to-sim-to-real manipulation. Particularly, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) supports efficient novel view synthesis~ kerbl_3d_2023 , and SplatSim, RE SIM, RoboSimGS, and GSWorld use Gaussian-based scene representations for simulated manipulation data or closed-loop policy interaction~ qureshi_splatsim:_2024, han_re sim:_2025, zhao_high-fidelity_2025, jiang_gsworld:_2025 . RL-GSBridge also demonstrates real-to-sim-to-real visual RL with Gaussian splat rendering~ wu_rl-gsbridge:_2024 . Some recent works employ real-to-sim for synthetic data generation. PRISM constructs semantically and geometrically aligned digital cousin scenes from a user-scene image and a language instruction, then uses task-and-motion planning to synthesize executable demonstrations without human teleoperation~ ko_prism:_2026 . DREAM reconstructs a captured workspace, translates a supplied instruction into symbolic goals and success criteria, and generates and augments planned trajectories for VLA fine-tuning without a task-specific human demonstration~ sato2026dreamdeploymenttimedemonstrationgeneration . SimFoundry reconstructs simulation-ready digital twins and generates object, scene, and task cousins, including feasible tasks proposed from the reconstructed objects and affordances~ ranawaka_simfoundry:_2026 . Recent agentic real-to-sim systems further automate simulation construction and downstream interaction. Agentic Real2Sim uses VLM-directed reconstruction and simulator-in-the-loop refinement to reproduce observed robot interactions as physically executable simulation episodes~ chen2026agenticreal2simphysicsbasedworld . Real2Gym reconstructs interactive simulation environments from demonstrations, enabling agents to practice and acquire reusable manipulation skills~ ren2026real2gymbuildinggymsvideos . More closely related to our pipeline, ARSTAG reconstructs task-specific simulation scenes from an image and language instruction, then generates demonstrations with task-consistent augmentations for VLA adaptation~ li2026arstagagenticreal2sim2realtaskspecific . title: Imagine the Future, Internalize the Gist: Efficient VLA Reasoning via Internalized Spatiotemporal Imagination
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. Extending such reasoning to explicit future rollouts at every inference step, however, introduces substantial computational overhead. We propose IG-VLA, a VLA reasoning framework that enables models to imagine the future and internalize the gist. Our Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, guiding action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. To further reduce inference overhead, we introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving the benefits of future reasoning while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IG-VLA. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate. The gist policy also achieves up to 6.38x speedup over baselines, reducing inference latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment.

Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable general-purpose robotic manipulation by mapping multimodal observations and language instructions to actions guan2025efficient,li2025vla,li2025comprehensive,sapkota2025vision,wang2025vision . However, learning an effective end-to-end mapping from multimodal perception to robotic actions requires extensive, high-quality demonstration data liu2025aligning,ma2026survey . To address this challenge, recent VLA models adopt a ``think-before-acting'' paradigm through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning guo2025vla,ye2025vla,yin2025deepthinkvla .By reasoning over task goals, visual observations, and object relations before execution, these models decompose complex instructions and adapt action plans to environmental feedback. Existing VLA paradigms include language-based reasoning zawalski2024robotic,lee2025molmoact,qu2508eo,huang2026fast , which carry out reasoning in language domain and reasoning in vision, exemplified by CoT-VLA's decomposition of predicted goals into visual subgoals zhao2025cotvla and VLA-Thinker's repeated incorporation of intermediate state images~ wang2026vla . As shown in Figure fig:compare (a), language-based reasoning loses fine-grained visual details and achieves lower success rates. In contrast, incorporating updated visual information during reasoning can mitigate drift from the actual environment wang2026vla (Figure fig:compare (b)). In general, existing approaches face two limitations: (i) reliance on observed states rather than future predictions, and (ii) substantial computational overhead from repeated reasoning rollouts. Specifically, existing approaches primarily reason over observed states and plan subsequent actions based on the current environment, without explicitly anticipating how the environment may evolve under different decisions. Meanwhile, reasoning in VLA models need to perform full spatiotemporal reasoning rollouts repeatedly at every inference step, introducing substantial computation overhead. To address these issues, we propose a visual reasoning framework for VLA models with two core mechanisms: latent spatiotemporal reasoning and scene gist memory. Latent spatiotemporal reasoning enables the model to imagine future scene evolution in visual representation space, exploring plausible action trajectories and their potential outcomes. These imagined futures guide action selection, as shown in Figure fig:compare (b). It is inspired by human reasoning process, which imagines how a scene might unfold under different candidate actions and makes decisions based on expected consequences atance2001episodic . For example, when crossing a street, we consider multiple possible futures conditioned on our own actions such as crossing, waiting, or speeding up, then choose the safest action. This anticipation evaluates candidate behaviors through the imagined consequences rather than merely extrapolating scene evolution independently of actions conti2021harnessing . To reduce computational overhead, our proposed Scene Gist Memory internalizes reasoning-derived scene--behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token. This token captures general scene context and corresponding action patterns rather than preserving the complete future reasoning trajectory. During inference, the gist encoder predicts the Scene Gist directly from the current context, allowing the model to bypass the explicit future-reasoning pathway while retaining reasoning-derived behavioral guidance (Figure fig:brain ). It's inspired by human behavioral psychology that repeated experience in familiar environments helps consolidate learned behaviors into procedural memory involving the basal ganglia~ wulf2010motor,wood2016psychology . This memory supports rapid responses with less deliberation, reducing cognitive effort and decision time. For example, familiarity with a home allows a person to head directly to the kitchen for coffee without searching the entire house. Repeated experience reinforces the association between the familiar scene and the corresponding navigation behavior. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: Our framework incorporates Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning, enabling VLA models to learn to imagine task-relevant scene evolution in visual representation space. These anticipated scene dynamics guide action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. We further introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene--behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token. It enables the model to reuse this knowledge in corresponding scenarios, preserving reasoning benefits while bypassing explicit future imagination and full reasoning rollouts at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our framework. For example, IG-VLA achieves an 85.6 success rate on LIBERO-Plus's challenging Language suite, outperforming the strongest baseline by nearly 6 . Meanwhile, the gist policy requires only 169.5\,ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000, achieving , and speedups over FastWAM-IDM (1,081\,ms), FastWAM (1-step) (302\,ms) and ImageWAM (263\,ms), respectively. Existing approaches mainly follow several directions. Prompting-based methods such as EcoT zawalski2024robotic use supervised reasoning traces to decompose tasks into intermediate subgoals before action execution. Data-centric methods, including RAD clark2025action , combine human videos with LLMs to construct reasoning-action demonstrations for policy learning. Another line of work, represented by CoT-VLA zhao2025cot , replaces textual reasoning with visual subgoal representations to better align planning with robot perception. Recently, reinforcement learning shao2024deepseekmath,guo2025deepseek has been adopted to optimize reasoning policies under verifiable rewards, where GRPO encourages more effective reasoning trajectories feng2026video,tan2025reason,liu2025visual . title: NovaSplat: Model-Free 6D Object Pose Estimation via 3D Gaussian Splatting Onboarding and Refinement
summary: 6D pose estimation of novel objects without CAD models remains an open challenge: model-free methods must build the object representation from scratch during onboarding and have long trailed their model-based counterparts. We present NovaSplat, a model-free pipeline that closes this gap. From a short smartphone video captured at onboarding, we train a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model that serves both as a template source for detection and coarse pose estimation and as a differentiable backbone for pose refinement. Our refiner optimizes the object-to-camera pose with combined photometric and geometric losses under a continuous rotation parametrization free of gradient singularities. On a household-object benchmark, NovaSplat surpasses all model-based methods. On a challenging industrial benchmark with textureless and specular surfaces, it outperforms all model-free competitors while substantially narrowing the gap to model-based ones. We further introduce NovaSplat-Lite, an inference variant that is $3.1\times$ faster at negligible accuracy cost. Code will be made available at \href{https://github.com/POSE-Lab/novasplat}{https://github.com/POSE-Lab/novasplat}.
full_text: 6D pose estimation of novel objects without CAD models remains an open challenge: model-free methods must build the object representation from scratch during onboarding and have long trailed their model-based counterparts. We present NovaSplat, a model-free pipeline that closes this gap. From a short smartphone video captured at onboarding, we train a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model that serves both as a template source for detection and coarse pose estimation and as a differentiable backbone for pose refinement. Our refiner optimizes the object-to-camera pose with combined photometric and geometric losses under a continuous rotation parametrization free of gradient singularities. On a household-object benchmark, NovaSplat surpasses all model-based methods. On a challenging industrial benchmark with textureless and specular surfaces, it outperforms all model-free competitors while substantially narrowing the gap to model-based ones. We further introduce NovaSplat-Lite, an inference variant that is faster at negligible accuracy cost. Code will be made available at https://github.com/POSE-Lab/novasplat . Introduction sec:introduction 6D object pose estimation, recovering the full position and orientation of an object relative to a camera, is a core capability for robotic manipulation, augmented reality, and industrial inspection. The highest-performing methods rely on a 3D CAD model of the object: they render templates at many viewpoints and extract geometric point clouds, which are then matched against the query image using powerful frozen foundation models~ Oernek_ECCV_2024,Caraffa_ECCV_2024 . In practice, however, CAD models are rarely available outside controlled environments, making these approaches impractical for real-world deployment. This motivates the model-free setting: given only a short video of a novel object captured during an onboarding phase, estimate its 6D pose in new scenes without any 3D model. Model-free methods face a fundamental reconstruction problem. Where model-based methods receive the object geometry by definition, model-free methods must recover it from video, a noisier and less complete substitute that degrades every downstream stage, from template rendering to correspondence matching. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:bridging_gap , this has historically resulted in a substantial performance gap between the two paradigms, limiting the practical utility of model-free approaches. We propose NovaSplat, a complete model-free pipeline that closes this gap and in some cases reverses it. During onboarding, we reconstruct a dense 3D representation of the object from video and train a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. This representation serves two roles simultaneously: rendering high-quality templates for object detection and coarse pose estimation and acting as a differentiable backbone for gradient-based pose refinement. Our 3DGS refiner freezes the learned scene representation and directly optimizes the object-to-camera pose by jointly minimizing appearance and geometric losses, using a continuous rotation parameterization that avoids singularities. This joint optimization proves considerably more robust than geometry-only refinement under the noisy reconstructions typical of video-based onboarding. We make the following contributions: A complete model-free onboarding pipeline that produces a high-quality 3DGS object representation from a short video, enabling model-based pose estimation methods to operate without a CAD model. A novel 3DGS-based pose refiner that jointly optimizes appearance and geometry, advancing model-free pose refinement. State-of-the-art results on two benchmarks spanning household and industrial objects, demonstrating that model-free methods can match and exceed model-based performance without CAD models. Related Work sec:related-work Taxonomy of 6D Object Pose Estimation sec:taxonomy Existing 6D object pose estimation methods can be broadly categorized by the level of prior object knowledge they require. Instance-based methods~ Hodan_CVPR_2020, Tremblay_CORL_2018, Su_CVPR_2022 leverage 3D object models during training to achieve high accuracy but are restricted to previously seen objects. Novel object methods~ Oernek_ECCV_2024, Caraffa_ECCV_2024, Nguyen_CVPR_2024, Moon_CVPR_2025, He_NEURIPS_2022, Liu_ECCV_2022, Jung_3DV_2026, Lee_CVPR_2025, Li_ICCVW_2023, Wen_CVPR_2023, Wen_CVPR_2024, Cao_CVPR_2025, Wang_ICRA_2026 generalize to unseen objects and can be further divided into category-based~ Wang_CVPR_2019, Tian_ECCV_2020 and unseen object approaches. Within the unseen object paradigm, model-based methods~ Oernek_ECCV_2024, Caraffa_ECCV_2024, Nguyen_CVPR_2024, Moon_CVPR_2024, Moon_CVPR_2025, Sun_CVPR_2022 require a CAD model at inference time, exploiting geometric priors from rendered templates and 3D point clouds, while model-free methods build an object representation from a short video sequence during an onboarding phase, without any 3D model. This work focuses on the model-free unseen object setting. Model-Based Novel Object Methods sec:model-based-methods Several recent methods follow a correspondence-based pipeline over CAD-rendered templates. FoundPose~ Oernek_ECCV_2024 matches DINOv2~ Oquab_TMLR_2024 descriptors between the query and rendered templates but relies solely on visual features. FreeZe~ Caraffa_ECCV_2024 and FreeZeV2~ Caraffa_ARXIV_2025 extend to depth input by fusing visual and geometric (GeDi~ Poiesi_PAMI_23 ) features for 3D-3D correspondence matching and refine the final pose using the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm, ranking among the top BOP methods. We build directly on FreeZeV2 as our coarse pose estimator. GigaPose~ Nguyen_CVPR_2024 is fast and supports both model-based and model-free settings on single RGB frames, though lacking depth limits its performance on small or occluded objects. GenFlow~ Moon_CVPR_2024 and its successor Co-op~ Moon_CVPR_2025 refine poses via optical flow and semi-dense correspondences, respectively, the latter using a CroCo-based~ Weinzaepfel_ICCV_2023 ViT with a differentiable PnP layer. Pos3R~ Deng_CVPR_2025 likewise matches over CAD-rendered templates, employing MASt3R~ Leroy_ECCV_2024 , a 3D reconstruction foundation model, to establish dense correspondences, select the best template by feature similarity, and recover pose via PnP-RANSAC, with optional refinement via render-and-compare. WALDO~ Pakdamansavoji_WACV_2026 extends the detect-segment-hypothesize-refine pipeline with dynamic non-uniform sampling, multi-hypothesis inference, and iterative refinement to exhibit robustness under occlusions. All these methods require a 3D CAD model at inference time. NovaSplat operates without one at any stage, replaces ICP with a differentiable 3DGS-based refiner, and surpasses those of them evaluated on HOPEv2 (Table~1). Model-Free Novel Object Methods sec:model-free-methods Model-free methods can be organized into three categories. Visual localization approaches~ Sun_CVPR_2022, He_NEURIPS_2022 apply Structure-from-Motion (SfM) during onboarding to build a sparse 3D point cloud, recovering pose via 2D-3D correspondences. They struggle, however, with low-texture objects and large viewpoint changes. Template-based methods~ Liu_ECCV_2022 use viewpoint retrieval over posed reference images for a coarse hypothesis before refinement but are sensitive to detection and bounding box quality. Few-shot methods operate from only one or a handful of RGB or RGB-D images:~ Jung_3DV_2026 generate a geometry-aware encoding from a few RGB views,~ Liu_CVPR_2025 compress a single RGB-D reference into a pose embedding via latent diffusion, and~ Lee_CVPR_2025 combine 2D-3D alignment with render-and-compare refinement from a single RGB-D anchor. Despite their practical appeal, these methods rely on strong assumptions, such as symmetry priors or scale constraints, to compensate for limited onboarding data, restricting generalization across object geometries. Neural Rendering for Object Pose Estimation sec:neural-rendering-methods Neural rendering approaches encode objects into differentiable implicit representations for CAD-free novel-view synthesis. Early NeRF-based methods such as LatentFusion~ Park_CVPR_2020 and NeRF-Pose~ Li_ICCVW_2023 use latent voxel grids and radiance fields, respectively. BundleSDF~ Wen_CVPR_2023 builds a Neural Object Field on-the-fly from an RGB-D stream, concurrently optimizing pose and a 3D representation. FoundationPose~ Wen_CVPR_2024 extends this into a unified foundation model supporting both model-based and model-free setups via large-scale synthetic training. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ Kerbl_TOG_2023 has largely displaced NeRF-based representations owing to superior rendering quality and real-time speed. GS-Pose~ Cai_3DV_2025 , iG-6DoF~ Cao_CVPR_2025 , and 6DOPE-GS~ Jin_2025_ICCV all leverage 3DGS for render-and-compare refinement or online tracking but evaluate primarily on simpler benchmarks (Linemod~ Hinterstoisser_ACCV_12 , HO3D~ Hampali_CVPR_2020 , YCBInEOAT~ Wen_IROS_2020 ) without testing on challenging multi-object scenes such as HOPEv2. The work that is most closely related to ours is GFreeDet2~ Wang_ICRA_2026 , which combines a 3DGS onboarding pipeline with template-based coarse pose estimation but relies exclusively on visual features, lacking the geometric integration we show is critical for accurate pose estimation on challenging objects. Method sec:method Overview sec:overview Our pipeline consists of two stages: onboarding and inference (Figure~ fig:pipeline ). During onboarding (Section~ ref:onboarding ), the goal is to build an object representation from a short video of the object captured from multiple viewpoints with a handheld device such as a smartphone. Given the video frames and corresponding object masks, we run a classical 3D reconstruction pipeline comprising SfM, Multi-View Stereo (MVS), and 3DGS training to produce a 3D mesh and an optimized 3DGS object representation. During inference, given an RGB-D query image containing instances of onboarded objects, the goal is to detect each object and estimate its 6D pose. We first run a modified CNOS~ Nguyen_ICCVW_2023 detection and segmentation module (Section~ ref:detection_segmentation ) to localize each object and produce its segmentation mask. We then employ the coarse pose estimation module of FreeZeV2~ Caraffa_ECCV_2024,Caraffa_ARXIV_2025 (Section~ ref:coarse_pose_estimation ), adapted to use templates rendered from the 3DGS representation and a 3D point cloud sampled from the mesh model, to obtain an initial 6D pose estimate. Finally, each coarse pose is passed to our 3DGS-based hybrid refiner (Section~ sec:refinement ), which produces the final 6D pose. Implementation details of the onboarding and inference stages are provided in Section~ sec:implementation . Onboarding ref:onboarding We assume access to a set of RGB video frames depicting the object from all viewpoints, along with corresponding object segmentation masks. When masks are unavailable, they can be obtained automatically using an off-the-shelf video segmentation model such as SAM3~ Carion_ARXIV_2025 . The raw frames are passed to a SfM pipeline~ Schoenberger_CVPR_2016, Pan_ECCV_2024 to estimate camera poses and a sparse 3D point cloud. The object masks are then applied to isolate the object point cloud from the background. The masked frames, camera poses, and object point cloud are used to train a 3DGS model~ Kerbl_TOG_2023 . The 3DGS representation consists of a set of 3D Gaussians, each parameterized by its mean, covariance, opacity, and view-dependent color encoded as Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. The model is optimized by differentiably rendering the Gaussians onto the image plane and minimizing the photometric error against the masked training frames. title: LAPT-Scale: Scaling Embodied Policies with Latent Action Pre-Training on Human Videos
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026; 24 pages including appendix
summary: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen visual conditions.
full_text: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3 to 85.0 as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen visual conditions. Introduction sec:intro Scaling data drives progress in vision and language, but embodied intelligence faces a sharper bottleneck: interaction data requires physical robots or simulators, making it far more expensive than text or static images. Large-scale human videos, especially egocentric ones, offer a promising way to relieve this bottleneck~ grauman2022ego4d . They naturally record diverse everyday interactions at a scale beyond robot-collected trajectories, and transforming such videos into action-like supervision could complement robot-only datasets such as Open X-Embodiment~ o2024open . The central challenge is that human videos lack robot action labels, and human motion cannot be directly mapped to robot control spaces. Existing methods, such as VITRA~ li2025vitra , often convert human videos into pseudo-actions through explicit motion estimation, where estimation errors can lead to noisy action annotations; simply adding more human video does not necessarily improve policies. Latent Action Models (LAMs) offer an alternative: they infer implicit actions between consecutive frames end-to-end, without predefined robot action labels~ bruce2024genie,ye2024latent,bu2025univla,bi2025motus . Because these implicit actions are optimized to explain visual transitions, they provide compact supervision for unlabeled videos. Despite this potential, existing LAMs are limited by their architectural priors and alignment signals. Many recent methods use Vector Quantized (VQ) latent spaces~ van2017neural,ye2024latent,bu2025univla . While compact, a fixed discrete codebook can over-compress the continuous changes that define egocentric manipulation, weakening the supervision needed for fine-grained policy learning. In addition, pixel-wise reconstruction signals such as MSE are often dominated by large static regions, providing weak signals for small but important hand-object interactions. As a result, learned latent actions may miss transition-relevant structure needed for downstream embodied policies. To address these limitations, we introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm for embodied policy learning. LAPT-Scale contains two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM, which constructs human-derived supervision with a continuous Latent Action Model trained on large-scale human videos, and LAPT-Scale-Policy, which uses this supervision to train a VLA policy. The policy training follows three stages: human-video latent-action pre-training, embodiment alignment with target-robot data, and task-specific post-training in simulation and the real world. Unlike discrete LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM parameterizes implicit actions in a continuous space to preserve fine-grained transition dynamics. To make this space perceptually grounded and temporally consistent, we train the LAM with alignment signals beyond pixel reconstruction: perceptual alignment for local contact fidelity~ zhang2018unreasonableeffectivenessdeepfeatures , semantic alignment with self-supervised features for hand-object structure~ oquab2023dinov2 , and optical-flow alignment for observed dynamics~ teed2020raft . We train LAPT-Scale-LAM on 23.3K hours of diverse egocentric videos and use it to annotate a 5.1K-hour cleaned human-video subset for policy pre-training. With 250 hours of self-collected robot data for embodiment alignment, LAPT-Scale reaches 90.0 /89.3 success on RoboTwin Easy/Hard, 64.8 on RoboCasa-GR1. Scaling LAM-annotated human video from 1K to 5K hours further improves real-robot success from 63.3 to 85.0 , suggesting that continuous latent action annotation is a promising route for benefiting from larger human-video corpora. On four harder real-robot tasks, it retains 70.0--75.0 success under unseen position, illumination, and background shifts. Our contributions are summarized as follows: LAPT-Scale-LAM: a continuous latent action model with perceptual, self-supervised feature, and optical-flow alignment signals for learning a more expressive latent action space from human videos. LAPT-Scale-Policy: a three-stage framework for human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and downstream post-training. Real-robot scaling: increasing only Stage-1 human-video pre-training data improves downstream real-robot success from 63.3 to 85.0 . Related Work sec:related_work Vision-language-action policy learning. Vision-language-action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language conditioning, and action generation for generalist manipulation. Recent systems scale VLA policies with web knowledge, robot data, flow-based action modeling, and cross-embodiment training~ zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel,intelligence2025pi_,bjorck2025gr00t,team2025gemini,wu2026pragmatic,yang2026abot,joyai2026ra05 , while other work studies backbone, adaptation, spatial-representation, and action-space choices~ li2024robovlms,wang2024vladapter,qu2025spatialvla,zheng2025uniact . However, VLA training remains constrained by action-labeled robot trajectories. Egocentric VLA methods such as VITRA and EgoScale reduce this bottleneck by converting human videos into action-like targets before robot alignment~ li2025vitra,zheng2026egoscale , but such targets depend on explicit motion estimation or retargeting signals. Simulation-mediated pipelines also convert reconstructed human demonstrations into physically checked robot-centered trajectories~ liu2026joyaisim . LAPT-Scale instead annotates human videos with LAM-derived implicit actions. Human video data for embodied learning. Human video datasets provide broad coverage of physical interaction, from object manipulation in Something-Something and EPIC-KITCHENS to daily-life egocentric video in Ego4D~ goyal2017something,damen2018scaling,grauman2022ego4d . Recent resources expand scale and annotation density with paired ego-exo views, factory videos, 3D/4D annotations, dexterous demonstrations, multimodal interaction labels, and filtered Ego4D text/action annotations~ grauman2025egoexo4d,buildai2025egocentric10k,xperience_10m,hoque2025egodex,punamiya2026egoverse,wang2024egovid . These datasets are useful visual experience, but their human observations and motion annotations do not directly specify robot-executable actions. LAPT-Scale learns latent actions to bridge this missing-label gap before robot embodiment alignment. Latent action models from videos. Latent Action Models infer action-like variables from observation transitions, making unlabeled videos useful for behavior learning. Related work learns compact transition variables through inverse-dynamics, world-model, or latent-action objectives and integrates them into VLA or world-model pipelines~ bruce2024genie,ye2024latent,chen2024igor,gao2025adaworld,gao2026dreamdojo,bu2025univla,bi2025motus,chen2025villa,zhang2026clap,liu2026wla3 . However, many LAMs rely on discrete or vector-quantized latents, which can over-compress continuous egocentric manipulation dynamics~ van2017neural,ye2024latent,bu2025univla . Reconstruction-only training can be dominated by static background regions. LAOF augments reconstruction with optical-flow constraints to improve robustness to visual distractors~ bu2025laof . LAPT-Scale-LAM therefore uses continuous latents together with perceptual, self-supervised semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to preserve fine-grained implicit actions for human-video policy pre-training~ zhang2018unreasonableeffectivenessdeepfeatures,oquab2023dinov2,teed2020raft . title: SplatQ: Interaction-Aware Pruning of 3D Gaussian Splatting via Quadratic Selection
comment: Under review at ICLR 2027 (main paper 9 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables; appendix included)
summary: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pruning methods primarily rely on global Top-K selection based on independent importance scores, lacking regional budget control and ignoring joint deletion effects. Consequently, they cannot ensure balanced reconstruction quality across a scene. We propose SplatQ, a combinatorial pruning algorithm that coordinates regional budget allocation and joint Gaussian selection under a fixed budget. SplatQ partitions Gaussians by spatial proximity and appearance similarity into size-limited blocks, decomposing global selection into subproblems of a specific size. It then smooths importance-based block retention quotas to prevent excessive budget concentration. Finally, it constructs a quadratic approximation of joint deletion effects using the responses of representative pixel colors to changes in Gaussian opacity. Individual responses, pairwise interactions, and quota penalties are incorporated into a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) objective, solved using simulated annealing (SA) or a coherent Ising machine (CIM) to jointly select Gaussians. Experiments on 5 benchmarks demonstrate that SplatQ outperforms state-of-the-art pruning methods in aggregate reconstruction quality, spatial quality balance, and rendering speed. Ablations confirm that budget smoothing improves local detail reconstruction, while interaction modeling improves Gaussian selection quality under a fixed budget.
full_text: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pruning methods primarily rely on global Top-K selection based on independent importance scores, lacking regional budget control and ignoring joint deletion effects. Consequently, they cannot ensure balanced reconstruction quality across a scene. We propose SplatQ, a combinatorial pruning algorithm that coordinates regional budget allocation and joint Gaussian selection under a fixed budget. SplatQ partitions Gaussians by spatial proximity and appearance similarity into size-limited blocks, decomposing global selection into subproblems of a specific size. It then smooths importance-based block retention quotas to prevent excessive budget concentration. Finally, it constructs a quadratic approximation of joint deletion effects using the responses of representative pixel colors to changes in Gaussian opacity. Individual responses, pairwise interactions, and quota penalties are incorporated into a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) objective, solved using simulated annealing (SA) or a coherent Ising machine (CIM) to jointly select Gaussians. Experiments on 5 benchmarks demonstrate that SplatQ outperforms state-of-the-art pruning methods in aggregate reconstruction quality, spatial quality balance, and rendering speed. Ablations confirm that budget smoothing improves local detail reconstruction, while interaction modeling improves Gaussian selection quality under a fixed budget. Introduction sec:introduction Gaussian Splatting ~ kerbl2023_3dgs enables high-quality real-time rendering through an explicit Gaussian representation, providing a practical foundation for the reconstruction and interaction of 3D digital assets. Complex scenes, however, often contain large numbers of Gaussians, whose storage, memory, and rendering costs limit asset transmission and deployment~ lightgaussian2024,eagles2024 . Gaussian pruning reduces these costs by removing primitives. Methods such as LightGaussian~ lightgaussian2024 and PUP 3D-GS~ pup3dgs2025 combine importance estimation with post-pruning fine-tuning to balance model size and rendering quality. Under a fixed budget and aggressive pruning, we observe that results with similar overall image-quality metrics can exhibit different patterns of local degradation: structures and textures remain clear in some regions, while other regions become visibly blurred or distorted. Existing methods also make different regional trade-offs. For example, PUP 3D-GS discusses the trade-off between foreground detail and background quality~ pup3dgs2025 , whereas GaussianPOP emphasizes the preservation of detail-rich regions~ gaussianpop2026 . These choices have their own motivations, but they raise a question: when the number of retained Gaussians is strictly limited, how can pruning preserve both overall rendering quality and reconstruction quality across different regions? We have two observations from previous global importance ranking works~ lightgaussian2024,pup3dgs2025,refine2026 : First, global ranking does not directly control how the retention budget is distributed across a scene. Such methods score each Gaussian separately and retain the highest-scoring Gaussians globally~ lightgaussian2024,pup3dgs2025,refine2026 . The number retained in each region therefore depends primarily on the score distribution. If Gaussians in certain regions consistently receive higher scores, the limited budget may concentrate there, leaving other regions with insufficient representational capacity. Thus,relying on a global ranking cannot guarantee that the rendering quality of all regions is well preserved under aggressive pruning Figure~ fig:teaser (a) illustrates this spatial quality imbalance: pruning baselines preserve some structures while losing detail in other regions of the same scene. Second, Gaussian pruning under a fixed budget is a combinatorial optimization problem. It requires selecting, subject to a retention constraint, a set of Gaussians that renders well together. Independent scoring followed by Top- ranking reduces this set-selection problem to a comparison of individual scores. Yet multiple Gaussians may jointly support the same pixel or make overlapping contributions during rendering~ kerbl2023_3dgs . Because Gaussian contributions overlap, the degradation caused by removing multiple Gaussians is not strictly additive and cannot be inferred from individual deletion costs.Highly overlapping Gaussians might all receive high individual scores and be redundantly retained, even though preserving just one would suffice. Consequently, accurate individual scores alone cannot determine which set of Gaussians should be retained. Ignoring interactions may prevent the limited budget from being used for a combination that achieves better reconstruction quality. To address these limitations, we propose SplatQ, a post-training Gaussian pruning framework that performs similarity-guided partitioning, budget assignment, and interaction-aware quadratic selection in sequence. SplatQ aims to reduce disparities in local reconstruction quality under aggressive pruning and use the retained Gaussian budget more effectively, improving overall and local reconstruction quality with the same number of Gaussians. First, SplatQ partitions Gaussians into local blocks according to spatial proximity and appearance similarity. These blocks provide units for budget assignment while keeping the selection problems at a specific size. Second, to control local retention counts, SplatQ derives an initial quota for each block from importance estimates and adjusts the quota distribution to reduce the risk of concentrating the budget in a few blocks while leaving others with insufficient capacity. Finally, to account for the joint effects of deleting multiple Gaussians, SplatQ uses rendering responses to changes in opacity multipliers to estimate individual deletion effects and pairwise interactions. Figure~ fig:teaser (b) illustrates how block quotas, budget assignment, and quadratic selection progressively improve detail preservation across the highlighted regions. It then formulates and solves a QUBO~ glover2018qubo under each block's quota to select a retained set with a smaller estimated joint deletion effect. Because solving QUBOs with classical methods requires more computation than direct Top- ranking, we also examine a coherent Ising machine (CIM) as a hardware solver backend and assess its potential to improve solving efficiency. After pruning, SplatQ fine-tunes the retained Gaussians to recover rendering quality. We conduct extensive experiments on 27 scenes from 5 benchmarks covering indoor, outdoor, and objects, comparing SplatQ with eight open-source pruning methods. Under a common 90 pruning setting, SplatQ achieves the best overall image quality and rendering speed among the compared methods, while providing more uniform reconstruction quality across image regions. We further evaluate different pruning ratios, fine-tuning budgets, and combinations of pruning rounds and per-round fine-tuning iterations, facilitating comparisons with the reported settings of methods without released code. SplatQ also remains effective in a picture-free setting, where neither pruning nor fine-tuning uses the original training photographs and fine-tuning relies on images rendered by the fixed pretrained model. Even under this constraint, SplatQ surpasses the strongest baseline, MesonGS~ mesongs2024 , in dataset-macro PSNR. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of partition-based budget assignment and interaction-aware combinatorial optimization, while experiments with CIM demonstrate that an alternative solver backend can also produce competitive selection results. Related work sec:related Gaussian compression and pruning. Existing 3DGS pruning methods often rank or sample Gaussians by rendering contributions, using compositing weights, coverage, volume, opacity, or gradients~ eagles2024,lightgaussian2024,mesongs2024,trimmingfat2024,coreset3dgs2026 . These criteria may overlook compensation by other Gaussians and undervalue sparsely observed regions. Other methods use parameter sensitivity or its approximations~ pup3dgs2025,refine2026,c3dgs2024 , or estimate single-Gaussian deletion error relative to renderings of the current or original model~ gaussianpop2026,potr2026 . However, sensitivity is not equivalent to actual deletion error, and individual deletion errors do not directly characterize joint removal. Learned scores, masks, or sparse representations enable reconstruction-driven adaptation but require additional learning~ rap2026,compact3dgs2024,lp3dgs2024,gaussianspa2025,maskgaussian2025 . Further methods consider relationships among Gaussians through neighboring appearance differences or local overlap~ omg2025,qirf2026 , or merge Gaussians into new representatives~ ghap2025 . In contrast, SplatQ partitions pretrained Gaussians by spatial and appearance similarity, initializes and smooths blockwise retention quotas under an exact global budget, and jointly selects Gaussians within each block using a quadratic objective built from individual and pairwise linearized rendering responses. Balancing Rendering Quality Across Image Regions. NeRF++~ nerfpp2020 , Mip-NeRF 360~ barron2022mipnerf360 , and HoGS~ hogs2025 study how to represent near and distant content during scene reconstruction. For a pretrained 3DGS model, pruning additionally requires deciding how many primitives to retain in different parts of the scene under a limited Gaussian budget. PUP 3D-GS reports a trade-off between foreground detail and background quality under aggressive pruning~ pup3dgs2025 . These regional differences motivate SplatQ to partition Gaussians with similar spatial positions and appearances into size-limited blocks, smooth the block quotas derived from importance estimates while preserving the exact global retention count, and perform joint selection within each block. In addition to overall reconstruction quality, we evaluate pruning results by measuring quality differences across image patches. Method sec:method Given a pretrained 3D Gaussian Splatting model with Gaussians, SplatQ aims to retain exactly \(K\) Gaussians while accounting for their joint effects on the rendered image and reducing disparities in retention across scene regions. We represent the model as where each Gaussian is parameterized by its center , scale , rotation quaternion , zeroth-order (DC) and higher-order spherical-harmonic coefficients and , and opacity . Previous methods suffer from two limitations: 1) They may produce imbalanced Gaussian retention across near and distant regions. 2) Moreover, independent Gaussian scores cannot capture the joint rendering effects of simultaneous deletions. SplatQ addresses these limitations through blockwise retention ratio allocation and interaction-aware quadratic selection, respectively. SplatQ decomposes this global selection problem into five stages. Partitioning in Section~ sec:partition first converts Gaussians into several size-limited blocks . Opacity response modeling in Section~ sec:response then produces a response matrix for each block. Budget allocation in Section~ sec:allocation uses part of the matrix to assign a retention quota to every block, with . Given and , quadratic selection in Section~ sec:selection determines which block members to retain. Finally, we fine-tune the retained attributes without changing the count of Gaussians in Section~ sec:refinement . Similarity Guided Partition sec:partition Independent importance scores do not capture how the image changes when several Gaussians are deleted together. To better describe these changes, we approximate their joint rendering effects using a quadratic objective over binary retention variables. Each variable equals 1 if the corresponding Gaussian is retained and 0 if it is deleted, as detailed in Section~ sec:selection . Formulating this optimization probl

title: Efficient Confidence-Aware Densification for 3DGS
summary: 3DGS-MCMC has replaced the gradient-driven density control of 3D Gaussian Splatting with opacity-based sampling and relocation, and is now the de facto standard for prior-free densification under a fixed primitive budget. Because opacity stays high where the scene is already well reconstructed, this sampling sends most new primitives to the foreground and leaves the background under-reconstructed. At low budgets, prior-based methods such as ConeGS and EDGS outperform it, at the cost of a pre-trained radiance field or dense image matches and a separate initialization stage. We argue for a comeback of error-driven densification within the fixed-budget MCMC framework. Our confidence-aware densification keeps the fixed budget and gradual growth of 3DGS-MCMC, but places primitives by the image error instead of the opacity. New primitives are drawn mostly where screen-space gradients are large. We favor primitives with a low learned confidence, which marks regions the reconstruction still explains poorly, and relocate the primitives that contribute least to the rendered images to these places. Averaged over 24 scenes, our method outperforms 3DGS-MCMC in PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS at every budget from 100k to 2M primitives. At 100k, without a prior or an initialization stage, it recovers 0.84dB of the 1.05dB PSNR by which ConeGS leads 3DGS-MCMC, and from 500k on, it has the highest PSNR and SSIM of all fixed-budget methods we compare with, including ConeGS and EDGS. While inherently prior-free, our densification can also exploit priors: from the ConeGS or EDGS initialization, it matches ConeGS in PSNR and SSIM at 100k and is best in all three metrics at 500k.

We train all our runs for 30k iterations. If the initial SfM point cloud exceeds the budget, we subsample it by farthest point sampling. We regularize scale and opacity with for all scenes, and keep the regularizer active until densification ends at iteration 25k. We use the confidence loss of Equation~ throughout training, with and the learning rate of CoMe~ radl2026come , and we clamp the confidence map to . Datasets and Comparison Methods. Following Power Foam~ govindarajan2026powerfoam , we add 11 scenes from DL3DV~ ling2023dl3dv , for 24 real-world scenes in total. We downsample the Mip-NeRF 360 outdoor scenes by 4 and the indoor scenes and DL3DV by 2, use Tanks Temples and Deep Blending at the provided resolution, and hold out every eighth image for testing. The main baselines for our fixed-budget method areConeGS~ baranowski2026conegs , EDGS~ Kotovenko2026edgs , Taming 3DGS~ mallick2024taming and 3DGS-MCMC~ kheradmand2024mcmc , which also never exceed the budget during optimization. We also compare against variable-budget methods, which determine the final primitive count dynamically during optimization: 3DGS~ kerbl20233dgs , DashGaussian~ chen2025dashgaussian and the simplification methods Mini-Splatting2~ Fang2024minisplatting2 and GaussianSpa~ zhang2025gaussianspa .
