title: Gaussian Splatting with Reflections Guided by What is Seen
summary: While novel view synthesis methods like Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have shown impressive performance on common scenes, they often struggle with capturing view-dependent specular effects, particularly near-field reflections. Existing methods utilize environment maps, which only represent lights from infinity, or environment Gaussians, which rely solely on indirect supervision from reflections, are insufficient for accurately modeling such effects. Here, we propose a framework based on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) that leverages directly observable environment information in input images. Our approach also integrates a hybrid reflection appearance representation and view-dependent specular modeling. Experiments on public benchmarks and a newly curated near-field reflection dataset demonstrate that our method achieves superior rendering quality and geometric accuracy.
full_text: While novel view synthesis methods like Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have shown impressive performance on common scenes, they often struggle with capturing view-dependent specular effects, particularly near-field reflections. Existing methods utilize environment maps, which only represent lights from infinity, or environment Gaussians, which rely solely on indirect supervision from reflections, are insufficient for accurately modeling such effects. Here, we propose a framework based on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) that leverages directly observable environment information in input images. Our approach also integrates a hybrid reflection appearance representation and view-dependent specular modeling. Experiments on public benchmarks and a newly curated near-field reflection dataset demonstrate that our method achieves superior rendering quality and geometric accuracy. Novel view synthesis, Gaussian splatting, Near-field reflection. Introduction sec:intro Novel view synthesis (NVS) aims to generate photorealistic images of a scene from unseen viewpoints using a set of captured images. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ nerf have significantly advanced the field by leveraging a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) as an implicit representation of the radiance field. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs has shifted the paradigm back toward explicit representations. 3DGS adopts anisotropic 3D Gaussians as primitives and enables real-time rendering via efficient rasterization without sacrificing quality. Despite its rapid progress, modeling view-dependent effects, particularly high-frequency specular reflections, remains an open challenge for 3DGS-based NVS. The original 3DGS framework does not explicitly model specular reflections. Instead, it utilizes Spherical Harmonics (SH) to model view-dependent appearance, which can only simulate reflections to a limited degree. This representation treats reflections as an anisotropic property of each surface point rather than modeling the physics of light transport. Consequently, reflections lack real supervision via reflected light rays, and observations from different input views cannot be properly correlated. This often results in blurred reflections or geometry distortions that arise to compensate for appearance modeling, particularly for near-field reflections. Recent works~ gaussianshader, 3dgsdr, refgs address this by introducing environment maps, but these assume light originates from infinity and thus fail to capture the spatially varying reflections from near-field objects in real-world scenes. While EnvGS~ envgs attempts to bridge this gap by replacing the environment map with environment Gaussians, it is optimized purely through indirect reflection supervision, leading to inaccurate environment geometry and degraded reflection quality. In this work, we propose a framework based on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) 2dgs to achieve high-quality NVS in scenes with near-field reflections. Our key insight is that the sources of the near-field environment light reflected by surfaces are often directly observable from other viewpoints in the input images. Leveraging this observation, we represent the scene using two sets of Gaussians: primary Gaussians for the base scene (objects directly observable from input images) and secondary Gaussians for nearby objects appearing as reflections. Rendering consists of a diffuse pass and a reflection pass. In the diffuse pass, the diffuse component is rendered from the primary Gaussians via rasterization. In the reflection pass, secondary rays are traced from the surfaces of the base scene, and intersected with the union of the primary and secondary Gaussians. Since the geometry of the primary Gaussians is directly constrained by the input images, using them in the reflection pass ensures that the environment light originates from accurate 3D positions. To enhance rendering quality, we adopt a hybrid representation that leverages both triplane-based color fields and SH in the reflection pass. We also assign a separate SH to each primary Gaussian in the reflection pass to avoid conflicts with the diffuse appearance modeling. Additionally, we incorporate a data-driven, view-dependent specular weight model using another set of SH to capture the complex lighting variations in real-world scenes. We evaluate our method on multiple widely used benchmarks and a new custom real-world dataset, NearRef, which consists of four indoor scenes with prominent near-field reflections. Quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate that our approach produces sharper reflections, more accurate geometry, and better disentanglement than prior methods, while reconstructing more faithful environment lighting. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: [itemsep=1pt] We propose a 2DGS-based framework for NVS with near-field reflections that leverages direct observation for environment light modeling. We introduce a hybrid appearance model for the reflection pass and a view-dependent specular model to enhance the quality. We achieve state-of-the-art results on both public benchmarks and the new NearRef dataset featuring near-field reflections. The code and dataset will be released publicly. Related Work sec:related Novel View Synthesis Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ nerf implicitly encode a scene into an MLP, which is optimized via differentiable volume rendering. title: SimVTA: Simulation-Grounded Video-Trajectory Alignment for Driving World Action Models
summary: Driving world action models (WAMs) learn from paired trajectories and future observations. Post-training with reinforcement learning allows the policy to explore alternative trajectories and improve planning using driving rewards. However, driving logs contain future videos only for the recorded trajectories, leaving these alternatives without corresponding visual supervision. Thus, we introduce SimVTA, a simulation-grounded post-training framework that combines trajectory optimization with video supervision. First, we sample candidate trajectories for each observation and use a real-world simulator (e.g., World Engine) to render future videos for high-reward candidates in real-world scenes reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). This provides trajectory-matched supervision independent of the model's own predictions. Under a limited rendering budget, we prioritize video supervision for higher-error futures among these rendered candidates. Finally, we optimize trajectory planning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and use a flow-matching loss on the matched videos to update shared representations. At inference time, the model predicts trajectories directly, without simulator calls. On NAVSIM v1, applying SimVTA to a WAM initialization improves PDMS from 86.2 to 91.3 (+5.1). It achieves 88.2 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and an average HD-Score of 38.8 in closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM. Ablations show that updating shared representations with video supervision improves planning, while prioritizing higher-error futures among high-reward trajectories further improves performance.

The results and demo are available at . Introduction Driving WAMs combine future-scene prediction with trajectory planning for the ego vehicle. Predicting future frames provides dense visual supervision that complements sparse trajectory targets and helps models learn representations for planning li2025drivevla . Recent driving models retain video prediction during training but predict trajectories directly at inference time, avoiding the computational cost of future-video generation zhao2026simwam . Reinforcement learning can refine a planner trained on demonstrations to explore alternative trajectories and learn from driving rewards zhou2025autovla . However, driving logs contain future videos only for recorded trajectories. For example, when a candidate turns while the recorded trajectory continues straight, the logged video does not show the visual consequences. Reusing such videos creates incorrect trajectory-video pairs, while omitting video training leaves these candidates without visual supervision. This creates a supervision gap during post-training: current-policy trajectories lack matched future-video targets (Figure~ fig:motivation ). To address this gap, we introduce , a simulation-grounded framework for video-trajectory alignment. A WAM's own video predictions provide no external reference for checking whether they follow a candidate trajectory. We use the 3DGS-based simulator in World Engine li2026worldengine to render reconstructed real-world scenes from camera poses along executed candidate paths (Figure~ fig:motivation ). These renderings provide prediction-independent targets that match the scene geometry and motion of each selected trajectory, establishing video-trajectory alignment. We jointly train video prediction with flow matching and trajectory planning with GRPO, allowing the video loss to update shared representations. The former teaches the model to predict the visual consequences of candidate trajectories; the latter compares driving rewards among candidates and favors higher-reward trajectories. Rendering videos for every sampled trajectory is costly. We first select high-reward candidates for rendering, then prioritize video supervision for higher-error futures among the rendered candidates. This separates trajectory exploration from video-supervision target selection. Our ablations examine shared representation updates, target selection, trajectory-video correspondence, and online versus offline rendering. At inference, the planner predicts trajectories directly, without simulator calls or future-video generation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=*,topsep=2pt,itemsep=1pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt] We introduce , a post-training framework that combines trajectory GRPO with simulator-based video supervision. It connects policy sampling, trajectory execution, rendering, and joint updates to learn the visual consequences of actions beyond those recorded in driving logs. We introduce a video-target selection strategy based on trajectory reward and video prediction error. It prioritizes higher-error futures of high-reward trajectories for video supervision without restricting trajectory exploration. Applying to a WAM initialization improves NAVSIM v1 PDMS by 5.1 points, from 86.2 to 91.3, and achieves 88.2 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and an average HD-Score of 38.8 on HUGSIM. Video-based approaches jointly model future frames and trajectories~ zhang2025epona,liu2026driveva, shi2026drivewam,liu2026universe . Video prediction can also be retained during training and omitted at inference, as explored in robotics by Fast-WAM yuan2026fastwam and in driving by SimWAM zhao2026simwam . focuses on trajectory-matched video supervision during driving WAM post-training. title: Make It Flow: Animating Water in 3D Gaussian Splatting Scenes
summary: Explicit 3D scene representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have recently enabled high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis. However, these methods assume static scenes, limiting realism in the presence of dynamic phenomena ubiquitous in real-world environments. While coherent motion (e.g., humans or vehicles) can be captured and reconstructed, high-frequency effects such as flowing water remain intractable under casual capture conditions, where dense multi-view, high-speed acquisition is not feasible. We present a method to animate water in static 3DGS scenes, enabling visually plausible motion without requiring dynamic capture or physical simulation. Our approach estimates 2D optical flow from reference images or model renderings and lifts it into a consistent 3D Eulerian motion field. We propose a cinemagraph-inspired algorithm that applies this motion field to deform Gaussian primitives, producing temporally seamless looping animations. The resulting representation retains real-time rendering performance, significantly enhances perceptual realism, and preserves free-viewpoint navigation within the scene. We evaluate our method on a newly captured dataset of in-the-wild waterfall scenes and demonstrate clear improvements over prior work in dynamic Gaussian splatting and 3D cinemagraph generation in visual quality and computational efficiency.
full_text: We generate seamlessly looping water animations in static 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes via a cinemagraph-inspired approach that lifts optical flow into a coherent 3D Eulerian motion field. This field is iteratively applied to Gaussians via an unscented transform, producing temporally coherent fluid motion and enabling real-time rendering and immersive free-viewpoint exploration of dynamically animated scenes with minimal overhead as evident in our video. fig:teaser Explicit 3D scene representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have recently enabled high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis. Recent progress in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3Dgaussians combines the visual fidelity of neural radiance field approaches~ mildenhall2020nerf with the efficiency of point-based rendering, enabling high-quality real-time rendering even on resource-constrained platforms. Despite these advances, reconstructed scenes remain predominantly static and often fail to capture dynamic phenomena that are essential for visual realism. This limitation is particularly evident in fluid regions, where 3D Gaussian primitives frequently produce temporally inconsistent or structurally unstable reconstructions. As a result, phenomena such as flowing water often appear unnaturally frozen. In this work, we show that introducing plausible motion specifically in these regions can substantially enhance the perceived realism and liveliness of reconstructed scenes. Recent dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods have made substantial progress toward extending static reconstruction frameworks to dynamic scenes, but primarily focus on explicitly moving foreground objects~ luiten2023dynamic, wu20244dgs, yang20244dgaussians . In contrast, subtle continuous background phenomena such as rivers or waterfalls remain largely underexplored. Moreover, many dynamic reconstruction approaches rely on multi-view synchronized capture setups, limiting their applicability to casually captured or in-the-wild data. An alternative direction augments static 3DGS reconstructions with synthesized dynamics. While physics-based methods~ xie2024physgaussian can produce convincing simulations across materials including fluids, they incur substantial computational cost and are difficult to apply in real-time or casual capture settings. Instead of targeting physically accurate simulation, which is often unnecessary for visual realism, we aim to generate visually plausible motion that improves scene perception while remaining efficient. To this end, we draw inspiration from cinemagraphs, which introduce temporally looping motion into otherwise static imagery and are particularly effective for fluid phenomena in 2D~ holynski2021animating . Prior work extending cinemagraphs to 3D either combines layered depth representations with neural networks~ li2023_3dcinemagraphy , resulting in slow rendering and limited free-viewpoint capability, or relies on self-similarity in Gaussian point clouds~ li2024loopgaussian , which provides insufficient structure to recover realistic fluid motion. These limitations motivate a more efficient approach for visually plausible water animation in static 3DGS scenes. Given a 3DGS model and its training views (or alternatively model renderings), we estimate per-view fluid flow with an existing pretrained network~ mahapatra2021controllable . Our first contribution is lifting these multi-view estimates into a grid-based 3D Eulerian motion field via depth-based reprojection, refined via static/dynamic voxel hit ratios and view-hit thresholding. Second, we adopt the concept of symmetric warping from 2D cinemagraphs~ holynski2021animating , which is defined for pixels, and reformulate it for 3D Gaussians treated as Lagrangian particles: volume-aware covariance propagation, density-preserving opacity blending, and randomized per-Gaussian temporal offsets replace the feature warping and inpainting used in 2D. The resulting method integrates directly into the 3DGS rendering pipeline, enabling real-time animation of static scenes with low overhead and allowing interactive exploration of dynamically enhanced environments (cf.\ ). For evaluation, we introduce a new dataset of seven casually captured 3DGS scenes containing fluid phenomena such as waterfalls. We compare against dynamic Gaussian Splatting~ yang20244dgaussians and recent 3D cinemagraph methods~ li2023_3dcinemagraphy, li2024loopgaussian qualitatively and in terms of efficiency. As evident in our video, our method produces more realistic and temporally coherent novel view renderings while remaining computationally efficient. In summary, we make the following contributions: The first method to animate fluid regions in a static 3DGS scene, without dynamic capture, retraining, or simulation. An efficient, 3DGS-based approach for lifting multi-view optical flow into a 3D Eulerian motion field. A deformation framework for temporally looping, visually plausible fluid animation, integrated into a real-time 3DGS rendering system for interactive exploration of animated scenes. A curated dataset of seven casual scenes with fluid motion. We will release our full implementation, including preprocessing scripts, interactive GUI, and dataset. Related Work sec:related_work Our work extends novel view synthesis by integrating cinemagraph-inspired motion into static 3D scene representations, with a focus on efficient and perceptually plausible fluid animation. Novel View Synthesis Early image-based rendering and light field methods~ debevec1996mar, gortler1996lumigraph, levoy1996lightfields are limited by sparse viewpoint coverage. Neural radiance fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2020nerf significantly advanced novel view synthesis, but are expensive to train and render, which motivated more efficient scene parameterizations~ yu2021plenoxels, sun2022dvgo, mueller2022instant, Chen2022tensorf . 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3Dgaussians models scenes as anisotropic Gaussians optimized for real-time rasterization and forms the basis of our approach. Extensions of both NeRF and 3DGS to dynamic scenes introduce temporal variation either through explicit time-conditioned representations or learned deformation fields~ pumarola2021dnerf, park2021nerfies, cao2023hexplane, fridovichkeil2023kplanes, fang2022tineuvox, lin2023gaussianflow, yang20244dgaussians, wu20244dgs . These methods achieve compelling results for structured and well-observed motion such as humans or rigid objects, but typically assume controlled multi-view capture setups or availability of strong data-driven priors. Such assumptions restrict their applicability to casually captured or in-the-wild scenes. Moreover, they are less suitable for subtle, continuous background phenomena such as water, where motion is locally smooth, temporally repetitive, and driven more by perceptual consistency than strict geometric reconstruction. Cinemagraphs and Motion Synthesis Cinemagraphs and the closely related video textures~ schodl2000vidtex introduce looping motion into static imagery while preserving spatial consistency. Early work focused on manual or semi-automatic creation, followed by numerous methods for automatic loop synthesis and fluid animation in videos~ liao2013automatedvideolooping, liao2015fastseamlessloops, tompkin2011towardsmomentimagery . These techniques have demonstrated that fluid regions such as waterfalls are particularly well-suited for perceptually convincing motion synthesis. Recent learning-based approaches extend cinemagraph generation to single-image or sparse-input settings using generative models or optical flow prediction~ hao2018vidgen, gao2018im2flow, endo2019animatinglandscape . More recently, diffusion-based image-to-video models have enabled controllable cinemagraph synthesis with localized motion editing and user-guided spatial constraints~ le2026cinemagraphvideodiffusion . While visually compelling, these approaches remain computationally expensive and typically require repeated inference for long-duration or seamlessly looping animations, limiting interactivity and real-time applicability. To address this, recent works learn static or quasi-static motion fields that enable efficient looping animations~ holynski2021animating, mahapatra2021controllable, halperin2021loops . These approaches are effective for synthesizing fluid motion and form the foundation of our motion generation framework. Recent work has further explored lifting cinemagraph synthesis into 3D scene representations. Approaches based on layered depth images or multi-view video synthesis project 2D motion into 3D representations, but remain limited in viewpoint flexibility or reconstruction quality~ li2023_3dcinemagraphy, ma2023videoloop . More recent methods leverage neural or Gaussian-based scene representations to synthesize motion directly in 3D~ li2024loopgaussian, jia2025physic . However, these methods often rely on appearance-based similarity, specialized motion priors, or computationally expensive learned pipelines, which work well for their specific application but limit their ability to model coherent directional fluid motion in unconstrained scenes. Related approaches also augment static Gaussian scenes with specialized scene dynamics such as snowfall using physics-guided diffusion models~ fiebelman2026letsnow , or fluids using physics-based simulation with artificially added fluid particles rather than animating reconstructed water~ feng2025splashing .
